children.title: 1. Entire Spectrum of Ethics
children.description: The Chapter Containing the Section on Ethics (Sīlakkhandhavagga) is a chapter of 13 discourses. Each of these contains a long passage on the Gradual Training in ethics, meditation, and wisdom. The chapter is named after the first of these sections. The two other known versions of the Dīrghāgama (in Chinese and Sanskrit) also contain a similar chapter. Despite the monastic nature of the central teaching, most of these discourses are presented in dialog with lay people, with a strong emphasis on the relation between the Buddha’s teachings and other contemporary movements.

children.title: The Divine Net
children.description: While others may praise or criticize the Buddha, they tend to focus on trivial details. The Buddha presents an analysis of 62 kinds of wrong view, seeing through which one becomes detached from meaningless speculations.

children.title: The Fruits of the Ascetic Life
children.description: The newly crowned King Ajātasattu is disturbed by the violent means by which he achieved the crown. He visits the Buddha to find peace of mind, and asks him about the benefits of spiritual practice. This is one of the greatest literary and spiritual texts of early Buddhism.

children.title: With Ambaṭṭha
children.description: A young brahmin student attacks the Buddha’s family, but is put in his place.

children.title: With Soṇadaṇḍa
children.description: A reputed brahmin visits the Buddha, despite the reservations of other brahmins. They discuss the true meaning of a brahmin, and the Buddha skillfully draws him around to his own point of view.

children.title: With Kūṭadanta
children.description: A brahmin wishes to undertake a great sacrifice, and asks for the Buddha’s advice. The Buddha tells a legend of the past, in which a king is persuaded to give up violent sacrifice, and instead to devote his resources to supporting the needy citizens of his realm. However, even such a beneficial and non-violent sacrifice pales in comparison to the spiritual sacrifice of giving up attachments.

children.title: With Mahāli
children.description: The Buddha explains to a diverse group of lay people how the results of meditation depend on the manner of development.

children.title: With Jāliya
children.description: This discourse is mostly quoted by the Buddha in the previous.

children.title: The Longer Discourse on the Lion’s Roar
children.description: The Buddha is challenged by a naked ascetic on the topic of spiritual austerities. He points out that it is quite possible to perform all kinds of austere practices without having any inner purity of mind.

children.title: With Poṭṭhapāda
children.description: The Buddha discusses with a wanderer the nature of perception and how it evolves through deeper states of meditation. None of these, however, should be identified with a self or soul.

children.title: With Subha
children.description: Shortly after the Buddha’s death, Venerable Ānanda is invited to explain the core teachings.

children.title: With Kevaddha
children.description: The Buddha refuses to perform miracles, explaining that this is not the right way to inspire faith. He goes on to tell the story of a monk whose misguided quest for answers led him as far as Brahmā.

children.title: With Lohicca
children.description: A brahmin has fallen into the idea that there is no point in trying to offer spiritual help to others. The Buddha goes to see him, and persuades him of the genuine benefits of spiritual teaching.

children.title: The Three Knowledges
children.description: A number of brahmins are discussing the true path to Brahmā. Contesting the claims to authority based on the Vedas, the Buddha insists that only personal experience can lead to the truth.

children.title: 2. The Great Chapter
children.description: This chapter contains a diverse range of discourses. Several focus on the events surrounding the Buddha’s death, while others range into fabulous scenarios set among the gods, and still others are grounded in detailed discussions of doctrine.

children.title: The Great Discourse on Traces Left Behind
children.description: The Buddha teaches about the six Buddhas of the past, and tells a lengthy account of one of those, Vipassī.

children.title: The Great Discourse on Causation
children.description: Rejecting Venerable Ānanda’s claim to easily understand dependent origination, the Buddha presents a complex and demanding analysis, revealing hidden nuances and implications of this central teaching.

children.title: The Great Discourse on the Buddha’s Extinguishment
children.description: The longest of all discourses, this extended narrative tells of the events surrounding the Buddha’s death. Full of vivid and moving details, it is an ideal entry point into knowing the Buddha as a person, and understanding how the Buddhist community coped with his passing.

children.title: King Mahāsudassana
children.description: An elaborate story of a past life of the Buddha as a legendary king who renounced all to practice meditation.

children.title: With Janavasabha
children.description: Beginning with an account of the fates of disciples who had recently passed away, the scene shifts to a discussion of Dhamma held by the gods.

children.title: The Great Steward
children.description: A minor deity informs the Buddha of the conversations and business of the gods.

children.title: The Great Congregation
children.description: When deities from all realms gather in homage to the Buddha, he gives a series of verses describing them. These verses, which are commonly chanted in Theravadin countries, give one of the most detailed descriptions of the deities worshiped at the the time of the Buddha.

children.title: Sakka’s Questions
children.description: After hearing a love song from a god of music, the Buddha engages in a deep discussion with Sakka on the conditioned origin of attachment and suffering.

children.title: The Longer Discourse on Mindfulness Meditation
children.description: The Buddha details the seventh factor of the noble eightfold path, mindfulness meditation. This discourse is essentially identical to MN 10, with the addition of an extended section on the four noble truths derived from MN 141.

children.title: With Pāyāsi
children.description: This is a long and entertaining debate between a monk and a skeptic, who went to elaborate and bizarre lengths to prove that there is no such thing as an afterlife. The discourse contains a colorful series of parables and examples.

children.title: 3. Pāṭikaputta
children.description: Like the previous chapter, this contains a diverse range of discourses. It is named after the first discourse in the chapter. Among the discourses here are legendary accounts of the history and future of our world, which are extremely famous and influential in Buddhist circles.

children.title: About Pāṭikaputta
children.description: When Sunakkhatta threatens to disrobe, the Buddha is unimpressed. Rejecting showy displays of asceticism or wondrous powers, he demonstrates his pre-eminence.

children.title: The Lion’s Roar at Udumbarikā’s Monastery
children.description: This discourse gives a specially good example of dialog between religions. The Buddha insists that he is not interested to make anyone give up their teacher or practices, but only to help people let go of suffering.

children.title: The Wheel-Turning Monarch
children.description: In illustration of his dictum that one should rely on oneself, the Buddha gives a detailed account of the fall of a kingly lineage of the past, and the subsequent degeneration of society. This process, however, is not over, as the Buddha predicts that eventually society will fall into utter chaos. But far in the future, another Buddha, Metteyya, will arise in a time of peace and plenty.

children.title: The Origin of the World
children.description: In contrast with the brahmin’s self-serving mythologies of the past, the Buddha presents an account of evolution that shows how human choices are an integral part of the ecological balance, and how excessive greed destroys the order of nature.

children.title: Inspiring Confidence
children.description: Shortly before he passes away, Venerable Sāriputta visits the Buddha and utters a moving eulogy of his great teacher.

children.title: An Impressive Discourse
children.description: Following the death of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, the leader of the Jains, the Buddha emphasizes the stability and maturity of his own community. He encourages the community to come together after his death and recite the teachings in harmony.

children.title: The Marks of a Great Man
children.description: This presents the brahmanical prophecy of the Great Man, and explains the 32 marks in detail. This discourse contains some of the latest and most complex verse forms in the canon.

children.title: Advice to Sigālaka
children.description: The Buddha encounters a young man who honors his dead father by performing rituals. The Buddha recasts the meaningless rites in terms of virtuous conduct. This is the most detailed discourse on ethics for lay people.

children.title: The Āṭānāṭiya Protection
children.description: Mighty spirits hold a congregation, and warn the Buddha that, since not all spirits are friendly, the mendicants should learn verses of protection.

children.title: Reciting in Concert
children.description: The Buddha encourages Venerable Sāriputta to teach the mendicants, and he offers an extended listing of Buddhist doctrines arranged in numerical sequence.

children.title: Up to Ten
children.description: This is similar to the previous, but with a different manner of exposition. These two discourses anticipate some of the methods of the Abhidhamma.

children.title: The Thoroughbred (1st)
children.description: A steed is worthy of the king for six reasons, and a mendicant is worthy for six similar reasons.

children.title: The Thoroughbred (2nd)
children.description: A steed is worthy of the king for six reasons, and a mendicant is worthy for six similar reasons.

children.title: The Thoroughbred (3rd)
children.description: A steed is worthy of the king for six reasons, and a mendicant is worthy for six similar reasons.

children.title: Unsurpassable
children.description: Six things that are unsurpassable.

children.title: Topics for Recollection
children.description: Six topics for recollection.

children.title: With Mahānāma
children.description: The Buddha teaches his relative Mahānāma that a noble disciple often practices the six recollections, which lead to joy and peace.

children.title: Warm-hearted (1st)
children.description: Six warm-hearted qualities practiced among the mendicants.

children.title: Warm-hearted (2nd)
children.description: Six warm-hearted qualities practiced among the mendicants.

children.title: Elements of Escape
children.description: The Buddha’s teachings are effective, so we can’t claim to have practiced them fully if we’re still afflicted by the various forms of suffering.

children.title: A Good Death
children.description: A mendicant who lives well and doesn’t waste time will have a good death.

children.title: Regret
children.description: A mendicant who lives well and doesn’t waste time dies without regret.

children.title: Nakula’s Father
children.description: A sick householder is consoled by his wife, who says there is no need for him to be worried about dying, as she is well able to support the family and practice the Dhamma. He recovers, and visits the Buddha, who sings the praises of his kind and wise wife.

children.title: Sleep
children.description: Neither a king nor a mendicant gets anything accomplished if they just sleep all the time.

children.title: A Fish Dealer
children.description: Those whose livelihood is the killing of animals do not prosper.

children.title: Mindfulness of Death (1st)
children.description: Many of those who practice mindfulness of death don’t do so urgently enough. Death might come to us at any moment.

children.title: Mindfulness of Death (2nd)
children.description: A method for recollecting one’s own death that leads to urgency, diligence, and joy.

children.title: At Sāma Village
children.description: Even the gods know that some monks are falling away from their practice.

children.title: Non-decline
children.description: In the past, future, and present, practicing six good qualities protects against decline.

children.title: Dangers
children.description: Sensual pleasures are perilous.

children.title: The Himalaya
children.description: A mendicant who has fully mastered meditation could even split apart the Himalayas.

children.title: Topics for Recollection
children.description: The six recollections are a way to escape from greed.

children.title: With Mahākaccāna
children.description: Mahākaccāna teaches that the six recollections are a way to escape from greed and lead to a mind as vast as space.

children.title: Proper Occasions (1st)
children.description: The right time to visit an esteemed mendicant is when you need spiritual guidance and support.

children.title: Proper Occasions (2nd)
children.description: Some senior mendicants discuss the right time to see an esteemed mendicant, and Mahākaccāna answers by quoting the Buddha from AN 6.27.

children.title: With Udāyī
children.description: When the Buddha asks about the topics for recollection, a monk reveals his ignorance. Ānanda then gives an unusual list of five recollections, which the Buddha supplements with a sixth.

children.title: Unsurpassable
children.description: There are things in the world considered to be unsurpassed, but none of them compare with the Dhamma.

children.title: A Trainee
children.description: Things leading to decline or non-decline.

children.title: Non-decline (1st)
children.description: A god speaks on things leading to decline or non-decline.

children.title: Non-decline (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha recounts the events of the previous discourse.

children.title: With Mahāmoggallāna
children.description: Mahāmoggallāna visits a Brahmā god who had formerly been a mendicant, and they discuss which of the gods are stream-enterers.

children.title: Things That Play a Part in Realization
children.description: Six kinds of perception that lead to wisdom.

children.title: Roots of Dispute
children.description: If a mendicant nurses six kinds of defilements it leads to bitterness and disputes in the Saṅgha.

children.title: A Gift With Six Factors
children.description: Seeing the laywoman Veḷukaṇṭakī preparing a meal for the Saṅgha, the Buddha celebrated by saying that giving is of great benefit when the donor and the recipient each possess three qualities.

children.title: One’s Own Volition
children.description: The Buddha rebuts a brahmin’s claim that there is no such thing as actions initiated by oneself.

children.title: Sources
children.description: Greed, hate, and delusion are the roots of deeds.

children.title: With Kimbila
children.description: The Buddha explains to Venerable Kimbila the reasons why Buddhism lasts long after the Buddha’s demise.

children.title: A Tree Trunk
children.description: Even a simple block of wood can be perceived in different ways by a mendicant with advanced meditation.

children.title: With Nāgita
children.description: When visited by a noisy crowd, the Buddha speaks to his attendant Nāgita of his love of seclusion and solitude, and of his regard for forest mendicants.

children.title: The Giant
children.description: When going for a bath, the Buddha encounters a giant royal elephant. But a spiritual giant is even more impressive.

children.title: With Migasālā
children.description: In response to criticism, the Buddha explains that it is difficult to compare the spiritual development of different individuals, so we should not be judgmental.

children.title: Debt
children.description: Poor people suffer when they get in debt. Spiritual practitioners who are devoid of good qualities suffer in a similar way.

children.title: By Mahācunda
children.description: In a discourse evidently set some time after the Buddha’s passing, Venerable Mahācunda urges different groups of meditators, whether they emphasize serenity or insight, to respect and support each other.

children.title: Apparent in the Present Life (1st)
children.description: The Buddha explains to the wanderer Moliyasīvaka how the teaching may be realized in the present life.

children.title: Apparent in the Present Life (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha explains a brahmin how the teaching may be realized in the present life.

children.title: With Khema
children.description: Two monks separately come to the Buddha and speak of awakening in terms of letting go conceit. The Buddha affirms that they are, in fact, awakened, and that such indirect means are the proper way to make such declarations.

children.title: Sense Restraint
children.description: Just as a tree without leaves cannot grow, sense restraint is the foundation for spiritual growth.

children.title: With Ānanda
children.description: Venerables Ānanda and Sāriputta discuss how a mendicant can further their learning and understanding.

children.title: Aristocrats
children.description: The Buddha explains to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī the ambition, quest, commitment, insistence, and ultimate goal of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, women, bandits, and ascetics.

children.title: Diligence
children.description: With a series of vivid similes, the Buddha shows how diligence leads to benefits in both this life and the next.

children.title: About Dhammika
children.description: The monk Dhammika annoys both the monks and the layfolk so badly that they banish him. He comes to the Buddha, who consoles him and raises his spirits with a story, while at the same time showing him the error of his ways.

children.title: With Soṇa
children.description: When Venerable Soṇa thinks of disrobing, the Buddha comes and encourages him with the famous simile of the lute that is tuned neither too loose nor too tight.

children.title: With Phagguna
children.description: The Buddha consoles Venerable Phagguṇa on his deathbed, and he dies at peace. The Buddha then explains to Ānanda the benefits of hearing the Dhamma at the right time.

children.title: The Six Classes of Rebirth
children.description: Ānanda asks the Buddha about the six classes of people described by the rival ascetic Pūraṇa Kassapa. The Buddha rejects them, and proposes an alternate scheme, emphasizing the importance ones deeds in this life.

children.title: Defilements
children.description: The Buddha explains diverse methods for overcoming diverse kinds of defilements.

children.title: With Dārukammika
children.description: The householder Dārukammika claims to give gifts to arahants. But the Buddha warns him that it’s hard to know who is really an arahant, and encourage him instead to make offerings to the Saṅgha.

children.title: With Hatthisāriputta
children.description: The junior monk Citta Hatthisāriputta rudely interrupts his seniors, and is admonished by Mahākoṭṭhita. His friends speak in his defense, but Mahākoṭṭhita warns them with a long explanation of how hard it is to know another’s mind. Ultimately, Citta disrobes.

children.title: In the Middle
children.description: Several senior mendicants discuss the “Questions of Metteyya” from the Pārāyana (Snp 5.3). Each propose an interpretation, and they then ask the Buddha. He praises each reading, but gives his own intended meaning.

children.title: Knowledge of the Faculties of Persons
children.description: A monk asks whether, when the Buddha said that Devadatta was going to hell, he was speaking metaphorically. The Buddha castigates him, wondering how anyone could misunderstand such a straightforward statement, and explains how he reads the minds of others and understands where their deeds will lead them.

children.title: Penetrative
children.description: A detailed analysis of several central themes, including sense perception, feeling, defilements, kamma, etc.

children.title: The Lion’s Roar
children.description: The Buddha possesses six spiritual powers that enable him to roar his lion’s roar.

children.title: The Fruit of Non-Return
children.description: Six things lead to non-return.

children.title: Perfection
children.description: Six things lead to perfection.

children.title: Friends
children.description: With bad friends, a mendicant cannot fulfill six good qualities, but with good friends they can.

children.title: Enjoying Company
children.description: A mendicant who loves to socialize can’t find peace in meditation, but one who loves solitude can.

children.title: A God
children.description: A god speaks on the factors of non-decline. When the Buddha repeats what he says, Sāriputta gives an explaination.

children.title: Immersion
children.description: Without samādhi or immersion it is impossible to realize the higher truths of the path.

children.title: Capable of Realizing
children.description: Six qualities that enable a mendicant to gain understanding.

children.title: Strength
children.description: Six qualities that enable a mendicant to gain strength in meditation.

children.title: First Absorption (1st)
children.description: Six qualities that enable a mendicant to gain the first absorption.

children.title: First Absorption (2nd)
children.description: Six qualities that enable a mendicant to gain the first absorption.

children.title: Suffering
children.description: Six qualities that lead to suffering, and whose absence leads to happiness.

children.title: Perfection
children.description: Qualities for realizing arahantship.

children.title: Superhuman States
children.description: Qualities for realizing superhuman states.

children.title: Joy and Happiness
children.description: Qualities leading to happiness.

children.title: Achievement
children.description: Qualities for gaining and strengthening good qualities.

children.title: Greatness
children.description: Possessing six qualities a mendicant attains to greatness.

children.title: Hell (1st)
children.description: Things leading to hell or heaven.

children.title: Hell (2nd)
children.description: Things leading to hell or heaven.

children.title: The Best Thing
children.description: Things leading to or obstructing the attainment of perfection.

children.title: Day and Night
children.description: Things leading to growth or deterioration by day or night.

children.title: Coolness
children.description: Possessing six qualities a mendicant attains to coolness.

children.title: Obstacles
children.description: Things that enable or obstruct true understanding while listening to the teachings.

children.title: A Murderer
children.description: Things that enable or obstruct true understanding while listening to the teachings.

children.title: Wanting to Listen
children.description: Things that enable or obstruct true understanding while listening to the teachings.

children.title: Not Giving Up
children.description: Requirements for becoming a stream-enterer.

children.title: Given Up
children.description: Things given up by a stream-enterer.

children.title: Can’t Give Rise
children.description: Things impossible for a stream-enterer.

children.title: Things That Can’t Be Done (1st)
children.description: Things impossible for a stream-enterer.

children.title: Things That Can’t Be Done (2nd)
children.description: Things impossible for a stream-enterer.

children.title: Things That Can’t Be Done (3rd)
children.description: Things impossible for a stream-enterer.

children.title: Things That Can’t Be Done (4th)
children.description: Things impossible for a stream-enterer.

children.title: Appearance
children.description: Things rare to find in the world.

children.title: Benefit
children.description: Benefits of stream-entry.

children.title: Impermanence
children.description: A mendicant on the path cannot see any condition as permanent.

children.title: Suffering
children.description: A mendicant on the path cannot see any condition as pleasurable.

children.title: Not-Self
children.description: A mendicant on the path cannot see any thing as not-self.

children.title: Extinguished
children.description: A mendicant on the path cannot see extinguishment as suffering.

children.title: Transience
children.description: Reasons for meditating on impermanence.

children.title: With a Drawn Sword
children.description: Reasons for meditating on suffering.

children.title: Not Determined by Anything
children.description: Reasons for meditating on not-self.

children.title: States of Existence
children.description: Giving up rebirth in the three realms of existence, and developing the three trainings.

children.title: Craving
children.description: Giving up conceit and craving.

children.title: Greed
children.description: Antidotes for greed, hate, and delusion.

children.title: Bad Conduct
children.description: Antidotes for bad conduct.

children.title: Thoughts
children.description: Antidotes for bad thoughts.

children.title: Perceptions
children.description: Antidotes for harmful perceptions.

children.title: Elements
children.description: Antidotes for harmful properties.

children.title: Gratification
children.description: Antidotes for views of gratification, self, and wrong views.

children.title: Discontent
children.description: Antidotes for discontent, cruelty, and misconduct.

children.title: Contentment
children.description: Antidotes for discontent, unawareness, and desire.

children.title: Hard to Admonish
children.description: Antidotes for being hard to correct, bad friendship, and distraction.

children.title: Restlessness
children.description: Antidotes for restlessness, lack of restraint, and heedlessness.

children.title: Observing the Body
children.description: Things that enable or obstruct meditation on the body.

children.title: Observing Principles, Etc.
children.description: Things that enable or obstruct meditation on various things.

children.title: About Tapussa
children.description: Possessing six qualities, the householder Tapussa sees the Dhamma.

children.title: About Bhallika, Etc.
children.description: Possessing six qualities, various householders see the Dhamma.

children.title: Pleasing (1st)
children.description: Seven qualities that make a mendicant either agreeable or disagreeable to their fellow monastics.

children.title: Pleasing (2nd)
children.description: Seven qualities that make a mendicant either agreeable or disagreeable to their fellow monastics.

children.title: Powers in Brief
children.description: The powers of faith, energy, conscience, prudence, mindfulness, samādhi, and wisdom.

children.title: Powers in Detail
children.description: The powers of faith, energy, conscience, prudence, mindfulness, samādhi, and wisdom.

children.title: Wealth in Brief
children.description: The wealth of faith, energy, conscience, prudence, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

children.title: Wealth in Detail
children.description: The wealth of faith, energy, conscience, prudence, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

children.title: With Ugga
children.description: Migāra of Rohaṇa is a wealthy man, but even his riches are vulnerable to the vicissitudes of life, unlike spiritual wealth.

children.title: Fetters
children.description: The fetters of compliance, repulsion, views, doubt, conceit, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

children.title: Giving Up
children.description: The purpose of the spiritual life is to give up the fetters of compliance, repulsion, views, doubt, conceit, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

children.title: Stinginess
children.description: The fetters of compliance, repulsion, views, doubt, conceit, envy, and stinginess.

children.title: Underlying Tendencies (1st)
children.description: The underlying tendencies of sensual desire, repulsion, views, doubt, conceit, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

children.title: Underlying Tendencies (2nd)
children.description: The purpose of the spiritual life is to give up the underlying tendencies of sensual desire, repulsion, views, doubt, conceit, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

children.title: A Family
children.description: Factors that make a family worth visiting.

children.title: Individuals
children.description: Seven persons who are worthy of gifts and veneration.

children.title: A Simile With Water
children.description: Seven people found in the world who are like those in water.

children.title: Observing Impermanence
children.description: Seven persons who are worthy of gifts and veneration.

children.title: Observing Suffering
children.description: Seven persons who are worthy of gifts and veneration.

children.title: Observing Not-self
children.description: Seven persons who are worthy of gifts and veneration.

children.title: Extinguishment
children.description: Seven persons who are worthy of gifts and veneration.

children.title: Qualifications for Graduation
children.description: A mendicant with seven qualities is qualified to graduate.

children.title: At Sārandada
children.description: The Buddha teaches the seven principles of non-decline to the Licchavis at the Sārandada shrine near Vesālī.

children.title: With Vassakāra
children.description: King Ajātasattu of Magadha wishes to invade the Vajjians, and sends his minister Vassakāra to tell the Buddha of his intentions. The Buddha recalls the time he taught the seven principles of non-decline to the Vajjians.

children.title: Non-Decline for Mendicants (1st)
children.description: The Buddha teaches the seven principles of non-decline to the mendicants.

children.title: Non-Decline for Mendicants (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha teaches seven principles of non-decline to the mendicants.

children.title: Non-Decline for Mendicants (3rd)
children.description: The Buddha teaches seven principles of non-decline to the mendicants.

children.title: Awakening Factors
children.description: The Buddha teaches seven principles of non-decline to the mendicants.

children.title: Perceptions
children.description: The Buddha teaches seven principles of non-decline to the mendicants.

children.title: Non-decline for a Mendicant Trainee
children.description: Seven qualities leading to the decline of a mendicant who is a trainee.

children.title: Non-decline for a Lay Follower
children.description: Seven qualities leading to the decline of a lay follower.

children.title: Failures for a Lay Follower
children.description: Seven failures for a lay follower.

children.title: Downfalls for a Lay Follower
children.description: Seven ruins for a lay follower.

children.title: Respect for Diligence
children.description: A god speaks of the the seven principles of non-decline to the Buddha, who repeats it to the mendicants.

children.title: Respect for Conscience
children.description: The Buddha tells of hearing the seven principles of non-decline from a god.

children.title: Easy to Admonish (1st)
children.description: The Buddha tells of hearing the seven principles of non-decline from a god.

children.title: Easy to Admonish (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha tells of hearing the seven principles of non-decline from a god. Sāriputta offers additional explanation.

children.title: A Friend (1st)
children.description: When a friend has seven factors, one should associate with them.

children.title: A Friend (2nd)
children.description: When a mendicant has seven factors, one should stay close to them even if they send you away.

children.title: Textual Analysis (1st)
children.description: With seven qualities, a mendicant will soon realize the four kinds of textual analysis.

children.title: Textual Analysis (2nd)
children.description: With seven qualities, Sāriputta realized the four kinds of textual analysis.

children.title: Mastery of the Mind (1st)
children.description: Seven qualities leading to mastery of meditation.

children.title: Mastery of the Mind (2nd)
children.description: With seven qualities, Sāriputta became a master of meditation.

children.title: Graduation (1st)
children.description: Sāriputta visits a sectarian hermitage and hears them saying that someone who lives the spiritual life for twelve years is fit to graduate. The Buddha rejects this, saying that a mendicant is qualified to graduate not merely by completing a certain number of years, but because of their spiritual qualities.

children.title: Graduation (2nd)
children.description: Ānanda visits a sectarian hermitage and hears them saying that someone who lives the spiritual life for twelve years is fit to graduate. The Buddha rejects this, saying that a mendicant is qualified to graduate not merely by completing a certain number of years, but because of their spiritual qualities.

children.title: Planes of Consciousness
children.description: Seven planes of consciousness in which beings may be reborn.

children.title: Prerequisites for Immersion
children.description: The path factors are the prerequisite for right immersion.

children.title: Fires (1st)
children.description: Seven fires, some physical, some psychological.

children.title: Fires (2nd)
children.description: The brahmin Uggatasarīra has arranged a great sacrifice. On Ānanda’s advice, he asks the Buddha how to make a sacrifice beneficial.

children.title: Perceptions in Brief
children.description: Meditating on seven perceptions leads to the deathless, in brief.

children.title: Perceptions in Detail
children.description: Meditating on seven perceptions leads to the deathless, in detail.

children.title: Sex
children.description: The brahmin Jāṇussoṇī asks the Buddha about behaviors that are a blemish to the celibate life.

children.title: Yoking and Unyoking
children.description: By focusing on their own gendered attributes, a man or woman becomes attached to them and develops lust for the opposite sex.

children.title: A Very Fruitful Gift
children.description: The lay followers of Campā seek a teaching from the Buddha. Together with Sāriputta, they ask the Buddha about what makes a gift fruitful.

children.title: Nanda’s Mother
children.description: Sāriputta and Moggallāna are on tour in the southern hills. A deity informs the laywoman Veḷukaṇṭakī that they are approaching. When Sāriputta expresses his amazement that she speaks with the gods, she goes on to list many other of her own amazing qualities.

children.title: The Undeclared Points
children.description: The Buddha explains why a noble disciple has no doubt when it comes to the unexplained points.

children.title: Places People Are Reborn
children.description: Seven kinds of rebirth for non-returners, as well as extinguishment by not grasping.

children.title: Tissa the Divinity
children.description: Two gods come to the Buddha on Vulture’s Peak and declare that the nuns are liberated. Moggallāna interrogates one of the deities on what he means, and the Buddha adds further explanation.

children.title: General Sīha
children.description: The Buddha explains the benefits of giving that are visible in the present life, and one that is only apparent in the next.

children.title: Nothing to Hide
children.description: Four areas where the Realized One has nothing to hide, and three ways he is irreproachable.

children.title: With Kimbila
children.description: Venerable Kimbila asks the Buddha the reasons for the long-lasting of Buddhism after the Buddha’s demise.

children.title: Seven Qualities
children.description: Qualities required for arahantship.

children.title: Nodding Off
children.description: Before his awakening, Moggallāna is struggling with sleepiness in meditation. The Buddha visits him and gives seven ways to dispel drowsiness, and other important teachings.

children.title: Don’t Fear Good Deeds
children.description: The incalculable benefits of merit that last for many aeons.

children.title: Kinds of Wives
children.description: Anāthapiṇḍika’s home was in an uproar due to the badly behaved Sujātā, newly wedded to one of his sons. The Buddha speaks to her on the different kinds of wives.

children.title: Irritable
children.description: When someone is angry, they wish ill upon their enemy, and are disappointed if they do well. This sutta includes a powerful set of verses.

children.title: Conscience and Prudence
children.description: A sense of conscience is the foundation that leads step by step to liberation.

children.title: The Seven Suns
children.description: A rare discourse on cosmic evolution. The Buddha describes the successive appearance of seven suns and how even the earth will be burned up.

children.title: The Simile of the Citadel
children.description: When a king’s fortress is well supplied with seven things and has four kinds of food supplies it is impregnable. Similarly, a noble disciple with seven qualities and the four absorptions is impregnable.

children.title: One Who Knows the Teachings
children.description: A mendicant who has seven qualities is worthy, with a special emphasis on listening to and learning the teaching.

children.title: The Shady Orchid Tree
children.description: The blossoming of the Shady Orchid Tree delights the gods of the Thirty-Three, and in the same way, the renunciation of a Buddhist ascetic is delightful.

children.title: Honor
children.description: Sāriputta reflects on what a mendicant should revere in order to develop the wholesome. He reports to the Buddha that these things are indeed found in himself.

children.title: Committed to Development
children.description: Liberation doesn’t happen because you wish for it, but because you develop the path.

children.title: The Simile of the Great Mass of Fire
children.description: It would be better for a monk to embrace a blazing fire than to lie with a maiden.

children.title: About Sunetta
children.description: There have been many great teachers in the past, who should not be reviled. But reviling a single noble disciple is even more serious.

children.title: About Araka
children.description: Araka was a famous teacher long ago, when the life span was much greater than today. Nevertheless, he still taught impermanence; how much more is it relevant today!

children.title: An Expert in the Monastic Law (1st)
children.description: An expert in monastic conduct has seven qualities.

children.title: An Expert in the Monastic Law (2nd)
children.description: An expert in monastic conduct has seven qualities.

children.title: An Expert in the Monastic Law (3rd)
children.description: An expert in monastic conduct has seven qualities.

children.title: An Expert in the Monastic Law (4th)
children.description: An expert in monastic conduct has seven qualities.

children.title: Shines as an Expert in the Monastic Law (1st)
children.description: An expert in monastic conduct shines with seven qualities.

children.title: Shines as an Expert in the Monastic Law (2nd)
children.description: An expert in monastic conduct shines with seven qualities.

children.title: Shines as an Expert in the Monastic Law (3rd)
children.description: An expert in monastic conduct shines with seven qualities.

children.title: Shines as an Expert in the Monastic Law (4th)
children.description: An expert in monastic conduct shines with seven qualities.

children.title: The Teacher’s Instructions
children.description: The Buddha teaches the Vinaya expert Upāli a short summary of the teaching.

children.title: Settlement of Disciplinary Issues
children.description: Seven principles for settling issues and disputes that have arisen in the community.

children.title: A Mendicant
children.description: A mendicant destroys seven defilements.

children.title: An Ascetic
children.description: An ascetic  destroys seven defilements.

children.title: Brahmin
children.description: A brahmin destroys seven defilements.

children.title: Scholar
children.description: A scholar destroys seven defilements.

children.title: Bathed
children.description: A bathed initiate destroys seven defilements.

children.title: A Knowledge Master
children.description: A knowledge master destroys seven defilements.

children.title: A Noble One
children.description: A noble one destroys seven defilements.

children.title: A Perfected One
children.description: A perfected one destroys seven defilements.

children.title: Bad Qualities
children.description: Seven bad qualities starting with faithlessness.

children.title: Good Qualities
children.description: Seven good qualities starting with faith.

children.title: Observing Impermanence in the Eye
children.description: Seven people worthy of offerings due to observing impermanence in the eye.

children.title: Observing Suffering in the Eye, Etc.
children.description: Seven people worthy of offerings due to observing suffering, etc., in the eye, etc.

children.title: Untitled Discourse on Greed (1st)
children.description: Develop insight into greed through the awakening factors.

children.title: Untitled Discourse on Greed (2nd)
children.description: Develop insight into greed through seven perceptions starting with impermanence.

children.title: Untitled Discourse on Greed (3rd)
children.description: Develop insight into greed through seven perceptions starting with ugliness.

children.title: Untitled Discourses on Greed
children.description: Develop complete understanding, etc., of greed.

children.title: Untitled Discourses on Hate, Etc.
children.description: Develop complete understanding, etc., of hate, etc.

children.title: The Benefits of Love
children.description: The eight benefits of practicing the meditation on love.

children.title: Wisdom
children.description: Eight conditions that lead to the arising of wisdom, its growth and perfection.

children.title: Disliked (1st)
children.description: Due to eight qualities, a mendicant is displeasing to their fellow monastics, but with the opposite qualities is pleasing.

children.title: Disliked (2nd)
children.description: Due to eight qualities, a mendicant is displeasing to their fellow monastics, but with the opposite qualities is pleasing.

children.title: Worldly Conditions (1st)
children.description: The eight worldly conditions in brief: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, pleasure and pain.

children.title: Worldly Conditions (2nd)
children.description: The eight worldly conditions in detail: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, pleasure and pain.

children.title: Devadatta’s Failure
children.description: Devadatta’s downfall was the eight worldly conditions.

children.title: Uttara on Failure
children.description: In a discourse evidently set some time after the Buddha’s passing, Venerable Uttara, staying in a distant land, teaches that a mendicant should review their own failings and those of others. Questioned by Sakka, the Lord of Gods, Uttara affirms that he learned this from the Buddha.

children.title: Nanda
children.description: The Buddha praises the grace and restraint of Venerable Nanda.

children.title: Trash
children.description: When a certain monk was admonished, he responded by attacking his reprovers. The Buddha tells the other monks to expel him, explaining that when such a monk lives hidden in the Saṅgha, his corruption can spread to the other monks.

children.title: At Verañjā
children.description: The brahmin Verañja rebukes the Buddha for his lack of respect for senior brahmins. He levels a series of criticisms, each of which the Buddha deflects by redefining terms. The Buddha affirms that his claim to superiority is because he was the first to achieve awakening.

children.title: With Sīha
children.description: General Sīha, a prominent disciple of the Jains, visits the Buddha against the wishes of Mahāvīra, the Jain leader. He challenges the Buddha by bringing up the various ways that people criticize him. Convinced by the Buddha’s response, Sīha wishes to take refuge in the Buddha; but the Buddha urges him to be cautious and to continue supporting the Jains.

children.title: A Thoroughbred
children.description: With eight qualities a royal thoroughbred is worthy of a king. Likewise, with eight qualities a mendicant is worthy.

children.title: A Wild Colt
children.description: Eight flaws in wild horses, similar to eight flaws in mendicants.

children.title: Stains
children.description: Eight different kinds of stain.

children.title: Going on a Mission
children.description: A mendicant with eight qualities is worthy of being sent on a mission.

children.title: Catching (1st)
children.description: A woman imprisons a man in eight ways.

children.title: Catching (2nd)
children.description: A man imprisons a woman in eight ways.

children.title: With Pahārāda
children.description: Demons delight in the ocean for eight reasons, and likewise the mendicants delight in the Dhamma for eight reasons.

children.title: Sabbath
children.description: On a full-moon night, the Buddha was to recite the code of conduct for the monks. However, he remained silent until dawn, due to the presence of a corrupt monk.

children.title: With Ugga of Vesālī
children.description: The Buddha celebrates the eight amazing qualities of the householder Ugga of Vesālī. Ugga himself speaks of these qualities.

children.title: With Uggata of Elephant Village
children.description: The Buddha celebrates the eight amazing qualities of the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma. Ugga himself speaks of these qualities.

children.title: With Hatthaka (1st)
children.description: The Buddha celebrates the seven amazing qualities of the householder Hatthaka of Āḷavī. When he hears of this, Hatthaka is anxious to know that no lay people were present. Learning of this, the Buddha adds humility as an eight quality.

children.title: With Hatthaka (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha learns from Hatthaka of Āḷavī how he maintains a large following. He then celebrates Hatthaka’s eight good qualities.

children.title: With Mahānāma
children.description: Questioned by his relative Mahānāma, the Buddha explains what makes someone a Buddhist lay follower, a virtuous lay follower, and a lay follower practicing for the welfare of all.

children.title: With Jīvaka
children.description: Questioned by Jīvaka Komārabhacca, the Buddha explains what makes someone a Buddhist lay follower, a virtuous lay follower, and a lay follower practicing for the welfare of all.

children.title: Powers (1st)
children.description: Eight very different kinds of powers.

children.title: Powers (2nd)
children.description: Eight powers of a perfected one.

children.title: Lost Opportunities
children.description: Eight lost opportunities for spiritual practice.

children.title: Anuruddha and the Great Thoughts
children.description: Venerable Anuruddha reflects that the teachings is for someone who is of few wishes, content, secluded, energetic, mindful, peaceful, and wise. To these seven thoughts, the Buddha adds an eighth: the teaching is for those who delight in non-proliferation. Practicing in line with these eight thoughts of a great man, Venerable Anuruddha achieves perfection.

children.title: Giving (1st)
children.description: Eight ways of giving a gift.

children.title: Giving (2nd)
children.description: This verse on qualities of a good person appears to be a fragment of text, perhaps originally part of the previous sutta.

children.title: Reasons to Give
children.description: Eight grounds for giving.

children.title: A Field
children.description: The rewards of giving are compared to fields of different qualities.

children.title: Rebirth by Giving
children.description: When giving, if you expect a certain result in the next life, you can get it, if the conditions are right.

children.title: Grounds for Making Merit
children.description: The good deeds of giving, ethics, and meditation lead to good rebirths, depending on the level to which they are developed.

children.title: Gifts of a True Person
children.description: A good person gives gifts in eight ways.

children.title: A True Person
children.description: When a good person is born, it benefits eight kinds of people, like a rain-cloud showering all over the land.

children.title: Overflowing Merit
children.description: Eight streams of merit, consisting in going for refuge and five kinds of gifts.

children.title: The Results of Misconduct
children.description: Eight kinds of misdeed are conducive to bad outcomes.

children.title: The Sabbath With Eight Factors, In Brief
children.description: When the sabbath is observed by following the eight precepts, one lives for that day like the perfected ones. Such a sabbath is glorious.

children.title: The Sabbath With Eight Factors, In Detail
children.description: When the sabbath is observed by following the eight precepts, one lives for that day like the perfected ones. The benefits are explained at length.

children.title: With Visākhā on the Sabbath
children.description: The Buddha teaches the wealthy laywoman Visākhā that when the sabbath is observed by following the eight precepts, one lives for that day like the perfected ones.

children.title: With Vāseṭṭha on the Sabbath
children.description: The Buddha teaches the layman Vāseṭṭha that when the sabbath is observed by following the eight precepts, one lives for that day like the perfected ones. Vāseṭṭha exclaims that such a practice would be widely beneficial.

children.title: With Bojjhā on the Sabbath
children.description: The Buddha teaches the laywoman Bojjhā that when the sabbath is observed by following the eight precepts, one lives for that day like the perfected ones. Bojjhā exclaims that such a practice would be widely beneficial.

children.title: Anuruddha and the Agreeable Deities
children.description: Some “Agreeable” gods put on a display of music and dance for Venerable Anuruddha, but he is not impressed. He then asks the Buddha how women are reborn in such a heaven.

children.title: With Visākhā on the Agreeable Gods
children.description: The Buddha teaches the laywoman Visākhā eight qualities through which a woman may be reborn among the Agreeable gods.

children.title: With Nakula’s Mother on the Agreeable Gods
children.description: The Buddha teaches the housewife Nakulamātā eight qualities through which a woman may be reborn among the Agreeable gods.

children.title: Winning in This Life (1st)
children.description: The Buddha teaches the laywoman Visākhā four qualities through which a woman succeeds in this life, and four through which she succeeds in the next.

children.title: Winning in This Life (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha teaches the mendicants four qualities through which a woman succeeds in this life, and four through which she succeeds in the next.

children.title: With Gotamī
children.description: Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the Buddha’s foster mother, requests ordination from the Buddha. He declines, until urged to relent by Ānanda. He allows Mahāpajāpatī to go forth on eight conditions.

children.title: An Adviser for Nuns
children.description: With eight qualities a monk may be appointed to teach the nuns.

children.title: Brief Advice to Gotamī
children.description: Mahāpajāpatī wishes to go on retreat, so the Buddha teaches her eight principles that summarize the Dhamma in brief.

children.title: With Dīghajāṇu
children.description: Dīghajāṇu of the Koliyans asks the Buddha to teach in a way suitable for lay people who enjoy life. The Buddha teaches four practical ways to ensure success in this life, and another four ways to ensure success in the next.

children.title: With Ujjaya
children.description: The brahmin Ujjaya is going abroad, and asks the Buddha to teach him. The Buddha teaches four practical ways to ensure success in this life, and another four ways to ensure success in the next.

children.title: Danger
children.description: The Buddha explains how addiction to sensual pleasures is perilous.

children.title: Worthy of Offerings Dedicated to the Gods (1st)
children.description: With eight qualities, a mendicant is worthy.

children.title: Worthy of Offerings Dedicated to the Gods (2nd)
children.description: With eight qualities, a mendicant is worthy.

children.title: Eight Individuals (1st)
children.description: Eight kinds of person are worthy.

children.title: Eight Individuals (2nd)
children.description: Eight kinds of person are worthy.

children.title: Desire
children.description: The Buddha describes eight cases where a mendicant has a desire for material things. Sometimes they fall under the sway of that desire, but sometimes they rise above it.

children.title: Good Enough
children.description: Eight sets of qualities pertain to benefiting oneself and others.

children.title: A Teaching in Brief
children.description: A monk asks for teachings before going on retreat, but the Buddha rebukes him, as he has not practiced sincerely. Nevertheless, he persists, and the Buddha teaches him meditation in detail.

children.title: At Gayā Head
children.description: At Gayā, the Buddha describes his meditation before awakening. He was able to see lights and forms, converse with gods, and understand the deeds that made them gods.

children.title: Dimensions of Mastery
children.description: Eight dimensions of meditative mastery, based on the vision of certain shapes and colors.

children.title: Liberations
children.description: Eight meditative liberations, based on the vision of forms and the attainment of the formless.

children.title: Ignoble Expressions
children.description: Eight kinds of ignoble statement that misrepresent the truth.

children.title: Noble Expressions
children.description: Eight kinds of noble statement that convey the truth.

children.title: Assemblies
children.description: Eight kinds of assemblies: aristocrats, brahmins, householders, ascetics, and various deities. The Buddha has visited each of these in disguise.

children.title: Earthquakes
children.description: When the Buddha gives up his life-force, an earthquake is felt. The Buddha explains to Ānanda the eight causes of earthquakes.

children.title: Inspiring All Around (1st)
children.description: Beginning with faith, a mendicant completes all good qualities that fulfill liberation.

children.title: Inspiring All Around (2nd)
children.description: Beginning with faith, a mendicant completes all good qualities that fulfill liberation.

children.title: Mindfulness of Death (1st)
children.description: Various mendicants practice mindfulness of death, but do so inadequately. The Buddha explains how to do so with proper urgency,

children.title: Mindfulness of Death (2nd)
children.description: A mendicant should reflect each night on the dangers that lie around them, and practice mindfulness of death with urgency to give up the unwholesome.

children.title: Accomplishments (1st)
children.description: Eight accomplishments, both worldly and spiritual.

children.title: Accomplishments (2nd)
children.description: Eight accomplishments, both worldly and spiritual, in detail.

children.title: Desires
children.description: Sāriputta describes eight cases where a mendicant has a desire for material things. Sometimes they fall under the sway of that desire, but sometimes they rise above it.

children.title: Good Enough
children.description: Eight sets of qualities pertain to benefiting oneself and others, explained by Sāriputta.

children.title: Decline
children.description: Eight conditions for the decline or success of a trainee mendicant.

children.title: Grounds for Laziness and Arousing Energy
children.description: Eight grounds for laziness, and the corresponding eight grounds for energy.

children.title: Mindfulness and Situational Awareness
children.description: Mindfulness and situational awareness are a foundation for developing higher spiritual qualities leading to liberation.

children.title: With Puṇṇiya
children.description: Venerable Puṇṇiya asks the Buddha why he sometimes feels like teaching and other times doesn’t.

children.title: Rooted
children.description: The root of all things, and other factors that apply to all things.

children.title: A Master Thief
children.description: The Buddha teaches how to be a success as a master thief. Unusually, this discourse has no “spiritual” counterpart, so it sounds like the Buddha just giving a lesson in thievery!

children.title: Terms for the Realized One
children.description: Different titles for the Buddha.

children.title: With Nāgita
children.description: When the householders of Icchānaṅgala make a racket in the monastery, the Buddha asks his attendant Nāgita what is going on. The Buddha speaks strongly of his dislike for material gains, and his love of seclusion.

children.title: Turning the Bowl Upside Down
children.description: Eight reasons the Saṅgha may overturn the bowl against a lay follower.

children.title: A Proclamation of No Confidence
children.description: Eight reasons the lay followers may declare no confidence or confidence regarding a mendicant.

children.title: Reconciliation
children.description: Eight reasons the lay followers may enjoin an act of reconciliation on a mendicant, or relax said act.

children.title: Proper Behavior in a Case of Aggravated Misconduct
children.description: Eight things a mendicant charged with aggravated misconduct must observe.

children.title: Awakening
children.description: Beginning with good friendship, the Buddha teaches nine things that give rise to the qualities that lead to awakening.

children.title: Supported
children.description: The things that a mendicant relies on as supports in spiritual practice.

children.title: With Meghiya
children.description: Venerable Meghiya, while attending on the Buddha, wants to go off and meditate in a forest alone. The Buddha discourages him, but he goes anyway. When his meditation doesn’t go well, he returns chastened to the Buddha, who teaches him about the benefits of good companions and other fundamentals of a balanced spiritual practice.

children.title: With Nandaka
children.description: Nandaka is teaching the monks when the Buddha arrives. Unbeknown to those inside, the Buddha waits until the talk was finished, then enters. Nandaka is embarrassed at keeping the Buddha waiting, but the Buddha praises him and offers a teaching on the four things a mendicant should complete. Nandaka then teaches five benefits of listening to Dhamma.

children.title: Powers
children.description: A noble disciple who develops four powers overcomes five fears.

children.title: Association
children.description: Four kinds of person who one should or should not associate with. A similar distinction is made regarding robes, almsfood, lodgings, towns, and countries.

children.title: With Sutavā the Wanderer
children.description: The wanderer Sutavā asks the Buddha about five things a perfected one cannot do; the Buddha expands it to nine.

children.title: With the Wanderer Sajjha
children.description: The wanderer Sajjha asks the Buddha about five things a perfected one cannot do; the Buddha expands it to nine, which differ slightly from AN 9.7.

children.title: Individuals
children.description: Nine kinds of persons: the eight noble persons and the ordinary person.

children.title: Worthy of Offerings Dedicated to the Gods
children.description: Nine persons are worthy of gifts: the eight noble persons and a member of the spiritual family.

children.title: Sāriputta’s Lion’s Roar
children.description: After the rains season, Sāriputta takes leave of the Buddha. Another monk falsely accuses Sāriputta of hitting him before leaving. The Buddha calls Sāriputta to answer the accusation. Before the Saṅgha, Sāriputta denies it, uttering a powerful statement of spiritual prowess.

children.title: With Residue
children.description: Sāriputta visits some wanderers, who claim that only perfected ones are free from bad rebirth. Sāriputta has no opinion on this, but asks the Buddha, who replies that even stream-enterers are freed from lower rebirth.

children.title: With Koṭṭhita
children.description: Venerables Mahākoṭṭhita and Sāriputta discuss whether the spiritual path is for the purpose of changing the results of deeds.

children.title: With Samiddhi
children.description: Sāriputta questions Venerable Samiddhi on the basis of intentions and thoughts.

children.title: The Simile of the Boil
children.description: The body is compared to a boil with nine orifices.

children.title: Perceptions
children.description: Nine perceptions to be developed in meditation.

children.title: Families
children.description: Nine factors in how a family relates to the Saṅgha.

children.title: The Sabbath with Nine Factors
children.description: Nine factors for a glorious sabbath: the eight precepts and the meditation on love.

children.title: A Deity
children.description: Some deities come to the Buddha and speak of how their practice in their past life was limited and unsatisfactory.

children.title: About Velāma
children.description: The wealthy and devoted lay supporter Anāthapiṇḍika rather curiously says that only poor alms are given in his home. The Buddha praises gracious and bounteous generosity. But meditation surpasses even the greatest offering.

children.title: In Three Particulars
children.description: A comparison of the people of India, of Uttarakuru, and of the heaven of the Thirty-Three.

children.title: A Wild Colt
children.description: Nine kinds of horses are compared with nine kinds of monks.

children.title: Rooted in Craving
children.description: Nine things that are rooted in craving.

children.title: Abodes of Sentient Beings
children.description: Nine realms into which sentient beings may be reborn.

children.title: Consolidated by Wisdom
children.description: Nine reflections by which a mendicant knows their mind has wisdom.

children.title: The Simile of the Stone Post
children.description: Venerables Candikāputta and Sāriputta differ in their interpretation of a teaching proposed by the notorious schismatic Devadatta.

children.title: Fears and Enmities (1st)
children.description: A householder who has eliminated the perils that come with breaking the five precepts, and possesses the four factors of stream-entry is freed from lower rebirths.

children.title: Fears and Enmities (2nd)
children.description: A householder who has eliminated the perils that come with breaking the five precepts, and possesses the four factors of stream-entry is freed from lower rebirths.

children.title: Grounds for Resentment
children.description: Nine grounds for resentment.

children.title: Getting Rid of Resentment
children.description: Nine ways of removing resentment.

children.title: Progressive Cessations
children.description: Nine meditative states, each of which arises from the cessation of something present in the previous state.

children.title: Progressive Meditations
children.description: Nine progressive meditation states.

children.title: The Nine Progressive Meditative Attainments
children.description: Nine progressive meditation states, explained in detail.

children.title: Extinguishment is Bliss
children.description: Sāriputta declares that extinguishment is bliss, precisely because nothing is felt there. He explains this apparent paradox with reference to the nine progressive meditations.

children.title: The Simile of the Cow
children.description: Just as a foolish cow can get in trouble wandering the mountains, a foolish mendicant can get lost practicing absorption if they do it wrongly.

children.title: Depending on Absorption
children.description: The ending of defilements happens due to the practice of absorption meditation.

children.title: By Ānanda
children.description: Ānanda exclaims how amazing it is that the Buddha has found a way to freedom while still experiencing the world. Questioned by the monk Udāyī, Ānanda recounts a discussion on advanced meditation with the nun Jaṭilagāhiyā.

children.title: Brahmin Cosmologists
children.description: Two brahmin cosmologists ask the Buddha to decide between competing claims as to whether the cosmos is infinite. Rejecting metaphysical claims, the Buddha says that there is no end of the world that can be reached by traveling; but without reaching the end of the world you can’t be free of suffering.

children.title: The War Between the Gods and the Titans
children.description: In the wars between gods and demons, they find safety only in their own fortress. Similarly, a mendicant finds safety in absorption.

children.title: The Simile of the Bull Elephant in the Forest
children.description: A bull elephant, annoyed by living in the herd, goes off by himself. Similarly, a mendicant feeling crowded in a monastery goes off by themselves and happily meditates in seclusion.

children.title: With the Householder Tapussa
children.description: The householder Tapussa reflects that it is renunciation that distinguishes lay from monastic. The Buddha responds by giving a long account of his practice of absorption before awakening.

children.title: Cramped
children.description: At Udāyī’s request, Ānanda explains an obscure verse spoken (in SN 2.7) by a deity. The nine progressive meditations are the escape from confinement.

children.title: A Direct Witness
children.description: The Buddha speaks of a “direct witness’, that is, someone who personally has thorough and proficient experience of the different meditation states.

children.title: Freed by Wisdom
children.description: One liberated by wisdom first enters the meditation states, then understands them.

children.title: Freed Both Ways
children.description: One freed both ways is both proficient in and understands the meditation states.

children.title: In the Present Life
children.description: The teaching apparent in the present life is experienced provisionally in deep meditation, and completely when the defilements end.

children.title: Extinguishment is Apparent in the Present Life
children.description: Extinguishment apparent in the present life is experienced provisionally in deep meditation, and completely when the defilements end.

children.title: Weaknesses in Training and Mindfulness Meditation
Weaknesses in Training and the Bases of Psychic Power
What’s the Goal?
children.description: The purpose of ethics, leading step by step to liberation.

children.title: Making a Wish
children.description: There’s no need to make a wish to get enlightened; it happens naturally when the conditions are there.

children.title: Vital Conditions (1st)
children.description: The Buddha teaches how, like a tree that grows due to its leaves, liberation follows when ethics is present.

children.title: Vital Conditions (2nd)
children.description: Sāriputta teaches how, like a tree that grows due to its leaves, liberation follows when ethics is present.

children.title: Vital Conditions (3rd)
children.description: Ānanda teaches how, like a tree that grows due to its leaves, liberation follows when ethics is present.

children.title: Immersion
children.description: Ānanda asks the Buddha about a mysterious state of immersion in meditation where there is no normal perception, yet one is still conscious.

children.title: Sāriputta
children.description: Ānanda asks Sāriputta about a mysterious state of immersion in meditation where there is no normal perception, yet one is still conscious. Sāriputta confirms that there is, and claims to have attained it.

children.title: Inspiring All Around: the Absorptions
children.description: Ten factors, beginning with faith, that a mendicant should fulfill.

children.title: Inspiring All Around: the Peaceful Liberations
children.description: Ten factors, beginning with faith, that a mendicant should fulfill.

children.title: Inspiring All Around: the Three Knowledges
children.description: Ten factors, beginning with faith, that a mendicant should fulfill.

children.title: Lodgings
children.description: Five factors that a mendicant should have, and five factors of a lodging that they should occupy.

children.title: Five Factors
children.description: A mendicant should abandon the five hindrances and possess the five factors of the adept.

children.title: Fetters
children.description: Five lower and five higher fetters.

children.title: Hard-heartedness
children.description: Five kinds of emotional barrenness and five emotional shackles.

children.title: Diligence
children.description: Diligence is the foremost of all good qualities.

children.title: Worthy of Offerings Dedicated to the Gods
children.description: Ten persons who are worthy.

children.title: A Protector (1st)
children.description: Ten qualities that serve as protector.

children.title: A Protector (2nd)
children.description: Ten qualities that serve as protector, in detail.

children.title: Abodes of the Noble Ones (1st)
children.description: Ten noble abodes in which the noble ones of the past, present and future abide.

children.title: Abodes of the Noble Ones (2nd)
children.description: Ten noble abodes in which the noble ones of the past, present and future abide, in detail.

children.title: The Lion’s Roar
children.description: Like a lion, a Realized One roars his preeminence based on ten powers.

children.title: Hypotheses
children.description: The Buddha claims to be assured regarding the various different doctrinal hypotheses, based on the ten powers.

children.title: Body
children.description: Some things are to be given up by body, others by speech, and still others by wisdom.

children.title: By Mahācunda
children.description: Venerable Mahācunda teaches that, though a mendicant might claim to be free of greed, hate, and delusion, this is not always the case.

children.title: Meditation on Universals
children.description: Ten universal dimensions of meditation, or kasiṇas.

children.title: With Kāḷī
children.description: The female lay follower Kāḷī of Kuraraghara in Avantī asks Venerable Mahākaccāna about a verse spoken by the Buddha in “The Maidens’ Questions” (SN 4.25). He replies in terms of the ten universal dimensions of meditation.

children.title: The Great Questions (1st)
children.description: Some wanderers claim to teach the direct knowledge of all things, just like the Buddha. However the Buddha disputes this by presenting ten “Great Questions” that they cannot answer.

children.title: The Great Questions (2nd)
children.description: Some lay people ask the nun from Kajaṅgalā regarding the ten “Great Questions”. Though she has not heard this teaching herself, she explains from her own understanding, and is praised by the Buddha.

children.title: Kosala (1st)
children.description: Starting with a comparison with the King of Kosala, the Buddha teaches a series of ten advanced teachings. He culminates by affirming that he teaches the full understanding of sensual pleasures, forms, and feelings.

children.title: Kosala (2nd)
children.description: King Pasenadi returns victorious from battle and immediately goes to see the Buddha, bowing reverentially to his feet, and declaring ten reasons for his love and devotion to the Buddha.

children.title: With Upāli
children.description: The Buddha teaches Venerable Upāli the ten reasons for establishing the training rules.

children.title: Suspending the Recitation of the Monastic Code
children.description: Ten reasons for suspending the recitation of the code of conduct.

children.title: A Judge
children.description: Ten qualities a mendicant should have to be appointed to judge a dispute.

children.title: Ordination
children.description: Ten qualities a mendicant should have to give ordination.

children.title: Dependence
children.description: Ten qualities a mendicant should have to give dependence.

children.title: A Novice
children.description: Ten qualities a mendicant should have to be attended by a novice.

children.title: Schism in the Saṅgha
children.description: Ten reasons for schism in the Saṅgha.

children.title: Harmony in the Saṅgha
children.description: Ten reasons for harmony in the Saṅgha.

children.title: With Ānanda (1st)
children.description: The Buddha teaches Ānanda the ten reasons for schism in the Saṅgha, as well as the outcome of causing schism.

children.title: With Ānanda (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha teaches Ānanda the ten reasons for harmony in the Saṅgha, as well as the outcome of creating harmony.

children.title: Dispute
children.description: Ten reasons for disputes in the Saṅgha.

children.title: Roots of Dispute (1st)
children.description: Ten roots for disputes in the Saṅgha.

children.title: Roots of Dispute (2nd)
children.description: Ten roots for disputes in the Saṅgha.

children.title: At Kusinārā
children.description: A mendicant who wishes to admonish another should first reflect on five things in themselves and establish a further five.

children.title: Entering a Royal Compound
children.description: Ten dangers for a monk who enters a royal harem.

children.title: With the Sakyans
children.description: The Sakyans say that they don’t always observe the eight precepts on the sabbath. The Buddha strongly admonishes them to be more consistent.

children.title: With Mahāli
children.description: Mahāli the Licchavi asks the Buddha for the causes of bad deeds.

children.title: Ten Regular Reflections for a Renunciate
children.description: Topics for frequent reflection by one gone forth.

children.title: Existing Because of the Body
children.description: Ten things that depend on the body.

children.title: Fights
children.description: Some monks are arguing, so the Buddha teaches them ten warm-hearted principles.

children.title: Your Own Mind
children.description: The Buddha teaches that, if you can’t read anyone else’s mind, read your own by regular self-reflection.

children.title: With Sāriputta
children.description: Sāriputta teaches that, if you can’t read anyone else’s mind, read your own by regular self-reflection.

children.title: Stagnation
children.description: The Buddha doesn’t praise stagnation in wholesome qualities, let alone decline.

children.title: Serenity
children.description: The Buddha teaches that, if you can’t read anyone else’s mind, read your own by regular self-reflection. Includes a teaching on various things that should or should not be cultivated.

children.title: Decline
children.description: Sāriputta explains what the Buddha meant by a mendicant who is in decline.

children.title: Perceptions (1st)
children.description: Ten meditative perceptions that lead to the deathless.

children.title: Perceptions (2nd)
children.description: Ten meditative perceptions that lead to the deathless.

children.title: Rooted
children.description: The root of all things, and similar principles.

children.title: Going Forth
children.description: Ten reflections that strengthen the mind of a renunciate.

children.title: With Girimānanda
children.description: The monk Girimānanda is sick. The Buddha encourages Ānanda to visit him and speak of ten perceptions.

children.title: Ignorance
children.description: Even though ignorance has no discernible first point, it still has a cause.

children.title: Craving
children.description: Even though craving has no discernible first point, it still has a cause.

children.title: Come to a Conclusion
children.description: Those who have certainty in the Buddha may realize the final goal in this life or the next.

children.title: Experiential Confidence
children.description: Stream-enterers may realize the final goal in this life or the next.

children.title: Happiness (1st)
children.description: Sāriputta explains to the wanderer Sāmaṇḍakāni that rebirth is suffering, freedom from rebirth is happiness.

children.title: Happiness (2nd)
children.description: Sāriputta explains to the wanderer Sāmaṇḍakāni that dissatisfaction is suffering, enjoyment is happiness.

children.title: At Naḷakapāna (1st)
children.description: At Naḷakapāna the Buddha invites Sāriputta to teach. He speaks of ten qualities that lead to decline or non-decline.

children.title: At Naḷakapāna (2nd)
children.description: At Naḷakapāna the Buddha invites Sāriputta to teach. He speaks of ten qualities that lead to decline or non-decline.

children.title: Topics of Discussion (1st)
children.description: The monks are sitting around chatting about this and that. The Buddha admonishes them and teaches ten topics of conversation suitable for mendicants.

children.title: Topics of Discussion (2nd)
children.description: The monks are sitting around chatting about this and that. The Buddha admonishes them and teaches ten grounds of praise.

children.title: One Might Wish
children.description: If a mendicant wishes to attain spiritual heights, they should begin by practicing the code of training rules.

children.title: Thorns
children.description: When the Buddha receives noisy visitors, several monks withdraw to a nearby forest to meditate. The Buddha praises them, saying that noise is a thorn to absorption.

children.title: Likable
children.description: Ten desirable things that are hard to get.

children.title: Growth
children.description: Ten aspects of prosperity.

children.title: With Migasālā
children.description: The female lay disciple Migasālā questions Ānanda how the Buddha could have declared her father and her uncle had the same level of spiritual attainment, when one was much more strict than the other. Ānanda conveys this to the Buddha, who responds that only such as he can pass judgment, since the spiritual faculties of individuals are complex and hard to understand.

children.title: Three Things
children.description: Without rebirth, old age, and death, there would be no teaching of Dhamma. The Buddha teaches a series of sets of three things leading to liberation.

children.title: A Crow
children.description: A bad monk has ten bad qualities, like a crow.

children.title: Jains
children.description: Jain ascetics have ten bad qualities.

children.title: Grounds for Resentment
children.description: Ten ground for resentment.

children.title: Getting Rid of Resentment
children.description: Ten ways of removing resentment.

children.title: With Bāhuna
children.description: Giving up ten things, the Buddha lives free of limits.

children.title: With Ānanda
children.description: A mendicant cannot achieve progress if they have ten bad qualities starting with lack of faith.

children.title: With Puṇṇiya
children.description: Venerable Puṇṇiya asks why the Buddha sometimes feels like teaching, other times not.

children.title: Declaration
children.description: When a mendicant declares enlightenment, the Buddha or another accomplished meditator examines them.

children.title: A Boaster
children.description: Venerable Mahācunda teaches that when a mendicant boasts about spiritual attainments, the Buddha or another accomplished meditator examines them.

children.title: Overestimation
children.description: Venerable Mahākassapa teaches that when a mendicant declares enlightenment, the Buddha or another accomplished meditator examines them.

children.title: Disciplinary Issues
children.description: The Buddha, speaking in reference to the monk Kalandaka, explains ten qualities that lead to discord or unity.

children.title: An Abuser
children.description: A mendicant who insults their spiritual companions incurs ten disasters.

children.title: With Kokālika
children.description: The monk Kokālika accuses Sāriputta and Moggallāna of having evil wishes. The Buddha defends them. Later, Kokālika suffers calamity and is reborn in hell.

children.title: The Powers of One Who has Ended Defilements
children.description: Ten powers by which a mendicant knows that they have ended the defilements.

children.title: Pleasure Seekers
