children.description: The Buddha teaches Anāthapiṇḍika ten kinds of persons who enjoy sensual pleasures.

children.title: Dangers
children.description: A noble disciple has eliminated five perils, realized the four factors of stream-entry, and seen the noble process.

children.title: What is Your View?
children.description: Anāthapiṇḍika visits some wanderers, who ask him about the Buddha’s views. Anāthapiṇḍika asks them to explain their own view first. He then declares his own understanding of impermanence, leaving the wanderers speechless.

children.title: With Vajjiyamāhita
children.description: The householder Vajjiyamāhita visits some wanderers, who accuse the Buddha of condemning all asceticism. Vajjiyamāhita counters this by saying the Buddha only criticizes what is worthy of criticism. The Buddha praises him, and explains in detail what this means.

children.title: With Uttiya
children.description: The wanderer Uttiya asks the Buddha a series of ten metaphysical questions as to whether the cosmos is finite, etc. The Buddha responds by saying that he only teaches the end of suffering. Uttiya goes on to ask whether all beings will be liberated. The Buddha is silent, and Ānanda answers on his behalf.

children.title: With Kokanada
children.description: The wanderer Kokanada meets Ānanda at the baths and engages him on the topic of the ten metaphysical questions.

children.title: Worthy of Offerings Dedicated to the Gods
children.description: With ten qualities, a mendicant is worthy.

children.title: A Senior Mendicant
children.description: With ten qualities, a senior mendicant is at ease wherever they live.

children.title: With Upāli
children.description: When Upāli asks to go into retreat, the Buddha warns him that secluded wilderness dwellings are hard to endure unless one is accomplished in meditation. He gives a long account of the training required before going into solitude, and ends by encouraging Upāli to stay in the Saṅgha.

children.title: Cannot
children.description: Ten things must be given up before attaining perfection.

children.title: Perceptions for Ascetics
children.description: Three ascetic perceptions lead to seven results.

children.title: Awakening Factors
children.description: The seven factors of awakening lead to realizing the three knowledges.

children.title: The Wrong Way
children.description: The tenfold wrong path leads to failure, the tenfold right path leads to success.

children.title: A Seed
children.description: When a person has wrong view, all their path development is wrong. But when they have right view, everything good follows.

children.title: Knowledge
children.description: Ignorance is the precursor of wrong view and the other bad qualities, while right view is the opposite.

children.title: Wearing Away
children.description: Each of the ten path factors wears away its opposite.

children.title: The Bone-Washing Ceremony
children.description: The Buddha speaks of a southern land called “Bath”, but says that a spiritual bath is better.

children.title: Doctors
children.description: The Buddha speaks of a purgative for curing ailments, but says that a spiritual purgative is better.

children.title: Emetic
children.description: The Buddha speaks of a emetic for curing ailments, but says that a spiritual emetic is better.

children.title: Blown Away
children.description: The ten path factors each expel their opposite.

children.title: An Adept (1st)
children.description: An adept has fulfilled the ten path factors.

children.title: An Adept (2nd)
children.description: An adept has fulfilled the ten path factors.

children.title: Bad Principles (1st)
children.description: One should understand what is the teaching and what is contrary to the teaching, in brief.

children.title: Bad Principles (2nd)
children.description: One should understand what is the teaching and what is contrary to the teaching, in detail.

children.title: Bad Principles (3rd)
children.description: One should understand what is the teaching and what is contrary to the teaching. After hearing this in brief from the Buddha, the mendicants seek a detailed answer from Ānanda.

children.title: With Ajita
children.description: The wanderer Ajita informs the Buddha that a philosopher has proposed 500 cases for knowing that and argument has been won or lost. The Buddha asks the mendicants about these.

children.title: With Saṅgārava
children.description: The wrong path is the near shore where most people dwell; the right path is the far shore, where few have crossed over.

children.title: The Near Shore
children.description: The wrong path is the near shore where most people dwell; the right path is the far shore, where few have crossed over.

children.title: The Ceremony of Descent (1st)
children.description: The Buddha sees Jāṇussoṇī observing the brahmanical ceremony of “descent”. The Buddha teaches his revised version.

children.title: The Ceremony of Descent (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha teaches his revised version of the brahmanical ceremony of “descent” to the mendicants.

children.title: Forerunner
children.description: As the dawn is the forerunner of the sunrise, right view is the forerunner of the path.

children.title: The Ending of Defilements
children.description: The ten path factors lead to the end of the defilements.

children.title: The Teaching of the Noble Ones
The Teaching of the True Persons
The Brahmin Ceremony of Descent
children.description: The Buddha sees Jāṇussoṇī observing the brahmanical ceremony of “descent”. The Buddha teaches his revised version.

children.title: The Noble Descent
children.description: The Buddha teaches his revised version of the brahmanical ceremony of “descent” to the mendicants.

children.title: With Saṅgārava
children.description: The Buddha teaches the brahmin Saṅgārava that the wrong path is the near shore where most people dwell; the right path is the far shore, where few have crossed over.

children.title: The Near Shore
children.description: The wrong path is the near shore where most people dwell; the right path is the far shore, where few have crossed over.

children.title: Bad Principles (1st)
children.description: One should understand what is the teaching and what is contrary to the teaching, in brief.

children.title: Bad Principles (2nd)
children.description: One should understand what is the teaching and what is contrary to the teaching. After hearing this in brief from the Buddha, the mendicants seek a detailed answer from Mahākaccāna.

children.title: Bad Principles (3rd)
children.description: One should understand what is the teaching and what is contrary to the teaching, in detail.

children.title: Sources of Deeds
children.description: The various kinds of bad deeds are caused by greed, hate, and delusion.

children.title: The Bypass
children.description: Through the teaching one may avoid the various kinds of bad deeds.

children.title: With Cunda
children.description: Cunda the smith tells the Buddha of rites of purification practiced by the western brahmins. The Buddha explains purification in his teaching.

children.title: With Jānussoṇi
children.description: Jāṇussoṇī describes brahmanical memorial rites for the dead, and asks if giving gifts actually benefits dead relatives. The Buddha replies that it might do in some circumstances.

children.title: The Teaching of the Noble Ones
The Teaching of the True Persons
Principles That Should Be Made Much Of
Heaven and Hell (1st)
children.description: The ten kinds of bad deeds lead you to hell; the ten good deeds to heaven.

children.title: Creepy Creatures
children.description: Those who do the ten kinds of bad deeds are like creepy creatures.

children.title: Intentional (1st)
children.description: The Buddha asserts that one’s kamma must be exhausted before making an end of suffering. This statement precedes a long explanation of deeds and their causes.

children.title: Intentional (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha asserts that one’s kamma must be exhausted before making an end of suffering. This statement precedes a long explanation of deeds and their causes.

children.title: The Body Born of Deeds
children.description: The Buddha asserts that one’s kamma must be exhausted before making an end of suffering. If one develops the heart’s release through love, no bad deeds can persist there.

children.title: Unprincipled Conduct
children.description: The Buddha teaches a brahmin that bad conduct leads to hell, good conduct to heaven.

children.title: Untitled Discourses on Ten to Forty Qualities (1st)
Untitled Discourses on Ten to Forty Qualities (2nd)
Untitled Discourses on Ten to Forty Qualities (3rd)
What’s the Goal?
children.description: Good conduct leads to non-regret, to joy, and so on all the way to liberation.

children.title: Making a Wish
children.description: A virtuous person need not make a wish; it is natural for the path to flow on.

children.title: Vital Conditions (1st)
children.description: The Buddha teaches that ethical conduct is the vital cause of the good qualities that lead to awakening.

children.title: Vital Conditions (2nd)
children.description: Sāriputta teaches that ethical conduct is the vital cause of the good qualities that lead to awakening.

children.title: Vital Conditions (3rd)
children.description: Ānanda teaches that ethical conduct is the vital cause of the good qualities that lead to awakening.

children.title: Disasters
children.description: When a mendicant abuses their fellow monastics, eleven disasters follow.

children.title: Percipient
children.description: Ānanda asks the Buddha about a deep state of meditation where all normal perception has ceased, but there is still perception. The Buddha affirms that such a state exists. Ānanda puts the same question to Sāriputta, and gets the same answer.

children.title: Focus
children.description: Ānanda asks the Buddha about a deep state of meditation where all normal attention has ceased, but there is still attention. The Buddha affirms that such a state exists.

children.title: With Sandha
children.description: The Buddha tells Venerable Sandha to meditate like a trained thoroughbred, not like a wild colt. Doing so, they may attain a deep state.

children.title: At the Peacocks’ Feeding Ground
children.description: Possessing various sets of qualities, a mendicant is best among gods and men.

children.title: With Mahānāma (1st)
children.description: Mahānāma the Sakyan sees that the monks are preparing robes after the rains season. Knowing that the Buddha will soon depart, he asks how they are to live with their busy lives.

children.title: With Mahānāma (2nd)
children.description: Mahānāma the Sakyan sees that the monks are preparing robes after the rains season. Knowing that the Buddha will soon depart, he asks how they are to live with their busy lives.

children.title: With Nandiya
children.description: Nandiya the Sakiyan moves to Sāvatthī to be near the Buddha. At the end of the rains, he asks the Buddha’s advice on how to live.

children.title: With Subhūti
children.description: Venerable Subhūti brings the young monk Saddha to meet the Buddha. The Buddha goes on to teach the manifestations of faith.

children.title: The Benefits of Love
children.description: The meditation on love has eleven benefits.

children.title: The Wealthy Citizen
children.description: Asked by a householder to teach a path to freedom, Venerable Ānanda explains no less than eleven meditative states that may serve as doors to the deathless.

children.title: The Cowherd
children.description: A cowherd with eleven qualities is competent to look after a herd of cattle. Likewise, a mendicant with eleven qualities can grow in the Dhamma.

children.title: Immersion (1st)
children.description: The Buddha is asked by the mendicants about a deep state of meditation where all normal perception has ceased, but there is still perception.

children.title: Immersion (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha teaches the mendicants about a deep state of meditation where all normal perception has ceased, but there is still perception.

children.title: Immersion (3rd)
children.description: Sāriputta is asked by the mendicants about a deep state of meditation where all normal perception has ceased, but there is still perception.

children.title: Immersion (4th)
children.description: Sāriputta teaches the mendicants about a deep state of meditation where all normal perception has ceased, but there is still perception.

children.title: 1. Root of All Things
children.description: This chapter, though beginning with the abstruse Mūlapariyāya Sutta, mostly contains foundational teachings and can, as a whole, serve as an introduction to the discourses.

children.title: The Root of All Things
children.description: The Buddha examines how the notion of a permanent self emerges from the process of perception. A wide range of phenomena are considered, embracing both naturalistic and cosmological dimensions. An unawakened person interprets experience in terms of a self, while those more advanced have the same experiences without attachment.

children.title: All the Defilements
children.description: The diverse problems of the spiritual journey demand a diverse range of responses. Rather than applying the same solution to every problem, the Buddha outlines seven methods of dealing with defilements, each of which works in certain cases.

children.title: Heirs in the Teaching
children.description: Some of the Buddha’s students inherit from him only material profits and fame. But his true inheritance is the spiritual path, the way of contentment. Venerable Sāriputta explains how by following the Buddha’s example we can experience the fruits of the path.

children.title: Fear and Dread
children.description: The Buddha explains the difficulties of living in the wilderness, and how they are overcome by purity of conduct and meditation. He recounts some of the fears and obstacles he faced during his own practice.

children.title: Unblemished
children.description: The Buddha’s chief disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, use a simile of a tarnished bowl to illustrate the blemishes of the mind and conduct. They emphasize how the crucial thing is not so much whether there are blemishes, but whether we are aware of them.

children.title: One Might Wish
children.description: According to the Buddha, careful observance of ethical precepts is the foundation of all higher achievements in the spiritual life.

children.title: The Simile of the Cloth
children.description: The many different kinds of impurities that defile the mind are compared to a dirty cloth. When the mind is clean we find joy, which leads to states of higher consciousness. Finally, the Buddha rejects the Brahmanical notion that purity comes from bathing in sacred rivers.

children.title: Self-Effacement
children.description: The Buddha differentiates between peaceful meditation and spiritual practices that encompass the whole of life. He lists forty-four aspects, which he explains as “effacement”, the wearing away of conceit.

children.title: Right View
children.description: Venerable Sāriputta gives a detailed explanation of right view, the first factor of the noble eightfold path. At the prompting of the other mendicants, he approaches the topic from a wide range of perspectives.

children.title: The Discourse on Mindfulness Meditation
children.description: Here the Buddha details the seventh factor of the noble eightfold path, mindfulness meditation. This collects many of the meditation teachings found throughout the canon, especially the foundational practices focusing on the body, and is regarded as one of the most important meditation discourses.

children.title: 2. Lion’s Roar
children.description: Beginning with two discourses containing a “lion’s roar”, this chapter deals with suffering, community life, and practical meditation advice.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse on the Lion’s Roar
children.description: The Buddha declares that only those following his path can genuinely experience the four stages of awakening. This is because, while much is shared with other systems, none of them go so far as to fully reject all attachment to the idea of a self.

children.title: The Longer Discourse on the Lion’s Roar
children.description: A disrobed monk, Sunakkhatta, attacks the Buddha’s teaching because it merely leads to the end of suffering. The Buddha counters that this is, in fact, praise, and goes on to enumerate his many profound and powerful achievements.

children.title: The Longer Discourse on the Mass of Suffering
children.description: Challenged to show the difference between his teaching and that of other ascetics, the Buddha points out that they speak of letting go, but do not really understand why. He then explains in great detail the suffering that arises from attachment to sensual stimulation.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse on the Mass of Suffering
children.description: A lay person is puzzled at how, despite their long practice, they still have greedy or hateful thoughts. The Buddha explains the importance of absorption meditation for letting go such attachments. But he also criticizes self-mortification, and recounts a previous dialog with Jain ascetics.

children.title: Measuring Up
children.description: Venerable Moggallāna raises the topic of admonishment, without which healthy community is not possible. He lists a number of qualities that will encourage others to think it worthwhile to admonish you in a constructive way.

children.title: Emotional Barrenness
children.description: The Buddha explains various ways one can become emotionally cut off from one’s spiritual community.

children.title: Jungle Thickets
children.description: While living in the wilderness is great, not everyone is ready for it. The Buddha encourages meditators to reflect on whether one’s environment is genuinely supporting their meditation practice, and if not, to leave.

children.title: The Honey-Cake
children.description: Challenged by a brahmin, the Buddha gives an enigmatic response on how conflict arises due to proliferation based on perceptions. Venerable Kaccāna draws out the detailed implications of this in one of the most insightful passages in the entire canon.

children.title: Two Kinds of Thought
children.description: Recounting his own experiences in developing meditation, the Buddha explains how to understand harmful and harmless thoughts, and how to go beyond thought altogether.

children.title: How to Stop Thinking
children.description: In a practical meditation teaching, the Buddha describes five different approaches to stopping thoughts.

children.title: 3. Similes
children.description: A diverse chapter including biography, non-violence, not-self, and an influential teaching on the progress of meditation.

children.title: The Simile of the Saw
children.description: A discourse full of vibrant and memorable similes, on the importance of patience and love even when faced with abuse and criticism. The Buddha finishes with the simile of the saw, one of the most memorable similes found in the discourses.

children.title: The Simile of the Snake
children.description: One of the monks denies that prohibited conduct is really a problem. The monks and then the Buddha subject him to an impressive dressing down. The Buddha compares someone who understands only the letter of the teachings to someone who grabs a snake by the tail, and also invokes the famous simile of the raft.

children.title: The Ant-Hill
children.description: In a curious discourse laden with evocative imagery, a deity presents a riddle to a mendicant, who seeks an answer from the Buddha.

children.title: Prepared Chariots
children.description: Venerable Sāriputta seeks a dialog with an esteemed monk, Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāniputta, and they discuss the stages of purification.

children.title: Fodder
children.description: The Buddha compares getting trapped by Māra with a deer getting caught in a snare, illustrating the ever more complex strategies employed by hunter and hunted.

children.title: The Noble Search
children.description: This is one of the most important biographical discourses, telling the Buddha’s experiences from leaving home to realizing awakening. Throughout, he was driven by the imperative to fully escape from rebirth and suffering.

children.title: The Shorter Elephant’s Footprint Simile
children.description: The Buddha cautions against swift conclusions about a teacher’s spiritual accomplishments, comparing it to the care a tracker would use when tracking elephants. He presents the full training of a monastic.

children.title: The Longer Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint
children.description: Sāriputta gives an elaborate demonstration of how, just as any footprint can fit inside an elephant’s, all the Buddha’s teaching can fit inside the four noble truths. This offers an overall template for organizing the Buddha’s teachings.

children.title: The Longer Simile of the Heartwood
children.description: Following the incident with Devadatta, the Buddha cautions the mendicants against becoming complacent with superficial benefits of spiritual life and points to liberation as the true heart of the teaching.

children.title: The Shorter Simile of the Heartwood
children.description: Similar to the previous. After the incident with Devadatta, the Buddha cautions the mendicants against becoming complacent and points to liberation as the true heart of the teaching.

children.title: 4. The Greater Chapter on Pairs
children.description: Discourses arranged as pairs of longer and shorter texts.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse at Gosiṅga
children.description: The Buddha comes across three mendicants practicing diligently and harmoniously, and asks them how they do it. Reluctant to disclose their higher attainments, they explain how they deal with the practical affairs of living together. But when pressed by the Buddha, they reveal their meditation attainments.

children.title: The Longer Discourse at Gosiṅga
children.description: Several senior mendicants, reveling in the beauty of the night, discuss what kind of practitioner would adorn the park. They take their answers to the Buddha, who praises their answers, but gives his own twist.

children.title: The Longer Discourse on the Cowherd
children.description: For eleven reasons a cowherd is not able to properly look after a herd. The Buddha compares this to the spiritual growth of a mendicant.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse on the Cowherd
children.description: Drawing parallels with a cowherd guiding his herd across a dangerous river, the Buddha presents the various kinds of enlightened disciples who cross the stream of transmigration.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse With Saccaka
children.description: Saccaka was a debater, who challenged the Buddha to a contest. Despite his bragging, the Buddha is not at all perturbed at his attacks.

children.title: The Longer Discourse With Saccaka
children.description: In a less confrontational meeting, the Buddha and Saccaka discuss the difference between physical and mental development. The Buddha gives a long account of the various practices he did before awakening, detailing the astonishing lengths he took to mortify the body.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse on the Ending of Craving
children.description: Moggallāna visits the heaven of Sakka, the lord of gods, to see whether he really understands what the Buddha is teaching.

children.title: The Longer Discourse on the Ending of Craving
children.description: To counter the wrong view that a self-identical consciousness transmigrates from one life to the next, the Buddha teaches dependent origination, showing that consciousness invariably arises dependent on conditions.

children.title: The Longer Discourse at Assapura
children.description: The Buddha encourages the mendicants to live up to their name, by actually practicing in a way that meets or exceeds the expectations people have for renunciants.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse at Assapura
children.description: The labels of being a spiritual practitioner don’t just come from external trappings, but from sincere inner change.

children.title: 5. The Lesser Chapter on Pairs
children.description: A similar arrangement to the previous.

children.title: The People of Sālā
children.description: The Buddha explains to a group of brahmins the conduct leading to rebirth in higher or lower states, including detailed explanations of the ten core practices which lay people should undertake, and which also form the basis for liberation.

children.title: The People of Verañja
children.description: Similar to the previous. The Buddha explains the conduct leading to rebirth in higher or lower states, including detailed explanations of the ten core practices.

children.title: The Great Classification
children.description: A series of questions and answers between Sāriputta and Mahākoṭṭhita, examining various subtle and abstruse aspects of the teachings.

children.title: The Shorter Classification
children.description: The layman Visākha asks the nun Dhammadinnā about various difficult matters, including some of the highest meditation attainments. The Buddha fully endorses her answers.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse on Taking Up Practices
children.description: The Buddha explains how taking up different practices may have harmful or beneficial results. The memorable simile of the creeper shows how insidious temptations can be.

children.title: The Great Discourse on Taking Up Practices
children.description: While we all want to be happy, we often find the opposite happens. The Buddha explains why.

children.title: The Inquirer
children.description: While some spiritual teachers prefer to remain in obscurity, the Buddha not only encouraged his followers to closely investigate him, but gave them a detailed and demanding method to do so.

children.title: The Mendicants of Kosambi
children.description: Despite the Buddha’s presence, the monks of Kosambi fell into a deep and bitter dispute. The Buddha taught the reluctant monks to develop love and harmony, reminding them of the state of peace that they sought.

children.title: On the Invitation of Divinity
children.description: The Buddha ascends to a high heavenly realm where he engages in a cosmic contest with a powerful divinity, who had fallen into the delusion that he was eternal and all-powerful.

children.title: The Rebuke of Māra
children.description: Māra, the trickster and god of death, tried to annoy Moggallāna. He not only failed but was subject to a stern sermon warning of the dangers of attacking the Buddha’s disciples.

children.title: 1. Householders
children.description: This chapter is addressed to a diverse range of lay people.

children.title: With Kandaraka
children.description: The Buddha discusses mindfulness meditation with lay practitioners. Contrasting the openness of animals with the duplicity of humans, he explains how to practice in a way that causes no harm to oneself or others.

children.title: The Man From the City of Aṭṭhaka
children.description: Asked by a householder to teach a path to freedom, Venerable Ānanda explains no less than eleven meditative states that may serve as doors to the deathless.

children.title: A Trainee
children.description: The Buddha is invited by his family, the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, to inaugurate a new community hall. He invites Venerable Ānanda to explain in detail the stages of spiritual practice for a lay trainee.

children.title: With Potaliya the Householder
children.description: When Potaliya got upset at being referred to as “householder”, the Buddha quizzed him as to the true nature of attachment and renunciation.

children.title: With Jīvaka
children.description: The Buddha’s personal doctor, Jīvaka, hears criticisms of the Buddha’s policy regarding eating meat, and asks him about it.

children.title: With Upāli
children.description: The Buddha disagrees with a Jain ascetic on the question of whether physical or mental deeds are more important. When he hears of this, the Jain disciple Upāli decides to visit the Buddha and refute him, and proceeds despite all warnings.

children.title: The Ascetic Who Behaved Like a Dog
children.description: Some ascetics in ancient India undertook extreme practices, such as a vow to behave like an ox or a dog. The Buddha meets two such individuals, and is reluctantly pressed to reveal the kammic outcomes of such practice.

children.title: With Prince Abhaya
children.description: The leader of the Jains, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, gives his disciple Prince Abhaya a dilemma to pose to the Buddha, supposing that this will show his weakness. Things don’t go quite as planned.

children.title: The Many Kinds of Feeling
children.description: The Buddha resolves a disagreement on the number of kinds of feelings that he taught, pointing out that different ways of teaching are appropriate in different contexts, and should not be a cause of disputes. He goes on to show the importance of pleasure in developing higher meditation.

children.title: Unfailing
children.description: The Buddha teaches a group of uncommitted householders how to use a rational reflection to arrive at practices and principles that are guaranteed to have a good outcome, even if we don’t know all the variables.

children.title: 2. Mendicants
children.description: Ten discourses to monks, many of them focusing on matters of discipline.

children.title: Advice to Rāhula at Ambalaṭṭhika
children.description: Using the “object lesson” of a cup of water, the Buddha explains to his son, Rāhula, the importance of telling the truth and reflecting on one’s motives.

children.title: The Longer Advice to Rāhula
children.description: The Buddha tells Rāhula to meditate on not-self, which he immediately puts into practice. Seeing him, Venerable Sāriputta advises him to develop breath meditation, but the Buddha suggests a wide range of different practices first.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse With Māluṅkya
children.description: A monk demands that the Buddha answer his metaphysical questions, or else he will disrobe. The Buddha compares him to a man struck by an arrow, who refuses treatment until he can have all his questions about the arrow and the archer answered.

children.title: The Longer Discourse With Māluṅkya
children.description: A little baby has no wrong views or intentions, but the underlying tendency for these things is still there. Without practicing, they will inevitably recur.

children.title: With Bhaddāli
children.description: A monk refuses to follow the rule forbidding eating after noon, but is filled with remorse and forgiven.

children.title: The Simile of the Quail
children.description: Again raising the rule regarding eating, but this time as a reflection of gratitude for the Buddha in eliminating things that cause complexity and stress. The Buddha emphasizes how attachment even to little things can be dangerous.

children.title: At Cātumā
children.description: After dismissing some unruly monks, the Buddha is persuaded to relent, and teaches them four dangers for those gone forth.

children.title: At Naḷakapāna
children.description: Those who practice do so not because they are failures, but because they aspire to higher freedom. When he speaks of the attainments of disciples, the Buddha does so in order to inspire.

children.title: With Gulissāni
children.description: A monk comes down to the community from the wilderness, but doesn’t behave properly. Venerable Sāriputta explains how a mendicant should behave, whether in forest or town.

children.title: At Kīṭāgiri
children.description: A third discourse that presents the health benefits of eating in one part of the day, and the reluctance of some mendicants to follow this.

children.title: 3. Wanderers
children.description: The Buddha in dialog with ascetics and wanderers.

children.title: To Vacchagotta on the Three Knowledges
children.description: The Buddha denies being omniscient, and sets forth the three higher knowledges that form the core of his awakened insight.

children.title: With Vacchagotta on Fire
children.description: Refusing to take a stance regarding useless metaphysical speculations, the Buddha illustrates the spiritual goal with the simile of a flame going out.

children.title: The Longer Discourse With Vacchagotta
children.description: In the final installment of the “Vacchagotta trilogy”, Vacchagotta lets go his obsession with meaningless speculation, and asks about practice.

children.title: With Dīghanakha
children.description: Deftly outmaneuvering an extreme skeptic, the Buddha discusses the outcomes of belief and disbelief. Rather than getting stuck in abstractions, he encourages staying close to the feelings one experiences.

children.title: With Māgaṇḍiya
children.description: Accused by a hedonist of being too negative, the Buddha recounts the luxury of his upbringing, and his realization of how little value there was in such things. Through renunciation he found a far greater pleasure.

children.title: With Sandaka
children.description: Venerable Ānanda teaches a group of wanderers how there are many different approaches to the spiritual life, many of which lead nowhere.

children.title: The Longer Discourse with Sakuludāyī
children.description: Unlike many teachers, the Buddha’s followers treat him with genuine love and respect, since they see the sincerity of his teaching and practice.

children.title: With Uggāhamāna Samaṇamaṇḍikāputta
children.description: A wanderer teaches that a person has reached the highest attainment when they keep four basic ethical precepts. The Buddha’s standards are considerably higher.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse With Sakuludāyī
children.description: A wanderer teaches his doctrine of the “highest splendor” but is unable to give a satisfactory account of what that means. The Buddha memorably compares him to someone who is in love with an idealized women who he has never met.

children.title: With Vekhanasa
children.description: Starting off similar to the previous, the Buddha goes on to explain that one is not converted to his teaching just because of clever arguments, but because you see in yourself the results of the practice.

children.title: 4. Kings
children.description: Various dialogs with kings and princes, many of whom followed the Buddha.

children.title: With Ghaṭīkāra
children.description: The Buddha relates an unusual account of a past life in the time of the previous Buddha, Kassapa. At that time he was not interested in Dhamma, and had to be forced to go see the Buddha. This discourse is important in understanding the development of the Bodhisattva doctrine.

children.title: With Raṭṭhapāla
children.description: A wealthy young man, Raṭṭhapāla, has a strong aspiration to go forth, but has to prevail against the reluctance of his parents. Even after he became a monk, his parents tried to persuade him to disrobe. The discourse ends with a moving series of teachings on the fragility of the world.

children.title: About King Maghadeva
children.description: A rare extended mythic narrative, telling of an ancient kingly lineage and their eventual downfall.

children.title: At Madhurā
children.description: In Madhurā, towards the north-eastern limit of the Buddha’s reach during his life, King Avantiputta asks Venerable Mahākaccāna regarding the brahmanical claim to be the highest caste.

children.title: With Prince Bodhi
children.description: Admitting that he used to believe that pleasure was to be gained through pain, the Buddha explains how his practice showed him the fallacy of that idea.

children.title: With Aṅgulimāla
children.description: Ignoring warnings, the Buddha ventures into the domain of the notorious killer Aṅgulimāla and succeeds in converting him to the path of non-violence. After becoming a monk Aṅgulimāla still suffered for his past deeds, but only to a small extent. He uses his new commitment to non-violence to help a woman in labor.

children.title: Born From the Beloved
children.description: A rare glimpse into the marital life of King Pasenadi, and how he is led to the Dhamma by his Queen, the incomparable Mallikā. She confirms the Buddha’s teaching that our loved ones bring us sorrow; but that’s not something a husband, father, and king wants to hear.

children.title: The Imported Cloth
children.description: King Pasenadi takes a chance to visit Venerable Ānanda, where he asks about skillful and unskillful behavior, and what is praised by the Buddha. He offers Ānanda a valuable cloth in gratitude.

children.title: Shrines to the Teaching
children.description: King Pasenadi, near the end of his life, visits the Buddha, and shows moving devotion and love for his teacher.

children.title: At Kaṇṇakatthala
children.description: King Pasenadi questions the Buddha on miscellaneous matters: caste, omniscience, and the gods among them.

children.title: 5. Brahmins
children.description: The Buddha engages with the powerful caste of brahmins, contesting their claims to spiritual authority.

children.title: With Brahmāyu
children.description: The oldest and most respected brahmin of the age sends a student to examine the Buddha, and he spends several months following his every move before reporting back. Convinced that the Buddha fulfills an ancient prophecy of the Great Man, the brahmin becomes his disciple.

children.title: With Sela
children.description: A brahmanical ascetic named Keṇiya invites the entire Saṅgha for a meal. When the brahmin Sela sees what is happening, he visits the Buddha and expresses his delight in a moving series of devotional verses.

children.title: With Assalāyana
children.description: A precocious brahmin student is encouraged against his wishes to challenge the Buddha on the question of caste. His reluctance turns out to be justified.

children.title: With Ghoṭamukha
children.description: A brahmin denies that there is such a thing as a principled renunciate life, but Venerable Udena persuades him otherwise.

children.title: With Caṅkī
children.description: The reputed brahmin Caṅkī goes with a large group to visit the Buddha, despite the reservations of other brahmins. A precocious student challenges the Buddha, affirming the validity of the Vedic scriptures. The Buddha gives a detailed explanation of how true understanding gradually emerges through spiritual education.

children.title: With Esukārī
children.description: A brahmin claims that one deserves service and privilege depending on caste, but the Buddha counters that it is conduct, not caste, that show a person’s worth.

children.title: With Dhanañjāni
children.description: A corrupt tax-collector is redeemed by his encounter with Venerable Sāriputta.

children.title: With Vāseṭṭha
children.description: Two brahmin students ask the Buddha about what makes a brahmin: birth or deeds? the Buddha points out that, while the species of animals are determined by birth, for humans what matters is how you chose to live. This discourse anticipates the modern view that there are no such things as clearly defined racial differences among humans.

children.title: With Subha
children.description: Working hard is not valuable in and of itself; what matters is the outcome. And just as in lay life, spiritual practice may or may not lead to fruitful results.

children.title: With Saṅgārava
children.description: Angered by the devotion of a brahmin lady, a brahmin visits the Buddha. He positions himself against traditionalists and rationalists, as someone whose teaching is based on direct experience.

children.title: 1. Devadaha
children.description: Diverse teachings.

children.title: At Devadaha
children.description: The Buddha tackles a group of Jain ascetics, pressing them on their claim to be practicing to end all suffering by self-mortification. He points out a series of fallacies in their logic, and explains his own middle way.

children.title: The Five and Three
children.description: A middle length version of the more famous Brahmajāla Sutta (DN1), this surveys a range of speculative views and dismisses them all.

children.title: Is This What You Think Of Me?
children.description: The Buddha teaches the monks to not dispute about the fundamental teachings, but to always strive for harmony.

children.title: At Sāmagāma
children.description: Hearing of the death of the Jain leader Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, the Buddha encourages the Saṅgha to swiftly resolve any disputes. He lays down a series of seven methods for resolving disputes. These form the foundation for the monastic code.

children.title: With Sunakkhatta
children.description: Not all of those who claim to be awakened are genuine. The Buddha teaches how true spiritual progress depends on an irreversible letting go of the forces that lead to suffering.

children.title: Conducive to the Imperturbable
children.description: Beginning with profound meditation absorption, the Buddha goes on to deeper and deeper levels, showing how insight on this basis leads to the detaching of consciousness from any form of rebirth.

children.title: With Moggallāna the Accountant
children.description: The Buddha compares the training of an accountant with the step by step spiritual path of his followers. But even with such a well explained path, the Buddha can only show the way, and it is up to us to walk it.

children.title: With Moggallāna the Guardian
children.description: Amid rising military tensions after the Buddha’s death, Venerable Ānanda is questioned about how the Saṅgha planned to continue in their teacher’s absence. As the Buddha refused to appoint a successor, the teaching and practice that he laid down become the teacher, and the Saṅgha resolves issues by consensus.

children.title: The Longer Discourse on the Full-Moon Night
children.description: On a lovely full moon night, one of the mendicants presents the Buddha with a series of questions that go to the heart of the teaching. But when he hears of the doctrine of not-self, another mendicant is unable to grasp the meaning.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse on the Full-Moon Night
children.description: A good person is able to understand a bad person, but not vice versa.

children.title: 2. One By One
children.description: Many of the discourses in this chapter delve into complex and analytical presentations of core teachings. It includes important discourses on meditation.

children.title: One by One
children.description: The Buddha describes in technical detail the process of insight of Venerable Sāriputta. Many ideas and terms in this text anticipate the Abhidhamma.

children.title: The Sixfold Purification
children.description: If someone claims to be awakened, their claim should be interrogated with a detailed series of detailed questions. Only if they can answer them clearly should the claim be accepted.

children.title: A True Person
children.description: The Buddha explains that a truly good person does not disparage others or feel superior because of their attainment.

children.title: What Should and Should Not Be Cultivated
children.description: The Buddha sets up a framework on things to be cultivated or avoided, and Venerable Sāriputta volunteers to elaborate.

children.title: Many Elements
children.description: Beginning by praising a wise person, the Buddha goes on to explain that one becomes wise by inquiring into the elements, sense fields, dependent origination, and what is possible and impossible.

children.title: At Isigili
children.description: Reflecting on the changes that even geographical features undergo, the Buddha then recounts the names of sages of the past who have lived in Mount Isigili near Rājagaha.

children.title: The Great Forty
children.description: A discourse on the prerequisites of right samādhi that emphasizes the interrelationship and mutual support of all the factors of the eightfold path.

children.title: Mindfulness of Breathing
children.description: Surrounded by many well-practiced mendicants, the Buddha teaches mindfulness of breathing in detail, showing how it relates to the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: Mindfulness of the Body
children.description: This focuses on the first aspect of mindfulness meditation, the observation of the body. This set of practices, simple as they seem, have far-reaching benefits.

children.title: Rebirth by Choice
children.description: The Buddha explains how one can make a wish to be reborn in different realms.

children.title: 3. Emptiness
children.description: Named after the first discourses, which deal with emptiness, this chapter presents less analytical and more narrative texts.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse on Emptiness
children.description: The Buddha describes his own practice of the meditation on emptiness.

children.title: The Longer Discourse on Emptiness
children.description: A group of mendicants have taken to socializing too much, so the Buddha teaches on the importance of seclusion in order to enter fully into emptiness.

children.title: Incredible and Amazing
children.description: Venerable Ānanda is invited by the Buddha to speak on the Buddha’s amazing qualities, and proceeds to list a series of apparently miraculous events accompanying his birth. The Buddha caps it off by explaining what he thinks is really amazing about himself.

children.title: With Bakkula
children.description: Venerable Bakkula, regarded as the healthiest of the mendicants, explains to an old friend his strict and austere practice. The unusual form of this discourse suggests it was added to the canon some time after the Buddha’s death.

children.title: The Level of the Tamed
children.description: A young monk is unable to persuade a prince of the blessings of peace of mind. The Buddha offers similes based on training an elephant that would have been successful, as this was a field the prince was familiar with.

children.title: With Bhūmija
children.description: Success in the spiritual life does not depend on any vows you may or may not make, but on whether you practice well.

children.title: With Anuruddha
children.description: A lay person becomes confused when encouraged to develop the “limitless” and “expansive” liberations, and asks Venerable Anuruddha to explain whether they are the same or different.

children.title: Corruptions
children.description: A second discourse set at the quarrel of Kosambi, this depicts the Buddha, having failed to achieve reconciliation between the disputing mendicants, leaving the monastery. He spends time in the wilderness before encountering an inspiring community of practicing monks. There he discusses in detail obstacles to meditation that he encountered before awakening.

children.title: The Foolish and the Astute
children.description: A fool suffers both in this life and the next, while the astute benefits in both respects.

children.title: Messengers of the Gods
children.description: Expanding on the previous, this discourse contains the most detailed descriptions of the horrors of hell.

children.title: 4. Analysis
children.description: A series of discourses presented as technical analyses of shorter teachings.

children.title: One Fine Night
children.description: This discourse opens with a short but powerful set of verses extolling the benefits of insight into the here and now, followed by an explanation.

children.title: Ānanda and One Fine Night
children.description: The same discourse as MN 131, but spoken by Venerable Ānanda.

children.title: Mahākaccāna and One Fine Night
children.description: The verses from MN 131 are explained in a different way by Venerable Mahakaccāna.

children.title: Lomasakaṅgiya and One Fine Night
children.description: A monk who does not know the verses from MN 131 is encouraged by a deity to learn them.

children.title: The Shorter Analysis of Deeds
children.description: The Buddha explains to a brahmin how your deeds in past lives affect you in this life.

children.title: The Longer Analysis of Deeds
children.description: Confronted with an overly simplistic version of his own teachings, the Buddha emphasizes the often overlooked nuances and qualifications in how karma plays out.

children.title: The Analysis of the Six Sense Fields
children.description: A detailed analysis of the six senses and the relation to emotional and cognitive processes.

children.title: A Summary Recital and its Analysis
children.description: The Buddha gives a brief and enigmatic statement on the ways consciousness may become attached. Venerable Mahākaccāna is invited by the mendicants to draw out the implications.

children.title: The Analysis of No Strife
children.description: Achieving peace is no simple matter. The Buddha explains how to avoid conflict through contentment, right speech, understanding pleasure, and not insisting on local conventions.

children.title: The Analysis of the Elements
children.description: While staying overnight in a potter’s workshop, the Buddha has a chance encounter with a monk who does not recognize him. They have a long and profound discussion based on the four elements. This is one of the most insightful and moving discourses in the canon.

children.title: The Analysis of the Truths
children.description: Expanding on the Buddha’s first sermon, Venerable Sāriputta gives a detailed explanation of the four noble truths.

children.title: The Analysis of Religious Donations
children.description: When his step-mother Mahāpajāpatī wishes to offer him a robe for his personal use, the Buddha encourages her to offer it to the entire Saṅgha instead. He goes on to explain that the best kind of offering to the Saṅgha is one given to the dual community of monks and nuns, headed by the Buddha.

children.title: 5. Six Senses
children.description: Most discourses in this chapter deal with the six sense fields.

children.title: Advice to Anāthapiṇḍika
children.description: As the great lay disciple Anāthapiṇḍika lies dying, Venerable Sāriputta visits him and gives a powerful teaching on non-attachment.

children.title: Advice to Channa
children.description: The monk Channa is suffering a painful terminal illness and wishes to take his own life.

children.title: Advice to Puṇṇa
children.description: On the eve of his departure to a distant country, full of wild and unpredictable people, Venerable Puṇṇa is asked by the Buddha how he would respond if attacked there.

children.title: Advice from Nandaka
children.description: When asked to teach the nuns, Venerable Nandaka proceeds by inviting them to engage with his discourse and ask if there is anything that needs further explanation.

children.title: The Shorter Advice to Rāhula
children.description: The Buddha takes Rāhula with him to a secluded spot in order to lead him on to liberation.

children.title: Six By Six
children.description: The Buddha analyzes the six senses from six perspectives, and demonstrates the emptiness of all of them.

children.title: The Great Discourse on What Relates to the Six Sense Fields
children.description: Explains how insight into the six senses is integrated with the eightfold path and leads to liberation.

children.title: With the People of Nagaravinda
children.description: In discussion with a group of householders, the Buddha helps them to distinguish those spiritual practitioners who are truly worthy of respect.

children.title: The Purification of Alms
children.description: The Buddha notices Venerable Sāriputta’s glowing complexion, which is the result of his deep meditation. He then presents a series of reflections by which a mendicant can be sure that they are worthy of their alms-food.

children.title: The Development of the Faculties
children.description: A brahmin teacher advocates that purification of the senses consists in simply avoiding seeing and hearing things. The Buddha explains that it is not about avoiding sense experience, but understanding it and learning to not be affected by sense experience.

children.title: 1. Verses
children.description: The “Book With Verses” is the first of the five books of the Linked Discourses. It is divided into eleven saṁyuttas or “sections”, with a total of 271 suttas. Most of these are further subdivided into vaggas of ten suttas. The word vagga is thus used of both the major overarching “book” and the subsidiary “chapter”. Each of the suttas in this collection contains verse with a prose narrative structure, although in many cases the prose has been omitted through abbreviation. Where most of the Saṁyutta is organized around subject matter, here the organizational principle is people. Each saṁyutta contains conversation involving the Buddha or his disciples with a different person or kind of person, such as gods, kings, nuns, or brahmins. A typical sutta has a bare narrative framework, where someone comes to the Buddha and utters a verse, and the Buddha replies with a better one. In some cases, notably the Sakkasaṁyutta, the narrative element is developed into a lively exchange. Some of the texts in this collection are well known and widely quoted, such as the invitation of Brahmā or the nun Vajirā’s simile of the person as a chariot. Most of the suttas here have parallels in the Chinese Saṁyuktāgama translations; the partial translations SA 2 and SA 3 include Sagāthāvagga material. In addition, many of the verses have parallels elsewhere throughout the Buddhist literature in all languages.

children.title: 1. Deities
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Deities” contains 81 discourses, each one of which depicts the Buddha in conversation with a deity. Typically a deity approaches the Buddha in the monastery at Sāvatthī, illuminating the night with their glory. The deity addresses the Buddha with a question or verse, which may be a praise, a challenge, a riddle, or simply a reflection. The Buddha responds, usually elevating the discourse to a higher plane. As always in Buddhist texts, a deity is not worshiped, but is regarded as a temporary rebirth in a higher plane; the deities learn from the Buddha, not the other way around. In most cases, the narrative framework is slim, and after a while it is dropped entirely, retaining just the verses. There’s no particular theme to the discourses, which range from the simple to the profound.

children.title: Crossing the Flood
children.description: The Buddha crossed the flood of suffering by neither standing nor swimming.

children.title: Liberation
children.description: Freedom comes when we end attachment to rebirth.

children.title: Led On
children.description: Life is short, so we should drop the world’s bait.

children.title: Time Flies
children.description: Time flies, so we should drop the world’s bait.

children.title: Cut How Many?
children.description: A cryptic set of questions, which the Buddha answers equally cryptically.

children.title: Awake
children.description: How many are awake while others are asleep?

children.title: Not Comprehending
children.description: Those who comprehend the teachings live smooth amid the rough.

children.title: Very Confused
children.description: Those who are unconfused live smooth amid the rough.

children.title: Fond of Conceit
children.description: Unless you give up conceit you’ll be trapped in the domain of Death.

children.title: Wilderness
children.description: Spiritual practitioners have clear complexions, despite their simple life.

children.title: The Garden of Delight
children.description: Even the divine Garden of Delight is impermanent.

children.title: Delight
children.description: We think our attachments bring us happiness, but they really bring sorrow.

children.title: There’s Nothing Like a Child
children.description: Like many of these discourses, here the Buddha repeats a god’s verses with a subtle twist towards the Dhamma.

children.title: Aristocrats
children.description: A god’s worldly values are improved by the Buddha’s version.

children.title: Whispering
children.description: The quiet murmuring of the jungle can be scary—but not to the Buddha.

children.title: Sleepiness and Sloth
children.description: Laziness is an obstruction to the path.

children.title: Hard to Do
children.description: Life is hard for an unrestrained ascetic; they should draw in their thoughts like a tortoise.

children.title: Conscience
children.description: Does anyone have a sense of conscience and shame?

children.title: Little Hut
children.description: Do you have a little hut and a little nest—or are you free?

children.title: With Samiddhi
children.description: A deity tries to tempt a monk to first enjoy sensual pleasures and then go forth.

children.title: A Sword
children.description: A mendicant should live as if their head was on fire.

children.title: Impact
children.description: The evil you do hurts yourself.

children.title: A Tangle
children.description: This generation is all tangled up like a nest of matted hair. But who can unravel the tangle?

children.title: Shielding the Mind
children.description: One should rein in the mind, but only from that which is evil.

children.title: A Perfected One
children.description: If a perfected one has gone beyond all sense of self, would they still refer to themselves as “I”?

children.title: Lamps
children.description: How many lights are there that light up the world?

children.title: Streams
children.description: The stream of rebirth stops flowing when name and form ceases.

children.title: Affluent
children.description: Even the rich are full of greed for more—is there anyone free of greed?

children.title: Four Wheels
children.description: A riddle on the topic of escape.

children.title: Antelope Calves
children.description: The Buddha is asked how to find release from suffering.

children.title: Virtuous
children.description: A series of deities give verses praising association with the good, and the Buddha gives his own response.

children.title: Stinginess
children.description: A series of deities give verses praising generosity, and the Buddha gives his own response.

children.title: Good
children.description: A series of deities give verses praising generosity, and the Buddha gives his own response, saying that practice of the Dhamma goes beyond this.

children.title: There Are None
children.description: Two deities exchange verses with the Buddha on how sensual pleasures give rise to suffering.

children.title: Fault-Finding Deities
children.description: Some deities come to find fault with the Buddha. He responds to their critique, which stimulates a further discussion on wrong-doing and forgiveness.

children.title: Faith
children.description: A series of Satullapa gods address the Buddha with verses on various topics. The identifications of the verses in this unclear, and comparison with the Chinese parallels suggests the Pali may have suffered textual loss.

children.title: The Congregation
children.description: A vast congregation of deities assembles to see the Buddha and the Saṅgha at Kapilavatthu.

children.title: A Splinter
children.description: A series of deities praise the Buddha’s resilience and composure when his foot is injured by a stone.

children.title: With Pajjunna’s Daughter (1st)
children.description: A goddess identifying herself as Kokanadā claims to confirm with her own experience the Buddha’s teachings on karma.

children.title: With Pajjunna’s Daughter (2nd)
children.description: A goddess identified as Kokanada, possibly the sister of the previous, sums up the teaching in a pithy verse.

children.title: On Fire
children.description: A deity recites to the Buddha some verses

children.title: Giving What?
children.description: Different kinds of gifts have different purposes.

children.title: Food
children.description: Gods and humans love to eat, so what kind of being does not like food?

children.title: One Root
children.description: A single verse in the form of a Dhamma riddle.

children.title: Peerless
children.description: A verse in praise of the Buddha.

children.title: Nymphs
children.description: To escape from the Forest of Delusion, one needs the vehicle of the Dhamma.

children.title: Planters
children.description: For those who give the gift of a monastery, merit always grows.

children.title: Jeta’s Grove
children.description: Verses in praise of the Jetavana monastery, the Dhamma, and venerable Sāriputta, apparently spoken by the deity Anāthapiṇḍika.

children.title: Stingy
children.description: The Buddha is asked about the future destiny of people who are stingy and those who are generous.

children.title: With Ghaṭīkāra
children.description: Ghaṭīkāra, a disciple of the former Buddha Kassapa, comes to the Buddha and speaks of his past life, and of the attainments of six friends.

children.title: Old Age
children.description: Morality is good even in old age.

children.title: Getting Old
children.description: Morality is good when it doesn’t decay.

children.title: A Friend
children.description: Things that are friends in this life and the next.

children.title: Grounds
children.description: What is it that sustains various beings? Unusually, this verse lacks a “Dhamma” counterpart.

children.title: Gives Birth (1st)
children.description: A person is created by craving and fears suffering.

children.title: Gives Birth (2nd)
children.description: A person is created by craving and is not freed from suffering

children.title: Gives Birth (3rd)
children.description: A person is created by craving and their destiny is shaped by their deeds.

children.title: Deviation
children.description: What is the wrong path?

children.title: A Partner
children.description: A person’s true companion is their faith.

children.title: A Poet
children.description: A pair of verses on the nature of poetry, and lacking a Dhamma counterpart.

children.title: Name
children.description: “Name” weighs everything down.

children.title: Mind
children.description: The mind leads the world around and controls it all.

children.title: Craving
children.description: The mind leads the world around and craving controls it.

children.title: Fetter
children.description: The world is fettered by craving.

children.title: Bonds
children.description: The world is bound by craving.

children.title: Beaten Down
children.description: The world is afflicted with death and old age, and burning with desire.

children.title: Ensnared
children.description: The world is caught by craving and built on suffering.

children.title: Fastened Shut
children.description: The world is shut in by death.

children.title: Desire
children.description: The world is bound by desire.

children.title: The World
children.description: A Dhamma riddle whose answer, enigmatically, is “six”.

children.title: Slain
children.description: The killing of anger is the only killing praised by the noble ones.

children.title: A Chariot
children.description: What is the sign or token of a chariot, a fire, a nation, and a woman?

children.title: Wealth
children.description: A series of questions on what is best.

children.title: Rain
children.description: A series of questions asked by one deity, answered by another, and then given a better answer by the Buddha.

children.title: Afraid
children.description: Why is it that, though the path has been taught, people still fear?

children.title: Getting Old
children.description: A series of questions on the path.

children.title: Authority
children.description: A series of questions on diverse matters.

children.title: Desire
children.description: What is it that one should not give away?

children.title: Provisions
children.description: A series of questions on diverse topics.

children.title: Lamp
children.description: A series of questions on diverse topics.

children.title: Free of Strife
children.description: A series of questions on diverse kinds of people

children.title: 2. Godlings
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Gods” contains 30 discourses, each one of which depicts the Buddha in conversation with a god. Here the term devaputta is used, rather than devatā in the previous saṁyutta. The difference is purely nominal and there is no difference in the meaning. The style of discourses is similar to the “Linked Discourses on Deities”, although here there is a greater emphasis on the theme of renunciation. A number of these discourses are regularly recited in modern Theravāda; the Tāyana verses on diligent striving at SN 2.8 are often recited by monastics, while the discourses on the sun and the moon (SN 2.9 and SN 2.10) are popular protection chants, which are also found in Tibetan.

children.title: With Kassapa (1st)
children.description: A deity named Kassapa comes to the Buddha and speaks of the training of a mendicant in seclusion and right speech.

children.title: With Kassapa (2nd)
children.description: The deity Kassapa speaks of how a mendicant should be a meditator, peaceful and free.

children.title: With Māgha
children.description: The god Māgha asks the Buddha about what one should slay in order to sleep well and be without sorrow.

children.title: With Maghada
children.description: The deity Māgadha asks the Buddha how many sources of light there are in the world. The Buddha speaks of five lights, but the Buddha is the best of them.

children.title: With Dāmali
children.description: Dāmali the god suggests that a true brahmin must strive to abandon desire. The Buddha disagrees, saying that a true holy one has already completed their work.

children.title: With Kāmada
children.description: The deity Kāmada addresses the Buddha with a series of cryptic statements lamenting the difficulty of spiritual practice. The Buddha agrees, but points out that true practitioners do it even though it’s hard.

children.title: With Pañcālacaṇḍa
children.description: Pañcālacaṇḍa praises the Buddha for finding the opening amid the confinement of the world. But the Buddha affirms that anyone with mindfulness and stillness may find such an escape.

children.title: With Tāyana
children.description: Tāyana, a deity who was in a past life was a leader of a non-Buddhist sect, speaks a series of verses in praise of strenuous exertion and discipline. These famous verses are commonly recited by Theravadin monks.

children.title: The Moon
children.description: In a parable of a lunar eclipse, the moon god Candimā is swallowed by the demon lord Rāhu. Candimā appeals to the Buddha, who tells Rāhu to let go. This sutta is recited as a protection verse.

children.title: The Sun
children.description: In a parable of a solar eclipse, the sun god Suriya is swallowed by the demon lord Rāhu. Suriya appeals to the Buddha, who tells Rāhu to let go. This sutta is recited as a protection verse.

children.title: With Candimasa
children.description: The deity Candimasa says that those who practice absorption will surely find escape. The Buddha adds that they must also be diligent and discard flaws.

children.title: With Vishnu
children.description: The deity Veṇhu celebrates the joy of those who follow the Buddha’s teaching. The Buddha affirms that such will escape death. Veṇhu is the Pali spelling of Sanskrit Viṣṇu, and this marks a rare appearance of a god of this name in the early texts.

children.title: With Dīghalaṭṭhi
children.description: Dīghalaṭṭhi the god comes to the Buddha at Rājagaha and praises a mendicant who is a meditator.

children.title: With Nandana
children.description: The deity Nandana asks the Buddha who is virtuous, wise, beyond suffering, worshiped by the gods themselves. The Buddha replies that such a person is an arahant.

children.title: With Candana
children.description: Candana asks who crosses the flood. The Buddha replies that it is one who is virtuous , wise, peaceful, and beyond attachment to rebirth.

children.title: With Vāsudatta
children.description: The deity Vasudatta says that a mendicant should live like their hair is on fire so as to give up lust. The Buddha changes his verse to emphasize giving up attachment to self.

children.title: With Subrahmā
children.description: Subrahmā the god asks for the escape from fear. The Buddha says there is no escape from fear without letting go of everything.

children.title: With Kakudha
children.description: At Sāketa the god Kakudha asks the Buddha if he delights or sorrows. The Buddha replies that since he has no attachments he neither delights nor sorrows.

children.title: With Uttara
children.description: The god Uttara speaks of the transience of life, saying one should do good to be reborn in a happy future life. The Buddha replies that one should let go attachment.

children.title: With Anāthapiṇḍika
children.description: A deity who had been the Buddha’s supporter Anāthapiṇḍika in his former life comes to Buddha and speaks verses in celebration of the Jeta’s Grove monastery—which he had offered for the Buddha’s use—good deeds, the Dhamma, and Venerable Sāriputta.

children.title: With Shiva
children.description: The deity Siva says one should associate only with the good, and this will lead to happiness. The Buddha adds that associating with the good leads to the end of suffering. Siva is the Pali spelling of Sanskrit Śiva, and this marks a rare appearance of a god of this name in the early texts.

children.title: With Khema
children.description: The deity Khema utters a series of verses in praise of good deeds. The Buddha responds with a simile for someone who departs the path of the good.

children.title: With Serī
children.description: The deity Serī speaks of how everyone loves food., to which the Buddha responds with verses in praise of giving. Serī speaks of his own generosity in a past life.

children.title: With Ghaṭīkāra
children.description: The deity Ghaṭīkāra speaks of the seven mendicants reborn in the Aviha realm. The sutta is similar to SN 1.50.

children.title: With Jantu
children.description: Some monks in Kosala fell into negligence, and were admonished by the deity Jantu.

children.title: With Rohitassa
children.description: Rohitassa asks the Buddha if it is possible to reach the end of the world by traveling. The Buddha says no; and Rohitassa tells of how in a past life as a seer he had tried to accomplish this very feat and failed. The Buddha says the end of the world is found in this body.

children.title: With Nanda
children.description: Nanda speaks of the transience of life, saying one should do good to be reborn in a happy future life. The Buddha replies that one should let go attachment.

children.title: With Nandivisāla
children.description: The god Nandivisāla gives an elaborate metaphor for the body, and asks how to escape from it.

children.title: With Susīma
children.description: The Buddha asks Ānanda if he likes Sāriputta, and when he replies that he does, the god Susīma and his assembly appear, rejoicing in Sāriputta’s praises, and radiating in lustrous colors.

children.title: The Disciples of Various Monastics of Other Religions
children.description: A series of deities who had formerly been ascetics in the non-Buddhist sects came to the Buddha, speaking verses in praise—or occasional criticism—of their former teachers

children.title: 3. King Pasenadi of Kosala
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with the Kosalan” contains 25 discourses featuring King Pasenadi of Kosala. Pasenadi shines through in the early texts as a complex human figure, one with foibles and foolishness, but with a great devotion and capacity to grow. He appears frequently elsewhere in the suttas; MN 87 tells the story of how Queen Mallikā led him to the Dhamma. Here Mallikā appears again, and in SN 3.8 she shows how she is not afraid to challenge her king. The suttas in this collection typically set the verses in substantive prose narratives, illustrating the struggles and problems that beset a king intent on Dhamma who must nonetheless rule in a world with spies, sacrifices, punishments, wars, and the many temptations of royal life.

children.title: Young
children.description: King Pasenadi meets the Buddha for the first time. He wonders how the Buddha can claim to be awakened when he is still so young. The Buddha teaches him four things that should not be looked down on for their youth.

children.title: A Person
children.description: Pasenadi asks of the things that cause suffering when they arise in oneself.

children.title: Old Age and Death
children.description: Pasenadi asks if anything that is born can escape from old age and death.

children.title: Loved
children.description: Reporting on a reflection that arose while on retreat, Pasenadi says that those who do bad deeds treat themselves as enemy. The Buddha expresses his agreement in verse.

children.title: Self-Protected
children.description: Even if protected by an entire army, one who does bad deeds is still unprotected.

children.title: Few
children.description: There are few in the world who do not become negligent and complacent once they obtain material luxuries.

children.title: Judgment
children.description: Pasenadi laments how in his judgment hall he sees people lying all the time for the sake of sensual pleasures.

children.title: With Queen Mallikā
children.description: Pasandi asks Queen Mallikā who is most dear. They both agree that the one most dear is oneself, and the Buddha agrees.

children.title: Sacrifice
children.description: A great sacrifice involving the slaughter of many animals was being prepared for King Pasenadi. The Buddha condemns such sacrifices and says a fruitful sacrifice involves a blameless and harmless offering.

children.title: Shackles
children.description: When many people are put in chains by Pasenadi, the matter is reported to the Buddha.

children.title: Seven Matted-Hair Ascetics
children.description: A diverse group of ascetics passes by, and Pasenadi asks the Buddha if any of them are perfected ones. The Buddha says it is not easy for one such as Pasenadi to judge the spiritual achievements of others. Pasenadi reveals that the men are, in fact, his spies.

children.title: Five Kings
children.description: Five kings including Pasenadi are enjoying themselves and wonder which of the senses affords the highest pleasure. They ask the Buddha, who replies that it is subjective, depending on a persons preferences. Inspired, the laymen Candanaṅgalika offers a verse in praise of the Buddha.

children.title: A Bucketful of Rice
children.description: In what is probably the world’s first weight loss diet, when Pasenadi shows up overweight and out of breath, the Buddha advises him to cut down his eating. He gives a verse to one of the king’s attendants, and asks him to recite it whenever the king is eating.

children.title: Battle (1st)
children.description: Pasenadi loses a battle against his nephew King Ajātasattu of Magadha.

children.title: Battle (2nd)
children.description: In a battle subsequent to SN 3.14, Pasenadi defeats Ajātasattu and takes him prisoner. Acting compassionately, he confiscates Ajātasattu’s military assets but releases him alive.

children.title: A Daughter
children.description: Pasenadi is disappointed to hear that Queen Mallikā has given birth to a daughter. But the Buddha consoles him, saying a woman may turn out better than a man.

children.title: Diligence
children.description: Pasenadi asks the Buddha if there is one thing that secures benefit both in this life and the next.

children.title: Good Friends
children.description: In answer to Pasenadi’s praise of good friendship, the Buddha recounts an earlier conversation with Ānanda on the topic. He then goes on to say that when one has good friends, it is important to develop diligence.

children.title: Childless (1st)
children.description: A wealthy man dies childless, having not enjoyed his riches. The Buddha says that wealth should be properly enjoyed and shared.

children.title: Childless (2nd)
children.description: A wealthy man dies childless, having not enjoyed his riches. The Buddha tells of how in the time of a solitary Buddha of the past named Tagarasikhī, a householder made an offering but later regretted it.

children.title: Individuals
children.description: The Buddha teaches Pasenadi of four kinds of person, going from dark to dark, dark to light, light to dark, and light to light.

children.title: Grandmother
children.description: Pasenadi laments the death of his aged grandmother.

children.title: The World
children.description: How many things give rise to suffering in oneself?

children.title: Archery
children.description: “Where should I give” and “Where is a gift is most fruitful” are two different questions.

children.title: The Simile of the Mountain
children.description: Old age and death roll in upon all like mountains approaching from the four directions, crushing all in their path

children.title: 4. Māra
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Māra” contains 25 discourses featuring Māra, the god of temptation, deceit, and death. In these discourses, Māra typically appears in some terrifying or beguiling form, hoping to disturb the Buddha, or else he challenges the Buddha with a critical verse. Like the previous section, the narrative prose here is substantive. The Buddha recognizes him at once and exposes his deceit in a verse. Māra also appears throughout the next collection, where the nuns take him on.

children.title: Mortification
children.description: Māra accuses the Buddha of having abandoned the path of true austerity.

children.title: In the Form of an Elephant King
children.description: Māra manifests before the Buddha in the form of a ferocious elephant in order to scare him.

children.title: Beautiful
children.description: Māra tries to scare the Buddha by taking on shifting forms both beautiful and hideous.

children.title: Māra’s Snares (1st)
children.description: When the Buddha explains to the mendicants how he realized freedom, Māra claims he is still trapped.

children.title: Māra’s Snares (2nd)
children.description: When the Buddha explains to the mendicants how he has realized freedom, and so have his mendicant followers, Māra claims he is still trapped.

children.title: A Serpent
children.description: Māra manifests as a huge serpent, but the Buddha is unshaken.

children.title: Sleeping
children.description: After meditating all night, the Buddha lies down to sleep at dawn, and Māra scolds him for being lazy.

children.title: Delighting
children.description: The Buddha and Māra exchange verses on whether attachments are a source of delight or suffering.

children.title: Lifespan (1st)
children.description: Though the Buddha says that life is short, Māra says it is long.

children.title: Lifespan (2nd)
children.description: Though the Buddha says that life is short, Māra says it is long.

children.title: Boulders
children.description: Māra smashes boulders in an attempt to scare the Buddha.

children.title: Lion
children.description: Māra criticizes the Buddha for his lion’s roar, asserting that the Buddha is not in fact peerless.

children.title: A Splinter
children.description: The Buddha rests after being struck by stone splinters, and Māra criticizes him for being lazy.

children.title: Appropriate
children.description: Māra discourages the Buddha from teaching, warning him that he will become corrupted by favoritism.

children.title: A Mental Snare
children.description: Māra threatens the Buddha with a “mental snare” in the sky.

children.title: The Alms Bowls
