children.description: While the mendicants are listening to the teachings, Māra takes the form of an ox and looks as if he will break their almsbowls.

children.title: The Six Fields of Contact
children.description: While the mendicants are listening to the teachings, Māra makes an awful roar to distract them.

children.title: Alms Food
children.description: Māra ensures that the Buddha fails to get alms, but the Buddha is happy to feed on joy.

children.title: A Farmer
children.description: While the mendicants are listening to the teachings, Māra takes the form of a farmer looking for lost oxen and addresses the Buddha.

children.title: Ruling
children.description: The Buddha wonders whether it is possible to rule justly, without violence. Māra appears and encourages the Buddha to pursue such a path.

children.title: Several
children.description: Māra approaches some young mendicants as an old brahmin, and tries to tempt them with talk of the pleasures of youth.

children.title: With Samiddhi
children.description: Māra repeatedly pesters the monk Samiddhi when he is on retreat. The Buddha encourages him, until eventually Samiddhi is able to recognize Māra for himself.

children.title: With Godhika
children.description: Venerable Godhika finds himself repeatedly falling away from his meditation attainments due to severe illness. Eventually he considers suicide, and Māra tries to get the Buddha to deter him. But the Buddha says Godhika has already attained awakening and has died blamelessly.

children.title: Seven Years of Pursuit
children.description: Māra has tried to distract the Buddha for seven years without success. He laments his failure with the similes of a crab whose limbs are smashed by a group of children, and a crow who tried to eat a stone.

children.title: Māra’s Daughters
children.description: Depressed, Māra laments to his three daughters of his failure to distract the Buddha. So they take on the task themselves, and assume a variety of sensuous forms to tempt him. But they fail too, and Māra castigates them for being so presumptuous

children.title: 5. Nuns
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Nuns” contains 10 discourses describing occasions when various nuns retreat to a forest for meditation, only to be challenged by Māra. The verses here partly overlap with the Therīgāthā, though there are some that are unique to this context, and we also have a prose narrative to flesh out the context. Māra’s challenges are various; sometimes he is sexist, alleging that women are weak in wisdom (SN 5.2). Several of these short texts are among the most frequently quoted of all the suttas.

children.title: With Āḷavikā
children.description: The nun Āḷavikā has entered the Dark Wood seeking seclusion when Māra comes to threaten her, claiming there is no escape and no point in seclusion. She recognizes him instantly and dismisses his taunts, asserting that she is beyond his control.

children.title: With Somā
children.description: When meditating in the Dark Wood, the nun Somā is taunted by Māra, who claims that a mere woman can never see the subtle truth. She rejects him, stating that gender does not matter when one is perceiving deep truths, and telling Māra to go see those still attached to gender.

children.title: With Kisāgotamī
children.description: Māra taunts the nun Kisāgotamī, alleging she is mourning sons and longing for a man. She rejects him, stating that she has no need for men, as she has destroyed the mass of darkness and conquered the army of Death.

children.title: With Vijayā
children.description: Māra comes to the nun Vijayā in the form of a handsome youth and tries to tempt her from her path. But she rejects sensual pleasures, as she delights in subtle meditation and has ended ignorance.

children.title: With Uppalavaṇṇā
children.description: Uppalavaṇṇā is rebuked by Māra, who says a beautiful woman like her should fear rogues when alone in the forest. However, she dismisses such fears, saying she can use her psychic powers to defeat thousands of rogues like him.

children.title: With Cālā
children.description: Māra asks the nun Cālā why she disapproves of rebith. She replies that it necessarily entails suffering.

children.title: With Upacālā
children.description: Māra asks the nun Upacālā where she wishes to be reborn. But as the world everywhere is burning, she rejects all forms of rebirth.

children.title: With Sīsupacālā
children.description: Māra asks the nun Sīsupacālā whose teaching she believes in. She replies that she rejects the various sectarians and follows the Buddha, as his teachings lead to freedom.

children.title: With Selā
children.description: Māra asks the nun Selā about who has created this “puppet”, i.e. the form that has been reincarnated. She replies that there is no creator, but it arises as a result of conditions, like the growing of a seed in a field.

children.title: With Vajirā
children.description: Māra asks the nun Vajirā about who has created this being. Recognizing him, she points out that the word “being” is nothing more than a convention used to designate the aggregates, just as the word “cart” is used when the parts are assembled

children.title: 6. Divinities
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Brahmās” contains 15 discourses featuring high brahmanical deities. Most commonly we meet the “Great Brahmā”, regarded as the creator God, but he is merely one of a class of deities, and here we meet several others. Brahmā is depicted here and elsewhere in early Buddhist texts in a respectful way, regarded as a glorious deity reborn in his realm due to powerful good kamma. As here, he frequently acts as a champion for the Buddhist cause. However, like all the gods, he is still under the influence of delusion and has nor escaped rebirth.

children.title: The Appeal of the Divinity
children.description: After his awakening, the Buddha hesitated to teach, thinking that the Dhamma is too subtle for people to understand. But the high divinity Brahmā Sahampati appears and encourages him to teach, pointing out that there are some with “little dust in their eyes” who will understand.

children.title: Respect
children.description: After his awakening, the Buddha reflects that one should live with reverence; but who is he to revere, since he is fully awakened? He realizes that he should live revering the Dhamma. Brahmā Sahampati appears and agrees with him, saying that this is how all Buddhas of past and future live too.

children.title: With Brahmadeva
children.description: Brahmā Sahampati appears before a woman who is a devotee of his, and tells her to offer food instead to her son, a Buddhist monk, as Brahmās don’t eat the food she offers.

children.title: With Baka the Divinity
children.description: Baka the Brahmā conceives the wrong view that his status is permanent and imperishable. The Buddha goes to dissuade him, and they have an exchange in verse, with the Buddha telling Baka of his past lives.

children.title: A Certain Divinity
children.description: An unnamed brahmā god thinks to himself that he is so powerful no asectic can approach him. The Buddha goes straight to his realm and appears wrapped in flame above his head. Mahāmoggallāna and several other disciples follow him. The brahmā and his retinue are sutiably impressed.

children.title: The Negligent Divinity
children.description: The brahmās Subrahmā and Suddhāvāsa note that a fellow-brahmā is living in negligence, overly impressed with his own glory, so they go to shake him from his complacence.

children.title: About Kokālika
children.description: The brahmās Subrahmā and Suddhāvāsa come to the Buddha’s hut and speak on the monk Kokālika, a follower of Devadatta.

children.title: About Katamorakatissaka
children.description: The brahmās Subrahmā and Suddhāvāsa come to the Buddha’s hut and speak on the monk Katamorakatissaka, a follower of Devadatta.

children.title: With the Divinity Tudu
children.description: The brahmā Tudu tries to persuade Kokālika to have faith in Sāriputta and Moggallāna, but Kokālika wants none of it.

children.title: With Kokālika
children.description: Kokālika goes to the Buddha and criticizes Sāriputta and Moggallāna. But having deliberately slandered such great monks, he dies and Brahmā Sahampati informs the Buddha he has been reborn in hell. The Buddha gives a memorable simile of the length of life in hell.

children.title: With Sanaṅkumāra
children.description: Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra appears to the Buddha and asserts that the aristocrat or khattiya is the best caste, but the Buddha is the best of people.

children.title: About Devadatta
children.description: Brahmā Sahampati, referring to Devadatta, points out that honors destroy a scoundrel.

children.title: At Andhakavinda
children.description: Brahmā Sahampati appears to the Buddha and speaks in praise of the renunciates staying fearless in the deep forest, and celebrates the many who have found freedom.

children.title: About Aruṇavatī
children.description: The Buddha tells a story of the past Buddha Sikhī and his disciple Abhibhū. They visit a brahmā realm where they perform many astounding feats and give teachings.

children.title: Full Extinguishment
children.description: After the Buddha became finally extinguished, Brahmā Sahampati led a series of distinguished beings who uttered verses in commemoration

children.title: 7. Brahmins
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Brahmins” contains 22 discourses featuring the Buddha interacting with various members of the brahmanical caste. The brahmins were the custodians of the brahmanical scriptures and traditions, and saw themselves as the spiritual elite of society. A central platform of the Buddha’s ethical teaching was that one’s worth is determined by one’s deeds, not by caste. This was a direct challenge to brahmanical authority, and a number of discourses have an understandably combative air to them. But the brahmins were a diverse community, and it’s just as common to find them relating to the Buddha with respect and gratitude.

children.title: With Dhanañjānī
children.description: When a brahmin lady expresses her confidence in the Triple Gem, her husband is annoyed. She encourages him to visit the Buddha, who soothes his anger.

children.title: With Bhāradvāja the Rude
children.description: A brahmin visits the Buddha and unleashes a tirade of abuse, but the Buddha refuses to accept it, showing that he remains free of anger.

children.title: With Bhāradvāja the Fiend
children.description: A brahmin visits the Buddha and abuses him, but the Buddha responds only with patience.

children.title: With Bhāradvāja the Bitter
children.description: Hearing that a brahmin had gone forth under the Buddha, another brahmin was upset. But once again the Buddha calms him down, pointing out that anger only harms oneself.

children.title: Harmless
children.description: A brahmin called “Harmless” visits the Buddha, who teaches him the true meaning of harmlessness.

children.title: With Bhāradvāja of the Matted Hair
children.description: A brahmin with matted hair asks the Buddha how we can become disentangled. This short set of verses became one of the most important in all of Theravāda Buddhism when it was used as the cornerstone of the commentarial treatise Visuddhimagga (Path of Purification).

children.title: With Bhāradvāja the Pure
children.description: The brahmin Suddhika makes the strikingly Buddhist assertion that mere austerities don’t lead to purity; only knowledge and conduct do.

children.title: With Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper
children.description: A brahmin conducting a fire sacrifice invites the Buddha to accept the blessed milk-rice, claiming that the Buddha is a true brahmin.

children.title: With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā
children.description: A brahmin conducting a fire sacrifice wishes to offer the sacrificial cake. He sees the Buddha meditating and wants to give it to him, but hesitates when he realizes he is a shaven-headed ascetic. He asks the Buddha’s caste, but the Buddha argues that conduct is the important thing, not caste. The Buddha gives a metaphorical reinterpretation of the elements of brahmanical ritual.

children.title: Many Daughters
children.description: A brahmin is searching for his lost oxen when he sees the Buddha meditating peacefully in the forest. He laments the many sorrows of his life, celebrating the Buddha’s happiness and freedom from such sorrows.

children.title: With Bhāradvāja the Farmer
children.description: A brahmin farmer criticizes the Buddha for failing to produce food, merely living off the work of others. But the Buddha shows that his true work is spiritual.

children.title: With Udaya
children.description: A brahmin complains when the Buddha visits for alms again and again. The Buddha takes the chance to point out that all natural phenomena repeat in cycles, and only an awakened one escapes the cycle.

children.title: With Devahita
children.description: The Buddha is ill and sends his attendant monk Upavāṇa to fetch some hot water. A brahmin gives him not just water, but also molasses to ease his stomach. Later the brahmin visits the Buddha to discuss generosity.

children.title: A well-to-do brahmin
children.description: A brahmin in shabby clothes has been kicked out of his home by ungrateful sons. The Buddha gives him a verse to recite in the village council, comparing his faithless sons to his trusty wooden staff. Ashamed, the sons take back their father, bathe and dress him.

children.title: Stuck-Up
children.description: A stuck-up brahmin listening to the Buddha teach is awestruck when the Buddha appears to read his mind. To the surprise of the crowd, he bows and kisses the Buddha’s feet. The Buddha tells him to take his seat, and they exchange verses on the topic of conceit.

children.title: The Contraphile
children.description: A brahmin who loves to contradict everyone approaches the Buddha thinking to challenge him. But when he hears the Buddha speak, he cannot find anything to contradict.

children.title: The Builder
children.description: A brahmin is enjoying his work in the woods. Seeing the Buddha in meditation, he wonders what sort of work the Buddha enjoys.

children.title: Collecting Firewood
children.description: Some brahmin students are collecting firewood when they see the Buddha in meditation. They return and inform their teacher, who visits the Buddha to ask him how he is so peaceful in the wild forest.

children.title: The Brahmin Who Provided for His Mother
children.description: A brahmin wonders whether the legitimate seeking of alms is a proper way to support his parents.

children.title: An Almsman
children.description: The Buddha explains that a true mendicant is one who has gone beyond evil.

children.title: With Saṅgārava
children.description: A brahmin believes that by bathing he can wash away his sins. But the Buddha speaks of the Dhamma as a lake for true purification.

children.title: At Khomadussa
children.description: When the Buddha approaches a brahmin council in session, they complain that he is out of order.

children.title: 8. Vaṅgīsa
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Vaṅgīsa” contains 12 discourses with verses spoken by Vaṅgīsa, the most renowned poet of early Buddhism. His verses have a sophistication and personal vulnerability that stamp them as perhaps the most distinctive literary voice of the early texts. Several of these discourses speak of his insecurities and struggles, and how he was helped to overcome them. Others speak from his joyous devotion to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, and of his final triumph.

children.title: Renounced
children.description: Enticed by the sight of beautiful women, the newly ordained monk Vaṅgīsa dispels desire and celebrates his commitment to the spiritual path in verse.

children.title: Dissatisfaction
children.description: Vaṅgīsa is troubled again by lust, but manages to dispel it through his own efforts. His verse speak of the way of the renunciate, letting go of desire and wrong views, and dedicated to ethical conduct and seclusion.

children.title: Good-Hearted
children.description: As a renowned poet, Vaṅgīsa looked down on less skilled mendicants. Ashamed of his conceit, he exhorted himself in verse to be humble and at peace.

children.title: With Ānanda
children.description: Troubled once more by lust, Vaṅgīsa turned to Ānanda for support. Ānanda tells him to shift his perception so that beautiful things no longer seem so.

children.title: Well-Spoken Words
children.description: The Buddha gives a simple teaching on four qualities of good speech. Vaṅgīsa is inspired to utter a more elaborate set of verses on the topic, praising especially the speech of the Buddha that leads to the Deathless.

children.title: With Sāriputta
children.description: Seeing Sāriputta speak on the Dhamma, and the rapt attention of the Saṅgha, Vaṅgīsa comes out with verses in his praise.

children.title: The Invitation to Admonish
children.description: On the Pavāraṇā day at the end of the rains retreat, the Buddha invites the Saṅgha to admonish him. But not only is the Buddha faultless, so are all the 500 monks present. Vaṅgīsa is inspired to utter a elaborate praise of the Buddha.

children.title: Over a Thousand
children.description: Seeing the Buddha speak on the Dhamma, and the rapt attention of the Saṅgha, Vaṅgīsa comes out with verses in his praise. When asked if the verses were spontaneous, he replies that they were, and the Buddha invites him to speak further.

children.title: With Koṇḍañña
children.description: Aññā Koṇḍañña, the very first disciple to realize the Dhamma, comes to visit the Buddha after long in seclusion. Inspired, Vaṅgīsa speaks verses in his praise.

children.title: With Moggallāna
children.description: Vaṅgīsa speaks in praise of Moggallāna and the Saṅgha.

children.title: At Gaggarā
children.description: Vaṅgīsa says the Buddha, like the moon or the sun, outshines the whole world.

children.title: With Vaṅgīsa
children.description: Remembering his past as a wandering poet, Vaṅgīsa celebrates the freedom he has found in the Dhamma

children.title: 9. in the Woods
children.description: The “Linked Discourses in the Woods” contains 14 discourses with verses telling the experiences of certain monks living the woods. Typically the monk is slack or negligent in some way, and a deity appears to call them out and encourage them to greater diligence.

children.title: Seclusion
children.description: A monk in the forest lets his mind drift to thoughts of the lay life, but is warned by a local deity.

children.title: Application
children.description: When a mendicant falls asleep in the middle of the day, a deity tries to rouse them up. But not all is at it seems.

children.title: With Kassapagotta
children.description: A monk named Kassapagotta encounters a hunter in the forest and tries to dissuade him from his violent purpose. But a deity warns him not to waste his time.

children.title: Several Mendicants Set Out Wandering
children.description: When a group of mendicants leave the forest in which they had been staying, the local deities lament their absence.

children.title: With Ānanda
children.description: A deity warns Ānanda about getting too involved with teaching lay folk.

children.title: With Anuruddha
children.description: A former partner of Venerable Anuruddha, now a deity named Jālinī, tries to tempt him with heavenly pleasures. But he has seen a higher happiness.

children.title: With Nāgadatta
children.description: When Venerable Nāgadatta spends too much time in the village, a deity admonishes him.

children.title: The Mistress of the House
children.description: A deity becomes concerned of the gossip about a certain monk who had become close with a family in the village. Taking the form of one of the women of the family, she tries to warn him; but he says a true practitioner is not concerned with gossip.

children.title: A Vajji
children.description: Hearing the sounds of a city festival, a mendicant feels lonely in the forest. A deity comes to give them solace and support.

children.title: Recitation
children.description: When a mendicant gives up their habit of reciting the texts, a deity questions them. But it seems they have now found peace.

children.title: Unskillful Thoughts
children.description: A mendicant plagued by bad thoughts is encouraged by a deity.

children.title: Midday
children.description: A deity speaks of the fearfulness of the murmuring forest. But to a mendicant it seems delightful.

children.title: Undisciplined Faculties
children.description: A group of mendicants in the forest had fallen into bad ways, becoming conceited and confused. A deity came to admonish them, making clear that they were only speaking of the badly behaved, not all mendicants.

children.title: The Thief of Scent
children.description: A mendicant takes a bath in a pond and sniffs a lotus. A deity accuses him of being a “thief of scent”. For a person living a life of purity, even such a small matter is a cause for concern

children.title: 10. Spirits
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Spirits” contains 12 discourses with verses telling the encounters between the Buddha—or in one case the monk Anuruddha—and various spirits (yakkha). The spirits were local deities worshiped in ancient India, of a lower order than the gods and Brahmās. While in later forms of Buddhism, such spirits were typically depicted as malevolent or dangerous, in the early texts they are more ambivalent, and many of them are friendly, merely asking Dhamma questions, or extolling Dhamma virtues like mindfulness. That’s not to say they couldn’t be scary, and several discourses reveal a more ferocious aspect. Particularly interesting is the emphasis on the love that the female spirits feel for their children.

children.title: With Indaka
children.description: A local spirit asks the Buddha how a body is produced if there is no soul.

children.title: Sakka In Name Only
children.description: A spirit tells the Buddha that if he is truly free he should not be instructing others.

children.title: With Spiky
children.description: The spirits Khara and Sūciloma argue about whether the Buddha is a true ascetic or not. They approach him initially with threats, but then ask as to the origin of greed and hate.

children.title: With Maṇibhadda
children.description: The spirit Maṇibhadda speaks in praise of mindfulness, opining that a mindful one is free of hate. The Buddha responds that yes, mindfulness is wonderful, but only through developing love is one free of hate.

children.title: With Sānu
children.description: It seems that the novice Sānu had returned to his home intending to disrobe. To prevent him, a spirit possessed him, encouraging him to pursue the path of good. Sānu’s mother, weeping for her son, also tries to make him stay in robes.

children.title: With Piyaṅkara
children.description: A female spirit hushes her son Piyaṅkara so she can hear the teaching and pursue harmlessness.

children.title: With Punabbasu
children.description: A female spirit hushes her children as she listens to the teaching. But her son Punabbasu says that he had not been talking, as he too wants to learn.

children.title: With Sudatta
children.description: When Anāthapiṇḍika heard that a Buddha had arisen in the world, he rose first thing in the morning to go and visit him. But a mysterious darkness caused him to hesitate, so a spirit repeatedly encouraged him to step forward. Finally he reached the Buddha, and asked if he had slept well.

children.title: With the Nun Sukkā (1st)
children.description: A spirit was full of faith in the nun Sukkā, so he went about the towns and villages encouraging people to listen to her teaching.

children.title: With the Nun Sukkā (2nd)
children.description: A spirit was full of faith in the nun Sukkā, so he went about the towns and villages singing the benefits of giving her offerings.

children.title: With the Nun Cīrā
children.description: A spirit was full of faith in the nun Cirā, so he went about the towns and villages singing the benefits of giving her offerings.

children.title: With Āḷavaka
children.description: The famous story of the spirit Āḷavaka, who tries to bully the Buddha, but is soon persuaded through a surprisingly insightful series of questions and answers. This discourse provided the background for several elaborate legends in the later traditions

children.title: 11. Sakka
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Sakka” contains 25 discourses with verses telling stories involving Sakka, the Lord of the Thirty-Three gods. Many of these discourses are relatively lengthy, featuring substantive prose and extended dialogues in verse. Sakka is shown devoted to the Buddha, defending Buddhist virtues of kindness and forgiveness, even in the waging of war with the demons.

children.title: With Suvīra
children.description: When Sakka, the Lord of Gods, tries to organize a counterattack against the demons, he is frustrated by his lazy general Suvīra. Sakka asks Suvīra how one might get what one wants without effort; but Suvīra apparently believes Sakka can grant any wish he wants. The Buddha emphasizes that if effort is valuable among the gods, how much more so for mendicants.

children.title: With Susīma
children.description: When Sakka, the Lord of Gods, tries to organize a conterattack against the demons, he is frustrated by his lazy general Susīma. Sakka asks Susīma how one might get what one wants without effort; but Susīma apparently believes Sakka can grant any wish he wants. The Buddha emphasizes that if effort is valuable among the gods, how much more so for mendicants.

children.title: The Banner’s Crest
children.description: Sakka rallies his troops with the sight of his banner. But the Buddha points out that the deities, powerful as they are, are not free of fear, but he is. He encourages the mendicants to recollect the Triple Gem to abandon fear.

children.title: With Vepacitti
children.description: In a battle between the gods and the demons, and the demon lord Vepacitti is captured and brought in chains to Sakka’s hall. Vepacitti abuses Sakka, who endures his harsh words in patience. The charioteer Mātali asks whether he is silent out of weakness or fear, but Sakka says there is no point is wasting words arguing with a fool.

children.title: Victory by Good Speech
children.description: The demon lord Vepacitti proposes to Sakka that they engage in a battle of wits in debate rather than war. Vepacitti speaks in praise of forceful punishment, while Sakka stands up for patience and forgiveness.

children.title: Bird Nests
children.description: Fleeing the demon host, Sakka’s chariot risks endangering the nests of little birds in the forest. Rather than render the birds homeless, Sakka instructs his charioteer to turn back, even at the cost of his life.

children.title: Not Betray
children.description: Sakka reflects that one should not harm even one’s enemy. Knowing this, Vepacitti immediately takes advantage of it.

children.title: Verocana, Lord of Titans
children.description: Sakka, lord of gods, and Verocana, lord of demons, approach the Buddha’s hut and speak in praise of effort.

children.title: Seers in the Wilderness
children.description: In days gone by, Sakka, lord of gods, and Vepacitti, lord of demons, visited a hermitage of seers. But Vepacitti behaves rudely, while Sakka honors them. However, the seers beg Sakka to leave, on account of the stink of their unwashed bodies. But he says he loves their smell.

children.title: Seers by the Ocean
children.description: In the past, when battle between the gods and demons loomed, some seers sought out the demon lord Sambara to beg for protection. But due to their devotion to Sakka, he rejected them, so they cursed him.

children.title: Vows
children.description: Sakka achieved his status because of seven vows he kept in the past.

children.title: Sakka’s Names
children.description: Sakka’s many names arose due to the diverse good deeds he did in the past.

children.title: With Mahāli
children.description: Mahāli the Licchavi is skeptical as to whether the Buddha has really seen Sakka.

children.title: Poor
children.description: The gods complain when a poor man is reborn in heaven. But Sakka points out that even though poor, he did many good deeds.

children.title: Delightful
children.description: When Sakka asks what place is truly delightful, the Buddha replies that it is wherever the perfected ones dwell.

children.title: Sponsoring Sacrifice
children.description: When Sakka asks where a gift is most fruitful, the Buddha replies that it is the Saṅgha.

children.title: Homage to the Buddha
children.description: Sakka and Brahmā Sahampati come to the Buddha’s hut and speak in his praise.

children.title: Homage of Householders
children.description: When Sakka sets out on a pleasure jaunt, he begins by lifting his joined palms to the four quarters . His charioteer Mātali points out that Sakka is venerated by gods and men, and asks who he is venerating. Sakka replies that he venerates both well-practiced mendicants as well as virtuous lay folk.

children.title: Homage of the Teacher
children.description: When Sakka sets out on a pleasure jaunt, he begins by lifting his joined palms to the Buddha. His charioteer Mātali points out that Sakka is venerated by gods and men, and asks who he is venerating. Sakka replies that he venerates the Buddha, the perfected mendicants as well as trainees on the path.

children.title: Homage of the Saṅgha
children.description: When Sakka sets out on a pleasure jaunt, he begins by lifting his joined palms to the Saṅgha of mendicants. His charioteer Mātal asks why Sakka venerates smelly mendicants. Sakka replies that he venerates them for their renunciation and peacefulness.

children.title: Slain
children.description: Anger is the only thing whose slaying the Buddha commends.

children.title: Ugly
children.description: When an ugly spirit takes Sakka’s throne, the gods were outraged. But the more they complained, the prettier he became. Sakka realized this was the so-called “anger eating spirit”, and treated him with kindness and respect.

children.title: The Sambari Sorcery
children.description: When Vepacitti fell ill, Sakka visited his old adversary, who begged to be cured. But Sakka demanded to be taught a powerful magic spell first.

children.title: Transgression
children.description: When two mendicants have a falling out, the Buddha recalls the wise words of Sakka on not letting anger ruin friendship.

children.title: Don’t Be Angry
children.description: The Buddha recalls the words of Sakka warning of how anger crushes people like an avalanche

children.title: 2. Causation
children.description: The “Book of Causation” is the second of the five books of the Linked Discourses. It is named after the first and longest saṁyutta, which deals with causation through the core Buddhist teaching of Dependent Origination. The remaining nine saṁyuttas deal with miscellaneous secondary themes, some organized by subject, others by person.

children.title: 1. Causation
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Causation” is a major collection containing 93 discourses on the core Buddhist teaching of dependent origination. Dependent origination presents a series of conditional links laying bare how suffering originates and how it ends. As such, it is an extended treatment of the second and third noble truths. It integrates psychological and existential aspects of suffering, showing how when bound by attachment we make choices that bind us to transmigrating into future lives. One of the core purposes is to explain how rebirth takes place without having to invoke metaphysical concepts such as a “soul”. The collection begins by defining each of the terms in the standard 12-linked chain, definitions which are assumed to apply throughout. Remaining discourses iterate on this theme, introducing new perspectives and formulations.

children.title: Dependent Origination
children.description: The famous twelve links of dependent origination are spelled out, showing the origin and cessation of suffering dependent on ignorance.

children.title: Analysis
children.description: The Buddha gives definitions for each of the twelve links. These are general definitions that apply wherever the twelve links are mentioned.

children.title: Practice
children.description: The origin of suffering is the wrong way, the end is the right way.

children.title: About Vipassī
children.description: In the far past, the Buddha Vipassī reflected on how the world had fallen into suffering, and became awakened by understanding dependent origination.

children.title: Sikhī
children.description: In the far past, the Buddha Sikhī reflected on how the world had fallen into suffering, and became awakened by understanding dependent origination.

children.title: Vessabhū
children.description: In the far past, the Buddha Vessabhū reflected on how the world had fallen into suffering, and became awakened by understanding dependent origination.

children.title: Kakusandha
children.description: In the far past, the Buddha Kakusandha reflected on how the world had fallen into suffering, and became awakened by understanding dependent origination.

children.title: Koṇāgamana
children.description: In the far past, the Buddha Koṇāgamana reflected on how the world had fallen into suffering, and became awakened by understanding dependent origination.

children.title: Kassapa
children.description: In the far past, the Buddha Kassapa reflected on how the world had fallen into suffering, and became awakened by understanding dependent origination.

children.title: Gotama
children.description: The current Buddha Gotama, reflecting on how the world had fallen into suffering, became awakened by understanding dependent origination.

children.title: Fuel
children.description: The Buddha defines the four kinds of “food” or “nutriment”, which include edible food, contact, intention, and consciousness. These are all produced by craving, and hence connect with dependent origination.

children.title: Phagguna of the Top-Knot
children.description: Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna asks who eats the consciousness food. The Buddha says the question is improper, as it assumes a self as agent. Rather, all the factors of dependent origination are simply natural conditions and have nothing to do with a “self”.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins
children.description: One who does not understand dependent origination is no true ascetic.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: One who does not understand dependent origination is no true ascetic.

children.title: Kaccānagotta
children.description: Venerable Kaccānagotta asks the Buddha about right view, and the Buddha answers that right view arises when one sees the origin and cessation of the world and is free of attachments. This sutta, brief but profound and difficult, became renowned as the only canonical reference named in Nāgārjuna’s Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, perhaps the most famous philosophical treatise in all Buddhism.

children.title: A Dhamma Speaker
children.description: One is qualified to be called a “Dhamma speaker” if one teaches for the ending of suffering.

children.title: With Kassapa, the Naked Ascetic
children.description: A naked ascetic named Kassapa approaches the Buddha while he is on alms round and asks whether suffering is created by oneself, by another, by both, or by chance. Explaining why he rejects all these options, the Buddha asserts that suffering arises due to conditions.

children.title: With Timbaruka
children.description: A wanderer named Timbaruka asks the Buddha whether pleasure and pain are created by oneself, by another, by both, or by chance. Explaining why he rejects all these options, the Buddha asserts that pleasure and pain arise due to conditions.

children.title: The Astute and the Foolish
children.description: Both the wise and the foolish have been reborn in this life due to their deeds conditioned by ignorance in past lives. But a fool continues to make the same mistakes and is reborn yet again, whereas a wise person does not.

children.title: Conditions
children.description: The Buddha distinguishes between “dependently originated phenomena”—the twelve factors—and “dependent origination”—the principle of conditionality. Someone who understands these things no longer worries about the past or future.

children.title: The Ten Powers
children.description: The Buddha’s teaching rests on his possession of ten powers and four grounds for self-confidence.

children.title: The Ten Powers (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha’s teaching rests on his possession of ten powers and four grounds for self-confidence. When hearing such an open teaching, a mendicant puts forth great effort, considering the good for both themselves and for others.

children.title: Vital Conditions
children.description: The ending of defilements comes only when the truth is seen. But seeing the truth comes about due to a vital condition. In this way, twelve factors leading to freedom are united with the twelve factors leading to suffering.

children.title: Followers of Other Religions
children.description: Sāriputta is asked by various ascetics as to the origin of suffering. He replies that the Buddha teaches that suffering originates by conditions. Moreover, all those who offer opinions as to the source of suffering are themselves part of the web of conditions, as they cannot state their views without contact. Ānanda reports the exchange to the Buddha, who praises Sāriputta’s answer.

children.title: With Bhūmija
children.description: Sāriputta is asked by Venerable Bhūmija as to the origin of pleasure and pain. He replies that the Buddha teaches that pleasure and pain originate by conditions. Moreover, all those who offer opinions on this question are themselves part of the web of conditions, as they cannot state their views without contact. Ānanda reports the exchange to the Buddha, who praises Sāriputta’s answer.

children.title: With Upavāṇa
children.description: The Buddha is asked by Venerable Upavāṇa as to the origin of suffering. He replies that suffering originates by conditions. Moreover, all those who offer opinions as to the source of suffering are themselves part of the web of conditions, as they cannot state their views without contact.

children.title: Dependency
children.description: Dependent origination is framed within the four noble truths.

children.title: A Mendicant
children.description: A mendicant who understands dependent origination is a trainee who is accomplished in view.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins
children.description: An ascetic who understands dependent origination will realize the goal of the ascetic life.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: An ascetic who understands dependent origination may well escape those conditions.

children.title: What Has Come to Be
children.description: The Buddha asks Sāriputta to explain a verse from “The Questions of Ajita” in the Parāyana (Snp 5.2). At first, Sāriputta hesitates, but proceeds when the Buddha indicates he is looking for an answer in terms of conditionality.

children.title: With Kaḷāra the Aristocrat
children.description: A mendicant named Kaḷāra the Khattiya informs Sāriputta that the mendicant Moḷiyaphagguna had disrobed. Overinterpreting Sāriputta’s reply, Kaḷāra reports to the Buddha that Sāriputta had claimed to have ended all defilements. The Buddha calls Sāriputta to clarify his statements, and Sāriputta explains in terms of dependent origination.

children.title: Grounds for Knowledge
children.description: An analysis of 44 contexts for developing insight with regard to dependent origination. This includes an important distinction between knowledge arising from direct vision of the present, and that derived from inference as to the past and future.

children.title: Grounds for Knowledge (2nd)
children.description: An analysis of 77 contexts for developing insight with regard to dependent origination.

children.title: Ignorance is a Condition
children.description: A mendicant asks who possesses old age and death, and the other factors. The Buddha says the question is improper, as it assumes a self as agent. Rather, dependent origination is the teaching “by the middle”, explaining phenomena according to natural conditions.

children.title: Ignorance is a Condition (2nd)
children.description: The content of this discourse is identical with SN 12.35, except presented as a general teaching by the Buddha, without an questioner.

children.title: Not Yours
children.description: The body is not yours, but is old kamma, generated by choices in past lives.

children.title: Intention
children.description: Intentions or choices are the force that propels consciousness from one life to the next.

children.title: Intention (2nd)
children.description: Intentions or choices are the force that propels consciousness from one life to the next.

children.title: Intention (3rd)
children.description: Intentions or choices are the force that propels consciousness from one life to the next.

children.title: Fears and Enmities
children.description: A noble disciple who is a layperson has eliminated the fear that comes from breaking precepts, possesses the four factors of stream-entry, and understands dependent origination.

children.title: Fears and Enmities (2nd)
children.description: A noble disciple who is a layperson has eliminated the fear that comes from breaking precepts, possesses the four factors of stream-entry, and understands dependent origination.

children.title: Suffering
children.description: The origin and ending of suffering are explained in terms of sense experience giving rise to craving.

children.title: The World
children.description: The origin and ending of the world are explained in terms of sense experience giving rise to craving and suffering.

children.title: At Ñātika
children.description: While on retreat, the Buddha exclaims how the origin and ending of the world are explained in terms of sense experience giving rise to craving and suffering. A mendicant overhears him, and the Buddha urges him to remember that teaching.

children.title: A Certain Brahmin
children.description: A brahmin asks whether the person who acts is the same or different to the person who receives the result. The Buddha rejects both views as extreme.

children.title: Jānussoṇi
children.description: The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asks the Buddha whether all exists or nothing exists. The Buddha rejects both views as extreme.

children.title: A Cosmologist
children.description: A brahmin cosmologist asks the Buddha whether all exists or nothing exists. The Buddha rejects both views as extreme.

children.title: A Noble Disciple
children.description: A noble disciple does not wonder about the links of dependent origination, as they see it for themselves, independent of others.

children.title: A Noble Disciple (2nd)
children.description: A noble disciple does not wonder about the links of dependent origination, as they see it for themselves, independent of others.

children.title: An Inquiry
children.description: A mendicant should thoroughly investigate the causes of suffering in accordance with dependent origination. If someone who still has ignorance makes a choice, their consciousness fares on to a suitable state of existence. But one who has eradicated ignorance is detached and is not reborn anywhere.

children.title: Grasping
children.description: Craving increases when you linger on pleasing things that stimulate grasping, illustrated with the simile of a bonfire.

children.title: Fetters
children.description: Craving increases when you linger on pleasing things that stimulate fetters, illustrated with the simile of a lamp.

children.title: Fetters (2nd)
children.description: Craving increases when you linger on pleasing things that stimulate fetters, illustrated with the simile of a lamp.

children.title: A Great Tree
children.description: Craving increases when you linger on pleasing things that stimulate grasping, illustrated with the simile of a tree.

children.title: A Great Tree (2nd)
children.description: Craving increases when you linger on pleasing things that stimulate grasping, illustrated with the simile of a tree.

children.title: A Sapling
children.description: Craving increases when you linger on pleasing things that stimulate fetters, illustrated with the simile of a sapling.

children.title: Name and Form
children.description: The mental and physical organism is reborn when you linger on pleasing things that stimulate fetters, illustrated with the simile of a tree.

children.title: Consciousness
children.description: Consciousness is reborn when you linger on pleasing things that stimulate fetters, illustrated with the simile of a tree.

children.title: Causation
children.description: When Ānanda suggests that dependent origination is simple, the Buddha rebukes him. The opening of this is similar to DN 15 Mahānidāna.

children.title: Unlearned
children.description: An ignorant person might become free of attachment to their body, but not their mind. Still, it would be better to attach to the body, as it is less changeable than the mind, which jumps about like a monkey.

children.title: Unlearned (2nd)
children.description: An ignorant person might become free of attachment to their body, but not their mind. Still, it would be better to attach to the body, as it is less changeable than the mind. But a noble disciple reflects on dependent origination.

children.title: A Child’s Flesh
children.description: The Buddha defines the four kinds of “food” or “nutriment”, which include edible food, contact, intention, and consciousness. He illustrates them with a series of powerful and horrifying similes.

children.title: If There is Desire
children.description: The Buddha defines the four kinds of “food” or “nutriment”, which include edible food, contact, intention, and consciousness, showing how they lead to suffering according to dependent origination.

children.title: The City
children.description: The Buddha tells the story of how his awakening came about through investigation into dependent origination. He compares it to a man discovering and ancient city, lost and overgrown with weeds.

children.title: Probing Within
children.description: The right way to investigate inside oneself is to see how suffering is created by craving and attachment, stimulated by pleasant experiences.

children.title: Sheaves of Reeds
children.description: Venerables Mahākoṭṭhita and Sāriputta discuss whether the factors of dependent origination are created by oneself, another, both, or by chance.

children.title: At Kosambī
children.description: Venerable Saviṭṭha questions Venerable Musīla about his attainments, and concludes he is an arahant. But Venerable Nārada offers an explanation showing that it is possible to see the Dhamma without having fully realized arahantship.

children.title: Surge
children.description: Like rivers flowing to the ocean, the factors of dependent origination lead to suffering.

children.title: The Wanderer Susīma
children.description: The wanderer Susı̄ma fraudulently enters the Sangha so that the wanderers can learn the secret to the Buddha’s fame and success. Hearing that some mendicants claimed to be perfected, Susīma approaches and asks them if they have developed psychic powers or the formless states, to which they say no. Perplexed, he asks the Buddha, who explains that awakening follows insight into the principles of impermanence and causality. Eventually Susı̄ma confesses his misdeed.

children.title: Old Age and Death
children.description: One who does not understand aging and death is no true ascetic.

children.title: A Set of Ten on Rebirth, Etc.
children.description: One who does not understand the various factors of dependent origination is no true ascetic.

children.title: The Teacher
children.description: One who does not understand the various factors of dependent origination should seek a teacher.

children.title: 2. Sets of Eleven on Training, Etc.
Sets of Eleven on Training, Etc.
2. Comprehension
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Breakthrough” contains 11 discourses on the value of realizing the Dhamma. Each discourse features a memorable simile illustrating the truly momentous implications of seeing the four noble truths.

children.title: A Fingernail
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the great earth; what remains is like the dirt under a fingernail.

children.title: A Lotus Pond
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the water in a massive dam; what remains is like a few drops on a blade of grass.

children.title: Where the Waters Join Together
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the water at the confluence of great rivers; what remains is like a few drops.

children.title: Where the Waters Join Together (2nd)
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the water at the confluence of great rivers; what remains is like a few drops.

children.title: The Earth
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the great earth; what remains is like seven balls of clay.

children.title: The Earth (2nd)
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the great earth; what remains is like seven balls of clay.

children.title: The Ocean
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the water in the ocean; what remains is like a few drops.

children.title: The Ocean (2nd)
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the water in the ocean; what remains is like a few drops.

children.title: A Mountain
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the Himalayas; what remains is like seven bits of gravel.

children.title: A Mountain (2nd)
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the Himalayas; what remains is like seven bits of gravel.

children.title: A Mountain (3rd)
children.description: For someone who has seen the truth, the suffering eliminated is like the Sineru, king of mountains; what remains is like seven bits of gravel

children.title: 3. Elements
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Elements” contains 39 discourses on various factors classified as “elements” (dhātu). In Buddhism, the term “element” is applied to a range of phenomena, most commonly the main material properties of earth, water, fire and air. Here, however, these four elements play only a small role, and much of the text is devoted to analysis of the perceptual process, and to various character traits. The relation or dependence of elements on each other is a major theme, and this chapter can be seen as an appendix to the chapter on causality.

children.title: Diversity of Elements
children.description: The senses function due to the various different elements of sense experience, namely, the internal sense organ, the external sense stimulus, and consciousness.

children.title: Diversity of Contacts
children.description: The diverse internal elements of sense experience give rise to diverse contacts.

children.title: Not Diversity of Contacts
children.description: It is not the case that diverse contacts give rise to the diverse elements of sense experience.

children.title: Diversity of Feelings
children.description: Diverse contacts give rise to diverse feelings.

children.title: Diversity of Feelings (2nd)
children.description: It is not the case that diverse feelings give rise to diverse contacts.

children.title: External Diversity of Elements
children.description: The senses function due to the various different external elements of sense experience, namely, the various sense stimuli.

children.title: Diversity of Perceptions
children.description: The diverse external elements of sense experience give rise to diverse perceptions, intentions, desires, passions, and quests.

children.title: No Diversity of Searches
children.description: It is not the case that diverse perceptions, intentions, desires, passions, and quests give rise to diverse external elements of sense experience.

children.title: Diversity of Gains
children.description: The diverse external elements of sense experience give rise to diverse perceptions, intentions, desires, passions, quests, and material possessions.

children.title: No Diversity of Gains
children.description: It is not the case that diverse perceptions, intentions, desires, passions, quests, and material possessions give rise to diverse external elements of sense experience.

children.title: Seven Elements
children.description: A rare group of seven elements: light, beauty, the four formless states, and the attainment of cessation. Each of these is known due to the negation of something: light vs. darkness, beauty vs. ugliness, and so on.

children.title: With a Cause
children.description: Thoughts of sensuality, ill-will, and cruelty arise due to a series of causes.

children.title: In the Brick Hall
children.description: When unenlightened people have the view that certain people are Buddhas, this is due to ignorance.

children.title: Inferior Convictions
children.description: People of poor character associate together, while people of good character associate together.

children.title: Walking Together
children.description: The Buddha points out that each of the great disciples has a retinue of students of a similar character. And the monks in Devadattas’s retinue all have evil wishes.

children.title: With Verses
children.description: People of poor character associate together, while people of good character associate together. Illustrated with similes and verses.

children.title: Faithless
children.description: The faithless and those of other bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Beginning With the Faithless
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Beginning With the Shameless
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Beginning With Imprudence
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Beginning With the Unlearned
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Beginning With the Lazy
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Lacking Immersion
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Unethical
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: The Five Precepts
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Seven Ways of Performing Deeds
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Ten Ways of Performing Deeds
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: The Eightfold Path
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Ten Factored Path
children.description: Those of bad qualities associate together, while those of good qualities associate together.

children.title: Four Elements
children.description: The four material elements of earth, water, heat, and air. Note that “air” is close in meaning to “wind”.

children.title: Before Awakening
children.description: Before his awakening the Buddha saw the gratification, the drawback, and the escape in the four material elements.

children.title: In Search of Gratification
children.description: The Buddha set out to discover the gratification, the drawback, and the escape in the four material elements, and found it.

children.title: If There Was No
children.description: Each of the three aspects of the four material elements performs its own function. Gratification stimulates desire; drawbacks lead to disillusionment, while escape opens the possibility of freedom.

children.title: Exclusively Painful
children.description: If the material elements were solely painful, beings would not get attached. If they were solely pleasurable, it would be impossible to become detached.

children.title: Taking Pleasure
children.description: When you seek pleasure in the material elements, you seek pleasure in suffering.

children.title: Arising
children.description: The arising of the material elements is the arising of suffering.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins
children.description: One who does not understand the four material elements is no true ascetic.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: One who does not understand the four material elements is no true ascetic.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (3rd)
children.description: One who does not understand the four material elements is no true ascetic.

children.title: 4. Unknowable Beginning
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Unknowable Beginning” contains 20 discourses that speak of how the ultimate origin of the process of transmigration (saṁsāra) is unknowable. This theme is a direct counter to the hubris of the creation myths found in most religions, which confidently recount events which are in fact permanently hidden from view. The Buddha emphasized that transmigration has been ongoing for a fathomless period of time, illustrating it with a series of powerful similes.

children.title: Grass and Sticks
children.description: Transmigration is endless, like the grass and twigs in India.

children.title: The Earth
children.description: Transmigration is endless, like the great earth.

children.title: Tears
children.description: The tears you have shed in transmigration are greater than the waters in the oceans.

children.title: Mother’s Milk
children.description: The mother’s milk you have drunk in transmigration is greater than the waters in the oceans.

children.title: A Mountain
children.description: A great mountain would erode before the end of the eon.

children.title: A Mustard Seed
children.description: A city filled with mustard seeds might be emptied before the end of an eon.

children.title: Disciples
children.description: Even recollecting 100,000 eons per day you’ll never remember the beginning of transmigration.

children.title: The Ganges
children.description: There have been more eons than the sands in the Ganges river.

children.title: A Stick
children.description: Like a stick falling on this side or that, beings are reborn in different realms.

children.title: A Single Individual
children.description: The bones you’ve left behind in transmigration are greater than a mountain.

children.title: In a Sorry State
children.description: When you see someone suffer, know that you too have experienced that.

children.title: In a Good Way
children.description: When you see someone happy, know that you too have experienced that.

children.title: Thirty Mendicants
children.description: The blood you have shed from being slaughtered or beheaded in transmigration is greater than the waters in the oceans.

children.title: Mother
children.description: It is not easy to find a being who has not been your mother.

children.title: Father
children.description: It is not easy to find a being who has not been your father.

children.title: Brother
children.description: It is not easy to find a being who has not been your brother.

children.title: Sister
children.description: It is not easy to find a being who has not been your sister.

children.title: Son
children.description: It is not easy to find a being who has not been your son.

children.title: Daughter
children.description: It is not easy to find a being who has not been your daughter.

children.title: Mount Vepulla
children.description: The Buddha recounts how peoples of the past had different names for the mountains of Rājagaha. Yet now they have all gone

children.title: 5. Kassapa
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Kassapa” contains 13 discourses featuring one of the most famous of the Buddha’s disciples, the monk Kassapa. Kassapa was an ascetic and diligent practitioner, whose sometimes critical voice was tempered by a love of nature and a tender concern for the lay community. These discourses show his magnificent spiritual attainments, and his overriding concern for the health and longevity of the Buddhist community.

children.title: Content
children.description: Kassapa is content with robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicines.

children.title: Imprudent
children.description: Sāriputta approaches Kassapa and asks how it is that only someone who is keen and conscientious can realize freedom.

children.title: Like the Moon
children.description: Kassapa approaches families like the moon, with humility, keeping his distance, and not getting involved. So when he teaches, it is with pure intentions.

children.title: Visiting Families
children.description: Some mendicants approach families in the hope of receiving fine gifts or respect—but not Kassapa.

children.title: Old Age
children.description: The Buddha points out that Kassapa has grown old, and urges him to give up his ascetic life and stay in a comfortable monastery.

children.title: Advice
children.description: The Buddha invites Kassapa to teach the mendicants, but he is reluctant, since certain students of Anuruddha and Ānanda have been competing to see who can teach better.

children.title: Advice (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha invites Kassapa to teach the mendicants, but he is reluctant, saying that the mendicants have become stubborn and their good qualities are declining.

children.title: Advice (3rd)
children.description: The Buddha invites Kassapa to teach the mendicants, but he is reluctant, saying that the senior mendicants used to set a good example, but now instead of respecting good practice, they respect fame and fortune.

children.title: Absorptions and Insights
children.description: The Buddha asserts that just as he has full mastery of all the meditation attainments and higher spiritual realizations, so does Kassapa.

children.title: The Nuns’ Quarters
children.description: When Kassapa is persuaded by Ānanda to go with him to teach the nuns, the nun Thullatissā compares him unfavorably to Ānanda, prompting Kassapa to issue a warning and make a bold claim of his spiritual mastery. This discourse appears to be set after the Buddha’s passing.

children.title: Robes
children.description: When several of Ānanda’s students disrobe, Kassapa admonishes him, calling him “boy”. The nun Thullanandā hears of this and criticizes Kassapa, claiming he formerly followed another teacher. But Kassapa refutes this, and gives an account of his going forth and first encounter with the Buddha.

children.title: The Realized One After Death
children.description: Sāriputta asks Kassapa about whether a Realized One survives death.

children.title: The Counterfeit of the True Teaching
children.description: Kassapa asks the Buddha why there are now more rules but fewer awakened mendicants. The Buddha replies that it is due to the arising of the counterfeit Dhamma, giving five factors that lead to decline

children.title: 6. Gains and Honor
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Gains and Honor” contains 43 discourses warning the mendicants of the terrible dangers inherent in material possessions and love of popularity and honors.

children.title: Grim
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are terrible things, obstructing spiritual progress.

children.title: A Hook
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are terrible things, which catch you like fish on a hook.

children.title: A Turtle
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are terrible things, which hit you like a harpoon hits a careless turtle.

children.title: A Fleecy Sheep
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are terrible things, which snare you like a long-haired goat in a briar patch.

children.title: A Dung Beetle
children.description: A mendicant who is proud on account of their material possessions, honor, and praise is like a dung beetle proud of their ball of dung.

children.title: A Bolt of Lightning
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are terrible things, like a lightning strike.

children.title: A Poisoned Arrow
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are terrible things, like a poison dart.

children.title: A Jackal
children.description: A mendicant who is proud on account of their material possessions, honor, and praise is never at peace, like a mangy jackal.

children.title: Gale-force Winds
children.description: A mendicant who is proud on account of their material possessions, honor, and praise is never at peace, like a bird in a gale.

children.title: With Verses
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are terrible things, and attachment to them leads to a bad rebirth.

children.title: A Gold Cup
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are terrible things, which can corrupt the mind even of a pure mendicant.

children.title: A Silver Pot
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are terrible things, which can corrupt the mind even of a pure mendicant.

children.title: A Gold Ingot, Etc.
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are terrible things, which can corrupt the mind even of a pure mendicant.

children.title: A Lady
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise can be even more tempting than a woman.

children.title: The Finest Lady in the Land
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise can be even more tempting than the finest lady in the land.

children.title: An Only Son
children.description: A laywoman should wish that if her son remains in the household life, he should be like Citta and Hatthaka. But if he becomes a monk, may material possessions, honor, and praise not come to him!

children.title: An Only Daughter
children.description: A laywoman should wish that if her daughter remains in the household life, she should be like Khujjuttarā and Veḷukaṇḍakiyā. But if she becomes a nun, may material possessions, honor, and praise not come to her!

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins
children.description: Someone who doesn’t fully understand material possessions, honor, and praise is no true ascetic.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: Someone who doesn’t fully understand material possessions, honor, and praise is no true ascetic.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (3rd)
children.description: Someone who doesn’t fully understand material possessions, honor, and praise is no true ascetic.

children.title: Skin
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise cut to the bone.

children.title: A Rope
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise cut to the bone, like a rope.

children.title: A Mendicant With Defilements Ended
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise are even a problem for a perfected one, as they interfere with their meditation.

children.title: Schism
children.description: Devadatta provoked a schism due to material possessions, honor, and praise.

children.title: Skillful Root
children.description: Devadatta’s wholesome root was cut off due to material possessions, honor, and praise.

children.title: Skillful Quality
children.description: Devadatta’s wholesome nature was cut off due to material possessions, honor, and praise.

children.title: Bright Quality
children.description: Devadatta’s bright nature was cut off due to material possessions, honor, and praise.

children.title: Shortly After He Left
children.description: Material possessions, honor, and praise led to Devadatta’s downfall, like the fruit of a plantain.

children.title: Five Hundred Carts
children.description: Prince Ajātasattu supplied devadatta with 500 carts of offerings, leading to his downfall.

children.title: Mother
children.description: Even someone who would not lie for the sake of their mother would so so when corrupted by material possessions.

children.title: Father, Etc.
children.description: Even someone who would not lie for the sake of their father and other relatives would so so when corrupted by material possessions.

children.title: 7. Rāhula
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Rāhula” contains 22 discourses with the Buddha interrogating his son Rāhula on fundamental doctrines such as the aggregates or sense fields.

children.title: The Eye, Etc.
children.description: The Buddha answers Rāhula’s request by teaching on the internal sense organs in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: Sights, Etc.
children.description: The Buddha answers Rāhula’s request by teaching on the external sense objects in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: Consciousness
children.description: The Buddha answers Rāhula’s request by teaching on sense consciousness in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: Contact
children.description: The Buddha answers Rāhula’s request by teaching on sense contact in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: Feeling
children.description: The Buddha answers Rāhula’s request by teaching on feelings in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: Perceptions
children.description: The Buddha answers Rāhula’s request by teaching on perceptions in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: Intention
children.description: The Buddha answers Rāhula’s request by teaching on intentions in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: Craving
children.description: The Buddha answers Rāhula’s request by teaching on cravings in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: Elements
children.description: The Buddha answers Rāhula’s request by teaching on the four material elements in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: The Aggregates
children.description: The Buddha answers Rāhula’s request by teaching on the five aggregates in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: The Eye, Etc.
children.description: The Buddha teaches Rāhula about the internal sense organs in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: The Nine Discourses on Sights, Etc.
children.description: The Buddha teaches Rāhula about the senses, aggregates, and elements in light of the three characteristics.

children.title: Tendency
children.description: Rāhula asks how to see so that conceit no longer occurs. The Buddha teaches him to investigate the five aggregates in terms of not-self.

children.title: Rid of Conceit
children.description: Rāhula asks how to see so conceit no longer occurs and one is peaceful. The Buddha teaches him to investigate the five aggregates in terms of not-self

children.title: 8. Lakkhaṇa
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Lakkhaṇa” contains 21 discourses with the Buddha featuring the monk Lakkhaṇa (“Mark”). Through his psychic powers he sees beings in various states of torment and distress, and describes them to the Buddha.

children.title: A Skeleton
children.description: While walking for alms down Vulture’s Peak, Venerable Moggallāna smiled at something invisible. Later, he told the Buddha it was a skeleton flying through the air, being pecked at by vultures. The Buddha confirmed that the man he had seen had been a butcher in his past life

children.title: 9. Similes
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Similes” contains 12 discourses with parables or similes illustrating diverse points of the teaching. This chapter highlights the Buddha’s skill in choosing vivid and suitable similes for any occasion.

children.title: A Roof Peak
children.description: As rafters depend on the roof-peak, unwholesome qualities depend on ignorance.

children.title: A Fingernail
children.description: As the dirt in a fingernail is smaller than the great earth, the beings reborn as humans are few.

children.title: Families
children.description: As a family with few men and many women is easily attacked, non-human beings may attack a mendicant without love.

children.title: Cauldrons
children.description: Love is more beneficial than generosity.

children.title: A Spear
children.description: As it is not possible to bend back a spear, it is not possible to overthrow a mendicant who has developed love.

children.title: The Archers
children.description: Only a speedster could catch arrows in flight, yet conditioned phenomena perish faster than that.

children.title: The Drum Called Plugger
children.description: As an ancient drum has disintegrated, so too will the true teachings disappear.

children.title: Wood Blocks
children.description: Warriors who sleep on wooden pillows remain vigilant, and so it is for the spiritual seeker.

children.title: A Bull Elephant
children.description: A mendicant who overly associates with the laity is like an elephant calf who tries to copy the great bull elephants.

children.title: A Cat
children.description: As a cat may suffer from eating too hastily, so a mendicant may suffer by not restraining senses.

children.title: A Jackal
children.description: A mangy jackal howls in discomfort, but even that would be a good rebirth for some.

children.title: A Jackal (2nd)
children.description: An old jackal howls at dawn, but even they have more gratitude than some

children.title: 10. Monks
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Monks” contains 12 discourses featuring different monks. Unlike the chapter on nuns, this does not use a consistent template, but depicts a diverse range of scenarios. Each case shows a personal challenge or spiritual triumph, shedding a light on the life of the monks.

children.title: With Kolita
children.description: Moggallāna reflects that second absorption is the true noble silence, and the Buddha encourages him to develop it.

children.title: With Upatissa
children.description: Sāriputta says that not even if the Buddha changed would it cause him sorrow.

children.title: A Mound of Salt
children.description: Sāriputta and Moggallāna come together for a discussion, which touches on the use of psychic powers and energy. The two great monks end up warmly praising each other.

children.title: A Junior Mendicant
children.description: When a certain monk neglects his duties in favor of solitude, other monks complain. The Buddha questions him, and finds that he is awakened.

children.title: With Sujāta
children.description: The Buddha praises Venerable Sujāta as beautiful both inside and out.

children.title: With Bhaddiya the Dwarf
children.description: Venerable Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya is a dwarf, considered to be ugly and unsightly. The Buddha warns the monks not to despise him as he had realized full awakening.

children.title: With Visākha, Pañcāli’s Son
children.description: The Buddha praises Venerable Visākha Pañcāliputta for teaching the Dhamma.

children.title: With Nanda
children.description: Venerable Nanda wore pretty robes, a fancy bowl, and makeup, so the Buddha encouraged him to embrace simplicity.

children.title: With Tissa
children.description: Venerable Tissa admonished others but got upset when he was admonished. The Buddha encourages him to let go of his anger.

children.title: Senior In Name Only
children.description: A monk named “Senior” likes to live alone, but the Buddha questions whether it is the true solitude.

children.title: With Mahākappina
children.description: The Buddha describes Venerable Mahākappina as thin, fair-skinned, with a big nose—and as awakened.

children.title: Companions
children.description: The Buddha praises two friends who are students of Venerable Mahākappina

children.title: 3. the Aggregates
children.description: The “Book of the Aggregates” is the third of the five books of the Linked Discourses. It is named after the first and longest saṁyutta, which deals with the core Buddhist teaching of the five aggregates. Of the remaining twelve saṁyuttas, three also take up the theme of the aggregates, while the remainder deal with miscellaneous secondary themes, some organized by subject, others by person.

children.title: 1. Aggregates
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Aggregates” contains 159 discourses on the core doctrinal topic of the five aggregates. This term was introduced in the first sermon as the summary of the noble truth of suffering, and became a foundational teaching in all forms of Buddhism. The basic idea of an “aggregate” is a set or class of phenomena. The five are form (rūpa, i.e. “physical phenomena”, or sometimes simply “body”; note that in Buddhism, rūpa includes all things with material properties such as shape and color, including visions perceived only in the mind), feeling (vedanā, i.e. the pleasant, painful, or neutral tone of experience), perception (saññā, i.e. the recognition or interpretation of experience, not sense awareness), choices (saṅkhārā, i.e. intention, will, or volition; the choice to perform an act, especially one with an ethical dimension), and consciousness (viññāṇa, i.e. the subjective process of awareness itself). The “aggregates” are the various different phenomena so classified. Almost always, they are referred to as the “aggregates connected with grasping” (upādānakkhandha). The relation between “grasping” and “aggregate” encompasses a number of aspects. The aggregates are the subject of grasping, in that they are the things that are normally attached to and taken to be the permanent “self”. But they are not merely passive spectators: they are also the functional support of grasping, the things that make grasping work. As active participants in the process of grasping, they stimulate grasping to themselves (upādāniya). And finally, they are the product of grasping in the sense that attachments in past lives have given rise to the aggregates in this life (upādinna). One of the key functions of the aggregates is to categorize theories of the self. From the discourses, non-Buddhists seem to be familiar with this, yet we cannot identify the aggregates in any pre-Buddhist texts. Regardless of whether the set of categories was pre-Buddhist, the Buddha treated them in his own distinctive way, emphasizing that nothing in the aggregates was a permanent self or soul.
