In this collection we find a large number of striking and lively narratives, showing how the aggregates could be a solace at the time of death, a guide to the knotty theoretical debates on identity, or a framework for insight meditation. Many of the short abbreviated texts are built from the same templates employed in the “Linked Discourses on the Six Sense Fields”.

children.title: Nakula’s Father
children.description: The householder Nakulapitā asks the Buddha for help in coping with old age. The Buddha says to reflect: “Even though I am afflicted in body, my mind will be unafflicted.” Later Sāriputta explains this in terms of the five aggregates.

children.title: At Devadaha
children.description: A number of mendicants are heading for lands west, but the Buddha advises them to speak with Sāriputta before they go. Sāriputta reminds them that in foreign lands they will be scrutinized for their understanding, so they need to be able to answer questions on the teaching. He goes on to explain that the Dhamma is for the removal of desire for the five aggregates.

children.title: With Hāliddikāni
children.description: The householder Hāliddakāni approaches the Venerable Mahākaccāna in the Avanti country and asks how to understand a verse from “The Questions of Māgandiya” of the Aṭṭhakavagga (Snp 4.9). Though the verse appears to be pitched at an ethical level, describing a sage intimate with none in the village, Mahākaccāna explains it in philosophical terms as non-attachment to the aggregates.

children.title: Hāliddikāni (2nd)
children.description: The householder Hāliddakāni approaches the Venerable Mahākaccāna in the Avanti country and asks how to understand a passage on liberation from “The Questions of Sakka” (see MN 37 and DN 21). Mahākaccāna explains it in terms of freedom from attachment to the aggregates.

children.title: Development of Immersion
children.description: A mendicant should develop immersion (samādhi) in order to truly understand the origin and ending of the five aggregates.

children.title: Retreat
children.description: A mendicant should make an effort in seclusion in order to truly understand the origin and ending of the five aggregates.

children.title: Anxiety Because of Grasping
children.description: An ordinary person identifies their self with the five aggregates and suffers anxiety when the aggregates change. But a noble disciple, free of such identification, does not suffer.

children.title: Anxiety Because of Grasping (2nd)
children.description: An ordinary person identifies their self with the five aggregates and suffers anxiety when the aggregates change. But a noble disciple, free of such identification, does not suffer.

children.title: Impermanence in the Three Times
children.description: The aggregates are impermanent in the past and future as in the present.

children.title: Suffering in the Three Times
children.description: The aggregates are suffering in the past and future as in the present.

children.title: Not-Self in the Three Times
children.description: The aggregates are not-self in the past and future as in the present.

children.title: Impermanence
children.description: Because the aggregates are impermanent, a noble disciple becomes disillusioned with them.

children.title: Suffering
children.description: Because the aggregates are suffering, a noble disciple becomes disillusioned with them.

children.title: Not-Self
children.description: Because the aggregates are not-self, a noble disciple becomes disillusioned with them.

children.title: That Which is Impermanent
children.description: One should truly understand the five aggregates as impermanent, etc.

children.title: That Which is Suffering
children.description: One should truly understand the five aggregates as suffering, etc.

children.title: That Which is Not-Self
children.description: One should truly understand the five aggregates as not-self.

children.title: Impermanence With Its Cause
children.description: Since the causes of the aggregates are impermanent, how can the aggregates be permanent?

children.title: Suffering With Its Cause
children.description: Since the causes of the aggregates are suffering, how can the aggregates be free of suffering?

children.title: Not-Self With Its Cause
children.description: Since the causes of the aggregates are not-self, how can the aggregates be self?

children.title: With Ānanda
children.description: Ānanda asks the Buddha what exactly is meant when we say that things cease. The Buddha explains it as the cessation of the aggregates.

children.title: The Burden of Responsibility
children.description: The aggregates are the burden, a person carries that burden, craving takes up the burden, and letting go puts down the burden.

children.title: Complete Understanding
children.description: The aggregates are to be fully understood, and the full understanding is the ending of defilements.

children.title: Directly Knowing
children.description: Only by directly knowing the aggregates can one end suffering.

children.title: Desire and Greed
children.description: By letting go desire, the aggregates come to an end.

children.title: Gratification
children.description: Before his awakening, the Buddha investigated the aggregates in terms of their gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: Gratification (2nd)
children.description: When the Buddha fully knew the gratification, drawback, and escape regarding the five aggregates he became awakened.

children.title: Gratification (3rd)
children.description: Beings are attached to the five aggregates due to gratification, repelled due to drawbacks, and find escape because there is an escape.

children.title: Taking Pleasure
children.description: If you enjoy the aggregates, you enjoy suffering.

children.title: Arising
children.description: The arising of the aggregates is the arising of suffering.

children.title: The Root of Gloom
children.description: The aggregates are misery, desire for them is the root of misery.

children.title: Brittle
children.description: The aggregates are fragile and their passing is not fragile.

children.title: It’s Not Yours
children.description: Let go of what is not yours: the five aggregates. You wouldn’t be upset if someone took the grass and sticks from the monastery grounds, so why worry over the aggregates?

children.title: It’s Not Yours (2nd)
children.description: Let go of what is not yours: the five aggregates.

children.title: A Mendicant
children.description: The Buddha teaches a mendicant who wants to go on retreat that one is reckoned by what one has an underlying tendency for. The mendicant gives a full explanation.

children.title: A Mendicant (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha teaches a mendicant who wants to go on retreat that one is measured by what one has an underlying tendency for. The mendicant gives a full explanation.

children.title: With Ānanda
children.description: The Buddha speaks to Ānanda on what at AN 3.47 described as the “characteristics of conditioned phenomena”: arising, ceasing, and change while persisting. This was to become a critical aspect of later theories on the nature of change. Ānanda explains in terms of the aggregates.

children.title: With Ānanda (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha speaks to Ānanda on what at AN 3.47 described as the “characteristics of conditioned phenomena”: arising, ceasing, and change while persisting, as applied to past, future, and present. Ānanda explains in terms of the aggregates.

children.title: In Line With the Teaching
children.description: To practice in line with the teachings a mendicant should meditate on disillusionment with the aggregates.

children.title: In Line With the Teaching (2nd)
children.description: To practice in line with the teachings a mendicant should meditate on the aggregates as impermanent.

children.title: In Line With the Teaching (3rd)
children.description: To practice in line with the teachings a mendicant should meditate on the aggregates as suffering.

children.title: In Line With the Teaching (4th)
children.description: To practice in line with the teachings a mendicant should meditate on the aggregates as not-self.

children.title: Be Your Own Island
children.description: Dwell with yourself as an island and refuge, with the Dhamma as an island and refuge. How? By investigating how suffering arises from identification with the aggregates.

children.title: Practice
children.description: Contemplation of the five aggregates as not-self is the path to the end of identity.

children.title: Impermanence
children.description: Seeing the five aggregates as impermanent, etc., leads to freedom.

children.title: Impermanence (2nd)
children.description: Seeing the five aggregates as impermanent, etc., leads to letting go of views and ultimately to freedom.

children.title: Ways of Regarding
children.description: When you identify anything as self, you always identify one or other of the five aggregates.

children.title: Aggregates
children.description: The distinction between “five aggregates” and “five grasping aggregates”.

children.title: With Soṇa
children.description: The Buddha teaches a householder named Soṇa not to be conceited about the five aggregates.

children.title: With Soṇa (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha teaches a householder named Soṇa that any true ascetic understands the five aggregates.

children.title: The End of Relishing
children.description: Right view is seeing the aggregates as they are, impermanent, and this leads to freedom.

children.title: The End of Relishing (2nd)
children.description: Focusing properly on the five aggregates you see them as they are and become free.

children.title: Involvement
children.description: Consciousness stands dependent on the other four aggregates, and this attachment is what fuels the cycle of rebirth.

children.title: Seeds of Plants
children.description: Consciousness is like a seed that is planted in the soil of the other four aggregates and watered with craving.

children.title: An Inspired Saying
children.description: The Buddha utters an enigmatic saying that non-identification leads to cutting off the fetters. A mendicant asks how to achieve this.

children.title: Rounds of the Grasping Aggregates
children.description: The Buddha did not claim to be awakened until he had fully understood each of the five aggregates in the light of each of the four noble truths. This discourse includes definitions of each of the aggregates.

children.title: Seven Cases
children.description: To be fully accomplished, a mendicant should investigate the five aggregates in light of the four noble truths, as well as their gratification, drawback, and escape. In addition, they should investigate the elements, sense fields, and dependent origination.

children.title: The Fully Awakened Buddha
children.description: The Buddha declares that a mendicant is freed by wisdom by non-attachment to the aggregates, in just the same way as he himself. He then explains that the difference between himself and another awakened mendicant is simply that he was the first to discover the path and teach it to others.

children.title: The Characteristic of Not-Self
children.description: In the Deer Park at Varanasi the Buddha teaches the famous second discourse, on not-self with regard to the aggregates, to the group of five monks. At the conclusion, they become perfected ones.

children.title: With Mahāli
children.description: Mahāli the Licchavi reports to the Buddha that the rival teacher Pūraṇa Kassapa asserts that there is no reason for beings to be either defiled or pure. The Buddha denies this, and goes on to explain how it happens.

children.title: Burning
children.description: The five aggregates are burning.

children.title: The Scope of Definition
children.description: All philosophers must accept that the five aggregates are described in language that refers to either the past, future, or present.

children.title: When You Grasp
children.description: A mendicant comes to the Buddha to ask for instructions before going on retreat. The Buddha teaches them that in clinging to the aggregates one is bound by Māra.

children.title: Conceiving
children.description: In conceiving regarding the aggregates one is bound by Māra.

children.title: When You Take Pleasure
children.description: In seeking enjoyment in the aggregates one is bound by Māra.

children.title: Impermanence
children.description: One should let go of desire for what is impermanent, namely the five aggregates.

children.title: Suffering
children.description: One should let go of desire for what is suffering, namely the five aggregates.

children.title: Not-Self
children.description: One should let go of desire for what is not-self, namely the five aggregates.

children.title: Not Belonging to Self
children.description: One should let go of desire for what does not belong to self, namely the five aggregates.

children.title: Definitely Arousing
children.description: One should let go of desire for what appears tantalizing, namely the five aggregates.

children.title: With Rādha
children.description: Venerable Rādha asks the Buddha how to see so as to let go of conceit. The Buddha tells him to contemplate the aggregates in terms of not-self.

children.title: With Surādha
children.description: Venerable Surādha asks the Buddha how to see so as to let go of conceit and be freed. The Buddha tells him to contemplate the aggregates in terms of not-self.

children.title: Gratification
children.description: Only a noble disciple truly understand the five aggregates’ gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: Origin
children.description: Only a noble disciple truly understand the five aggregates’ origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: Origin (2nd)
children.description: Only a noble disciple truly understand the five aggregates’ origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: The Perfected Ones
children.description: One who is freed after truly understanding the aggregates is a perfected one. They are the best of beings, even up to the pinnacle of existence. A set of verses extols the perfected ones.

children.title: The Perfected Ones (2nd)
children.description: One who is freed after truly understanding the aggregates is a perfected one. They are the best of beings, even up to the pinnacle of existence.

children.title: The Lion
children.description: When a lion emerges from its lair and roars, animals are terrified. Similarly, when the Buddha teaches of the impermanence of the aggregates, even the gods are filled with fear. This is illustrated with a set of verses.

children.title: Bitable
children.description: One of the most extensive discourses in this collection begins with the Buddha saying that when anyone recollects a past life, all they are recollecting is the five aggregates. He then gives a distinctive set of definitions of the aggregates in terms of their functions, and discusses them from various aspects.

children.title: Beggars
children.description: While staying at Kapilavatthu the Buddha dismissed the the Sangha for misbehaving. Later he decided to support them for the sake of the young mendicants. He reminds them that their livelihood is considered a lowly one, and that one should let go of bad thoughts and wrong views, and see the aggregates as impermanent.

children.title: At Pārileyyaka
children.description: Leaving behind the quarreling monks at Kosambi, the Buddha went to stay in the empty forest at Pārileyyaka. Ānanda brings some mendicants to receive a teaching, and one of them wonders how to see so as to end defilements in this very life. The Buddha teaches the 37 practices that lead to awakening, and then goes on to show that various ways of regarding the aggregates are conditioned phenomena.

children.title: A Full Moon Night
children.description: On a sabbath day with the Sangha at Sāvatthi, the Buddha answers a series of ten questions on the aggregates.

children.title: With Ānanda
children.description: Ānanda praises Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāniputta, and says that it was when hearing his teaching on the aggregates that he understood the Dhamma.

children.title: With Tissa
children.description: Venerable Tissa, the Blessed One’s paternal cousin, tells the monks that he is dissatisfied as a monk. When the Buddha hears of this, he calls Tissa to him, and questions him on the aggregates. As Tissa showed his understanding of each question, the Buddha praised him, lifting his spirits.

children.title: With Yamaka
children.description: Venerable Yamaka had the wrong view that one whose defilements have ended is annihilated at death. The monks ask Sāriputta to help, and he asks Yamaka whether a realized one in this very life may be identified as one of the aggregates, or apart from them. Convinced, Yamaka lets go of his view and sees the Dhamma.

children.title: With Anurādha
children.description: Venerable Anurādha is questioned by a number of ascetics, and ends up by saying that a realized one is described in terms other than “still existing after death” and so on. The wanderers say he’s a fool, so he checks with the Buddha, who says that a realized one is not even apprehended in this life, so how can he be described after death?

children.title: With Vakkali
children.description: Venerable Vakkali is ill, and asks the Buddha to visit him. The Buddha does so, but says there is no point in seeing his physical body, as one who sees the Dhamma sees him. Later, Vakkali is taken to the Black Rock on Isigili, where he declares that he has no attachment to the aggregates, and takes his own life. The Buddha says that he had attained final extinguishment.

children.title: With Assaji
children.description: Venerable Assaji is ill, and asks the Buddha to visit him. The Buddha does so, and learns that Assaji has difficulty maintaining his meditation. The Buddha encourages him to contemplate the impermanence of the aggregates.

children.title: With Khemaka
children.description: Venerable Khemaka is ill, and some senior mendicants ask Dāsaka to convey their concern to him. There follows a series of exchanges mediated by Dāsaka until eventually Khemaka, despite his illness, goes to see the other mendicants himself. The seniors are asking to determine Khemaka’s understanding of the Dhamma, and he says that although he has let go of the five lower fetters, he still has a residual attachment to the five aggregates.

children.title: With Channa
children.description: Hearing that the Buddha, while on his deathbed, had announced a special punishment for him, Venerable Channa asks for teachings from the mendicants. Unsatisfied, he seeks out Ānanda, who teaches him the address to Kaccāyana (SN 12.15).

children.title: Rāhula
children.description: Rāhula asks how to contemplate to let go of conceit. The Buddha urges him to see the aggregates as not-self.

children.title: Rāhula (2nd)
children.description: Rāhula asks how to contemplate to let go of conceit and be free. The Buddha urges him to see the aggregates as not-self.

children.title: A River
children.description: If you grasp at the aggregates as a self, you will meet with calamity, like a man swept down by a mountain river, grasping at grass or rushes.

children.title: Flowers
children.description: The Buddha doesn’t dispute with the world; the world disputes with him. He has understood the five aggregates and explains them. Like a lotus, he was born in the swamp, but rises above it.

children.title: A Lump of Foam
children.description: The Buddha gives a series of similes for the aggregates: physical form is like foam, feeling is like a bubble, perception is like a mirage, choices are like a coreless tree, and consciousness is like an illusion.

children.title: A Lump of Cow Dung
children.description: Nothing in the aggregates has even the tiniest bit of stability or permanence. In a past life, the Buddha was a great king with vast properties, but all those conditions have passed away.

children.title: A Fingernail
children.description: A mendicant asks whether anything in the aggregates has even the tiniest bit of stability or permanence. The Buddha answers using the simile of a little dirt under his fingernail.

children.title: Plain Version
children.description: A mendicant asks whether anything in the aggregates has even the tiniest bit of stability or permanence.

children.title: A Leash
children.description: Transmigration has no knowable beginning; even the oceans, mountains, and this great earth will perish. But like a dog on a leash running around a post, beings remain attached to the aggregates.

children.title: A Leash (2nd)
children.description: A dog leashed to a post will always remain close to that post. In the same way, beings remain close to aggregates in this endless cycle of transmigration. The Buddha refers to a well-known painting called “Conduct”, and says the mind is even more diverse than that; and indeed, the animal realm is the most diverse of them all, and it is produced by the mind.

children.title: The Adze
children.description: Contemplating the aggregates leads to liberation, but this may not be immediately apparent. The Buddha illustrates this with similes of a chook sitting on eggs, the wearing away of an axe handle, and the rotting of a ship’s rigging.

children.title: The Perception of Impermanence
children.description: The perception of impermanence eliminates lust, ignorance, and conceit. Illustrated with a long series of similes.

children.title: Ends
children.description: The aggregates considered in light of the four noble truths, phrased as “portions” or “sides”.

children.title: Suffering
children.description: The aggregates considered in light of the four noble truths in terms of suffering.

children.title: Substantial Reality
children.description: The aggregates considered in light of the four noble truths in terms of identity.

children.title: Should Be Completely Understood
children.description: The aggregates are to be fully understood, ending the defilements is the full understanding of them, and an arahant is the one who has achieved this.

children.title: Ascetics (1st)
children.description: Only a true ascetic fully understands the five aggregates.

children.title: Ascetics (2nd)
children.description: Only a true ascetic fully understands the five aggregates.

children.title: A Stream-Enterer
children.description: One who truly understand these five aggregates is a stream-enterer.

children.title: A Perfected One
children.description: One who truly understand these five aggregates and is freed from them is a perfected one.

children.title: Giving Up Desire
children.description: Give up desire for the aggregates and they will come to an end.

children.title: Giving Up Desire (2nd)
children.description: Give up desire for the aggregates and they will come to an end.

children.title: Ignorance
children.description: Ignorance is not understanding the aggregates.

children.title: Knowledge
children.description: Knowledge is understanding the aggregates.

children.title: A Dhamma speaker
children.description: A true Dhamma speaker teaches for letting go of the aggregates.

children.title: A Dhamma speaker (2nd)
children.description: A true Dhamma speaker teaches for letting go of the aggregates.

children.title: Shackles
children.description: An unawakened person is bound both internally and externally to the aggregates and grows old in bondage.

children.title: Questioning
children.description: The Buddha questions the mendicants on the aggregates.

children.title: Questioning (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha questions the mendicants on the aggregates.

children.title: Things That Tighten Fetters
children.description: The aggregates are the things that fetter, the craving is the fetter.

children.title: Things That Fuel Grasping
children.description: The aggregates are the things that are graspable, the craving is the grasping.

children.title: An Ethical Mendicant
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita asks what an ethical mendicant should focus on, and Sāriputta replies that if they focus on aggregates as impermanent, etc. they may become a stream-enterer. A stream-enterer contemplating in the same way may become a non-returner, a once-returner, and a perfected one.

children.title: Learned
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita asks what an educated mendicant should focus on, and Sāriputta replies that if they focus on aggregates as impermanent, etc. they may become a stream-enterer. A stream-enterer contemplating in the same way may become a non-returner, a once-returner, and a perfected one.

children.title: With Kappa
children.description: Venerable Kappa asks the Buddha how to see so as to let go of conceit. The Buddha tells him to contemplate the aggregates in terms of not-self.

children.title: With Kappa (2nd)
children.description: Venerable Kappa asks the Buddha how to see so as to let go of conceit and be freed. The Buddha tells him to contemplate the aggregates in terms of not-self.

children.title: Liable to Originate
children.description: The Buddha explains to a mendicant that ignorance is not understanding the aggregates in terms of arising and ceasing, while knowledge is understanding the aggregates.

children.title: Liable to Originate (2nd)
children.description: Sāriputta explains to Mahākoṭṭhita that ignorance is not understanding the aggregates in terms of arising and ceasing.

children.title: Liable to Originate (3rd)
children.description: Sāriputta explains to Mahākoṭṭhita that knowledge is understanding the aggregates in terms of arising and ceasing.

children.title: Gratification
children.description: Sāriputta explains to Mahākoṭṭhita that ignorance is not understanding the aggregates in terms of gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: Gratification (2nd)
children.description: Sāriputta explains to Mahākoṭṭhita that knowledge is understanding the aggregates in terms of gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: Origin
children.description: Sāriputta explains to Mahākoṭṭhita that ignorance is not understanding the aggregates in terms of arising and ceasing, gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: Origin (2nd)
children.description: Sāriputta explains to Mahākoṭṭhita that knowledge is understanding the aggregates in terms of arising and ceasing, gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: With Koṭṭhita
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita explains to Sāriputta that ignorance is not understanding the aggregates in terms of gratification, drawback, and escape, while knowledge is understanding the aggregates.

children.title: With Koṭṭhita (2nd)
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita explains to Sāriputta that ignorance is not understanding the aggregates in terms of arising and ceasing, gratification, drawback, and escape, while knowledge is understanding the aggregates.

children.title: With Koṭṭhita (3rd)
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita explains to Sāriputta that ignorance is not understanding the aggregates in terms of the four noble truths, while knowledge is understanding the aggregates.

children.title: Burning Chaff
children.description: The aggregates are like burning chaff.

children.title: Impermanence
children.description: Give up desire for what is impermanent, i.e. the aggregates.

children.title: Impermanence (2nd)
children.description: Give up lust for what is impermanent, i.e. the aggregates.

children.title: Impermanence (3rd)
children.description: Give up desire and lust for what is impermanent, i.e. the aggregates.

children.title: Suffering
children.description: Give up desire for what is suffering, i.e. the aggregates.

children.title: Suffering (2nd)
children.description: Give up lust for what is suffering, i.e. the aggregates.

children.title: Suffering (3rd)
children.description: Give up desire and lust for what is suffering, i.e. the aggregates.

children.title: Not-Self
children.description: Give up desire for what is not-self, i.e. the aggregates.

children.title: Not-Self (2nd)
children.description: Give up lust for what is not-self, i.e. the aggregates.

children.title: Not-Self (3rd)
children.description: Give up desire and lust for what is not-self, i.e. the aggregates.

children.title: Full of Disillusionment
children.description: One gone forth should dwell full of disillusionment for the aggregates.

children.title: Observing Impermanence
children.description: One gone forth should dwell contemplating impermanence in the aggregates.

children.title: Observing Suffering
children.description: One gone forth should dwell contemplating suffering in the aggregates.

children.title: Observing Not-Self
children.description: One gone forth should dwell contemplating not-self in the aggregates.

children.title: In Oneself
children.description: Pleasure and pain arise inside oneself due to grasping the aggregates.

children.title: This is Mine
children.description: The ideas of “me’ and “mine” arise due to grasping the aggregates.

children.title: This is My Self
children.description: The idea that the self is identical with the cosmos arises due to grasping the aggregates.

children.title: It Might Not Be Mine
children.description: Even subtle forms of self identification arise due to grasping the aggregates.

children.title: Wrong View
children.description: Wrong view arises due to grasping the aggregates.

children.title: Substantialist View
children.description: Identity view arises due to grasping the aggregates.

children.title: Theory of Self
children.description: View of self arises due to grasping the aggregates.

children.title: Insistence
children.description: Fetters and shackles arise due to grasping the aggregates.

children.title: Insistence (2nd)
children.description: Fetters and holding arise due to grasping the aggregates.

children.title: With Ānanda
children.description: When Ānanda wants to go on retreat, the Buddha advises him to contemplate the aggregates

children.title: 2. Rādha
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Rādha” contains 46 discourses with a monk named Rādha on the topic of the five aggregates, and may be considered as an appendix to the previous saṁyutta.

children.title: About Māra
children.description: Rādha asks the Buddha about Māra, and the Buddha explains in terms of the five aggregates. Seeing in this way leads to freedom.

children.title: Sentient Beings
children.description: Rādha asks the Buddha about a the term “sentient being”, and the Buddha explains in terms of craving for the five aggregates. He compares such craving to a child playing with sandcastles.

children.title: The Leash to Existence
children.description: Rādha asks the Buddha about the tie or conduit to rebirth, and the Buddha explains in terms of craving for the five aggregates.

children.title: Should Be Completely Understood
children.description: The aggregates are to be fully understood, ending the defilements is the full understanding of them, and an arahant is the one who has achieved this.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins
children.description: Only a true ascetic fully understands the five aggregates.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: Only a true ascetic fully understands the five aggregates.

children.title: A Stream-Enterer
children.description: One who truly understand these five aggregates is a stream-enterer.

children.title: A Perfected One
children.description: One who truly understand these five aggregates and is freed from them is a perfected one.

children.title: Desire and Greed
children.description: Give up desire for the aggregates and they will come to an end.

children.title: Desire and Greed (2nd)
children.description: Give up desire for the aggregates and they will come to an end.

children.title: About Māra

children.title: 3. Views
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Views” contains 96 discourses on views, methodically analyzed through the lens of the aggregates. A wide variety of views is assessed, most of which are familiar from elsewhere in the canon, although the first one is unique.

children.title: Winds
children.description: The Buddha mentions a strange view to the effect that all changing phenomena of the world are really still and motionless. Such a view arises from grasping to the five aggregates. But by seeing the aggregates, as well as what is seen, heard, thought, and known, as impermanent, such a view is given up and one becomes a stream-enterer.

children.title: This is Mine
children.description: The view of me and mine is given up by seeing the aggregates, as well as what is seen, heard, thought, and known, as impermanent.

children.title: This is My Self

children.title: It Might Not Be Mine

children.title: There’s No Meaning in Giving

children.title: Acting

children.title: Cause

children.title: The Extensive View

children.title: The Cosmos is Eternal
children.description: The view that the cosmos is eternal is given up by seeing the aggregates, as well as what is seen, heard, thought, and known, as impermanent.

children.title: The Cosmos is Not Eternal

children.title: The Cosmos is Infinite

children.title: The Soul and the Body are One and the Same
children.description: The view that the soul is the same thing as the body is given up by seeing the aggregates, as well as what is seen, heard, thought, and known, as impermanent.

children.title: The Soul is One Thing, the Body Another
children.description: The view that the soul and the body are different things is given up by seeing the aggregates, as well as what is seen, heard, thought, and known, as impermanent.

children.title: A Realized One Still Exists

children.title: A Realized One No Longer Exists

children.description: The view that a realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death is given up by seeing the aggregates, as well as what is seen, heard, thought, and known, as impermanent.

children.title: Winds

children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Arrival” is the first of three similar sections, each of which takes a set of ten doctrinal items (shared also with SN 18 Rāhula) and presents it according to a set pattern. children.title: 7. Sāriputta
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Sāriputta” describes Sāriputta’s deep meditation practice, and his conversations with Ānanda, who noticed how radiant and glowing he was. An exception to this pattern is the final sutta, which depicts Sāriputta responding to the challenges of a female wanderer.

children.title: Born of Seclusion
children.description: Sāriputta goes to Mirkwood for meditation, and afterwards Ānanda asks why his face is so radiant. Sāriputta replies that he was practicing first absorption without any thought of self.

children.title: Better

The current chapter shows him repeatedly raising the question of the ten speculative views, and why they appear. The discourses are entirely formulaic and appear to have been produced from a template. Unusually for a section of this length, it lacks vaggas.

4. the Six Sense Fields
children.description: The “Book of the Six Sense Fields” is the fourth of the five books of the Linked Discourses. It is named after the first and longest saṁyutta, which deals with the core Buddhist teaching of the six sense fields. The second saṁyutta on Feelings also deals with a major doctrinal topic. The remaining eight saṁyuttas deal with miscellaneous secondary themes, some organized by subject, others by person.

children.title: 1. Six Sense Fields
children.description: The number of discourses in the “Linked Discourses on the Six Sense Fields” varies between editions, mainly due to the way repetitions are counted; SuttaCentral follows Bhikkhu Bodhi’s translation in counting 248 discourses. The six sense fields complement the five aggregates as the summary of the noble truth of suffering. Where the aggregates focus on the functional structure of experience as basis for views of self, the emphasis here is on how sense experience stimulates desire. Despite this difference in orientation, the two collections share much in common, and often the exact same template is applied in both cases. The six sense fields are the means through which the world is known, and so each of them has an “inner” and an “outer” aspect—the “eye” and “sights”, etc. Though common, it’s best to avoid thinking of the external sense field as the “object”, since in the suttas they are depicted in relation to the observing mind, and not as independently existing entities. This is straightforward until we come to the last sense, the “mind” and “thoughts” or “mental phenomena”. Just to clear up a possible confusion, this “sixth sense” is simply the mental faculty, and has nothing to do with psychic powers. The outer aspect is dhammā, a term so ambiguous its translation is always difficult. Here it refers to anything that may be known directly by the mind, distinct from the five senses. The most technically correct translation is probably “mental phenomena”, but “thought’ may be used as a more colloquial rendering, so long as it includes ideas, imagination, and so on, not just verbalized cognition.

children.title: The Interior as Impermanent

children.description: In the past, future, and present, the six interior sense fields are impermanent, suffering, and not-self. When a noble disciple truly sees them like this, they become disillusioned and liberated.

children.title: The Interior as Suffering in the Three Times
children.description: In the past, future, and present, the six interior sense fields are suffering and not-self. When a noble disciple truly sees them like this, they become disillusioned and liberated.

children.title: The Interior as Not-Self in the Three Times
children.description: In the past, future, and present, the six interior sense fields are not-self. When a noble disciple truly sees them like this, they become disillusioned and liberated.

children.title: The Exterior as Impermanent in the Three Times
children.description: In the past, future, and present, the six exterior sense fields are impermanent, suffering, and not-self. When a noble disciple truly sees them like this, they become disillusioned and liberated.

children.title: The Exterior as Suffering in the Three Times
children.description: In the past, future, and present, the six exterior sense fields are suffering and not-self. When a noble disciple truly sees them like this, they become disillusioned and liberated.

children.title: The Exterior as Not-Self in the Three Times
children.description: In the past, future, and present, the six exterior sense fields are not-self. When a noble disciple truly sees them like this, they become disillusioned and liberated.

children.title: Before My Awakening (Interior)
children.description: The Buddha did not claim to be awakened until he had fully understood the gratification, drawback, and escape regarding the six interior sense fields.

children.title: Before My Awakening (Exterior)
children.description: The Buddha did not claim to be awakened until he had fully understood the gratification, drawback, and escape regarding the six exterior sense fields.

children.title: In Search of Gratification (Interior)
children.description: The Buddha set out to find the gratification, drawback, and escape regarding the six interior sense fields.

children.title: In Search of Gratification (Exterior)
children.description: The Buddha set out to find the gratification, drawback, and escape regarding the six exterior sense fields.

children.title: If There Were No Gratification (Interior)
children.description: Beings are attached to the six interior sense fields due to gratification, repelled due to drawbacks, and find escape because there is an escape.

children.title: If There Were No Gratification (Exterior)
children.description: Beings are attached to the six exterior sense fields due to gratification, repelled due to drawbacks, and find escape because there is an escape.

children.title: Taking Pleasure (Interior)
children.description: If you enjoy the six interior sense fields, you enjoy suffering.

children.title: Taking Pleasure (Exterior)
children.description: If you enjoy the six exterior sense fields, you enjoy suffering.

children.title: The Arising of Suffering (Interior)
children.description: The arising of the six interior sense fields is the arising of suffering.

children.title: The Arising of Suffering (Exterior)
children.description: The arising of the six exterior sense fields is the arising of suffering.

children.title: All
children.description: The “all” consists of the six interior and exterior sense fields.

children.title: Giving Up
children.description: The “all” consisting of the six interior and exterior sense fields should be given up.

children.title: Giving Up By Direct Knowledge and Complete Understanding
children.description: The “all” consisting of the six interior and exterior sense fields should be given up by understanding.

children.title: Without Completely Understanding (1st)
children.description: Without understanding the “all” consisting of the six interior and exterior sense fields and becoming dispassionate towards it, it is impossible to be free of suffering.

children.title: Without Completely Understanding (2nd)
children.description: Without understanding the “all” consisting of the six interior and exterior sense fields and the associated consciousness and becoming dispassionate towards it, it is impossible to be free of suffering.

children.title: Burning
children.description: The “all” consisting of the six interior and exterior sense fields is burning. This is the famous “third sermon” taught at Gayā’s Head to the followers of the three Kassapa brothers.

children.title: Overcome
children.description: The “all” consisting of the six interior and exterior sense fields, and the phenomena they condition, is weighed down.

children.title: The Practice Fit for Uprooting
children.description: The way to uproot all conceivings is to not conceive in relation to the six sense fields.

children.title: The Practice Conducive to Uprooting (1st)
children.description: The way to uproot all conceivings is to not conceive in relation to the six sense fields.

children.title: The Practice Conducive to Uprooting (2nd)
children.description: The way to uproot all conceivings is to investigate the six sense fields as impermanent, etc.

children.title: Ten on Liable to Be Reborn, Etc.
children.description: The “all” consisting of the six interior and exterior sense fields is liable to be reborn, to age, etc.

children.title: Nine on Impermanence, Etc.
children.description: The “all” consisting of the six interior and exterior sense fields is impermanent, etc.

children.title: Contaminated
children.description: The “all” consisting of the six interior and exterior sense fields is afflicted.

children.title: Giving Up Ignorance
children.description: A mendicant asks the Buddha how to see so as to give up ignorance. The Buddha says one should see the six interior and exterior sense fields as impermanent.

children.title: Giving Up Fetters
children.description: A mendicant asks the Buddha how to see so as to give up the fetters. The Buddha says one should see the six interior and exterior sense fields as impermanent.

children.title: Uprooting the Fetters
children.description: A mendicant asks the Buddha how to see so as to uproot the fetters. The Buddha says one should see the six interior and exterior sense fields as not-self.

children.title: Giving Up Defilements
children.description: A mendicant asks the Buddha how to see so as to give up the defilements. The Buddha says one should see the six interior and exterior sense fields as impermanent.

children.title: Uprooting Defilements
children.description: A mendicant asks the Buddha how to see so as to uproot the defilements. The Buddha says one should see the six interior and exterior sense fields as not-self.

children.title: Giving Up Tendencies
children.description: A mendicant asks the Buddha how to see so as to give up the underlying tendencies. The Buddha says one should see the six interior and exterior sense fields as impermanent.

children.title: Uprooting Tendencies
children.description: A mendicant asks the Buddha how to see so as to uproot the underlying tendencies. The Buddha says one should see the six interior and exterior sense fields as not-self.

children.title: The Complete Understanding of All Grasping
children.description: To fully understand grasping, see how sense experience gives rise to feeling.

children.title: The Depletion of All Fuel for Grasping (1st)
children.description: To end grasping, see how sense experience gives rise to feeling.

children.title: The Depletion of All Fuel for Grasping (2nd)
children.description: To end grasping, investigate the six sense fields as impermanent, etc.

children.title: With Migajāla (1st)
children.description: Venerable Migajāla asks how one lives alone, and how with a partner. The Buddha says that so long as one is bound by desire to the senses, one lives with a partner. A mendicant free of such desire dwells alone, even if they live in close association with worldly people.

children.title: With Migajāla (2nd)
children.description: Venerable Migajāla asks for a teaching to take on retreat. The Buddha teaches him that the senses are delightful, but if you hold to them you will suffer. Meditating on this while on retreat, Migajāla became awakened.

children.title: Samiddhi’s Question About Māra
children.description: Venerable Samiddhi asks the Buddha what Māra is. The Buddha says that Māra is present so long as the senses exist.

children.title: Samiddhi’s Question About a Sentient Being
children.description: Venerable Samiddhi asks the Buddha what a “sentient being” is. The Buddha says that a sentient being is present so long as the senses exist.

children.title: Samiddhi’s Question About Suffering
children.description: Venerable Samiddhi asks the Buddha what suffering is. The Buddha says that suffering is present so long as the senses exist.

children.title: Samiddhi’s Question About the World
children.description: Venerable Samiddhi asks the Buddha what the world is. The Buddha says that the world is present so long as the senses exist.

children.title: Upasena and the Viper
children.description: A viper bit Venerable Upasena, but he remained poised, declaring that he had no identification with the six senses.

children.title: Upavāṇa on What is Apparent in the Present Life
children.description: The teaching that can be realized in this very life is the desire for the senses, and letting go of that desire.

children.title: Six Fields of Contact (1st)
children.description: One who does not understand the six senses’ origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape is no true mendicant. A mendicant speaks up, saying that he does not truly understand these things, so the Buddha teaches him further.

children.title: Six Fields of Contact (2nd)
children.description: One who does not understand the six senses’ origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape is no true mendicant. A mendicant speaks up, saying that he does not truly understand these things, so the Buddha teaches him further.

children.title: Six Fields of Contact (3rd)
children.description: One who does not understand the six senses’ origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape is no true mendicant. A mendicant speaks up, saying that he does not truly understand these things, so the Buddha teaches him further.

children.title: Sick (1st)
children.description: Hearing that a newly-ordained mendicant was sick, the Buddha visited him to offer support and Dhamma encouragement.

children.title: Sick (2nd)
children.description: Hearing that a newly-ordained mendicant was sick, the Buddha visited him to offer support and Dhamma encouragement.

children.title: With Rādha on Impermanence
children.description: Venerable Rādha asks for a teaching to take on retreat. The Buddha told him to abandon desire for sense experience, which is impermanent.

children.title: With Rādha on Suffering
children.description: Venerable Rādha asks for a teaching to take on retreat. The Buddha told him to abandon desire for sense experience, which is suffering.

children.title: With Rādha on Not-Self
children.description: Venerable Rādha asks for a teaching to take on retreat. The Buddha told him to abandon desire for sense experience, which is not-self.

children.title: Giving Up Ignorance (1st)
children.description: Through giving up ignorance, knowledge arises. To do this, contemplate the six senses as impermanent.

children.title: Giving Up Ignorance (2nd)
children.description: Through giving up ignorance, knowledge arises. To do this, contemplate the six senses as impermanent. Then a mendicant truly understands, and sees everything differently.

children.title: Several Mendicants
children.description: Some mendicants check with the Buddha that it’s correct to say that the spiritual life is lived to end suffering. The Buddha answers that it is, and explains what that suffering is: the process of sense experience.

children.title: A Question On the World
children.description: The “world” consisting of six sense experience is said to be falling apart.

children.title: Phagguna’s Question
children.description: The Buddhas of the past cannot be described in terms of the six senses.

children.title: Liable to Wear Out
children.description: The Buddha tells Ānanda that in the training of the Noble One the “world” consisting of six sense experience is liable to wear out.

children.title: The World is Empty
children.description: The Buddha tells Ānanda that the “world” consisting of six sense experience is empty because it is empty of self and what belongs to self.

children.title: A Teaching In Brief
children.description: Ānanda asks for a teaching to take on retreat. The Buddha teaches him that the senses are impermanent, etc.

children.title: With Channa
children.description: Sāriputta and Mahācunda visit Channa, who is ill. Channa says that he lacks for no care, but is in such great pain that he wishes to take his own life, insisting that he will do so blamelessly. Sāriputta tries to dissuade him, and questions him closely about attachment to the six senses. Later Channa does take his own life, and the Buddha confirmed that, despite Sāriputta’s doubts, he was indeed blameless.

children.title: With Puṇṇa
children.description: Venerable Puṇṇa goes to the Buddha and asks for a teaching before he departs to the foreign land of Sunāparanta. The Buddha warns him that folk there are fierce, and questions whether he is ready for such a difficult assignment.

children.title: With Bāhiya
children.description: Venerable Bāhiya asks for a teaching to take on retreat. The Buddha teaches him that the senses are impermanent, etc.

children.title: Turbulence (1st)
children.description: Being stirred by craving is painful, so the Realized One lives unstirred, not identifying with any aspect of sense experience.

children.title: Turbulence (2nd)
children.description: Being stirred by craving is painful, so the Realized One lives unstirred, not identifying with any aspect of sense experience, or indeed, with the entire scope of the aggregates, elements, and senses.

children.title: A Duality (1st)
children.description: The dyad is the interior sense organ with its corresponding exterior sense stimulus.

children.title: A Duality (2nd)
children.description: Consciousness arises from the dyad of the interior sense organ with its corresponding exterior sense stimulus. All these things are conditioned, impermanent, and constantly falling apart.

children.title: Untamed, Unguarded
children.description: The six fields of contact lead to suffering if left unguarded, but if guarded lead to happiness. A lengthy set of verses illustrate this.

children.title: Māluṅkyaputta
children.description: Venerable Māluṅkyaputta asks for a teaching to take on retreat. The Buddha wonders how to teach an old monk like him, then questions him on his desire for sense experience that has been or might be, and encourages him to simply let sense experience be. Māluṅkyaputta says he understands, and expands the Buddha’s teaching in a series of verses.

children.title: Liable to Decline
children.description: When a mendicant tolerates evil thoughts that arise from the senses, they are liable to decline. If they don’t tolerate them, they’re not liable to decline. When such thoughts not longer arise, they have mastered the senses.

children.title: One Who Lives Negligently
children.description: When a mendicant lives without restraint regarding the senses, they are negligent. If they have restraint, they are diligent.

children.title: Restraint
children.description: Non-restraint is delighting in the senses, restraint is not delighting in them.

children.title: Immersion
children.description: Develop meditative immersion so as to truly understand the process of sense experience.

children.title: Retreat
children.description: Develop seclusion so as to truly understand the process of sense experience.

children.title: It’s Not Yours (1st)
children.description: Let go of what is not yours: the process of sense experience. You wouldn’t be upset if someone took the grass and sticks from the monastery grounds, so why worry over the aggregates?

children.title: It’s Not Yours (2nd)
children.description: Let go of what is not yours: the process of sense experience.

children.title: About Uddaka
children.description: The Buddha’s former teacher Uddaka Rāmaputta claimed to be a knowledge master, a universal victor, who had excised the tumor. But a true knowledge master understands the senses, a victor is freed from them, and excising the tumor is being free from attachment to the body.

children.title: Sanctuary from the Yoke
children.description: Someone who has given up attraction to the senses has arrived at the sanctuary.

children.title: Because of Grasping
children.description: Pleasure and pain arise inside oneself due to grasping the senses.

children.title: The Origin of Suffering
children.description: The origin and ending of suffering are explained in terms of sense experience giving rise to craving.

children.title: The Origin of the World
children.description: The origin and ending of the world are explained in terms of sense experience giving rise to craving and suffering.

children.title: I’m Better
children.description: Conceit stems from clinging to the senses.

children.title: Things That Tighten Fetters
children.description: The interior sense fields are the things that fetter, the craving is the fetter.

children.title: Things That Fuel Grasping
children.description: The interior sense fields are the things that are graspable, the craving is the grasping.

children.title: Complete Understanding of the Interior
children.description: Without understanding the six interior sense fields and becoming dispassionate towards them, it is impossible to be free of suffering.

children.title: Complete Understanding of the Exterior
children.description: Without understanding the six exterior sense fields and becoming dispassionate towards them, it is impossible to be free of suffering.

children.title: Listening In
children.description: While on retreat, the Buddha exclaims how the origin and ending of the world are explained in terms of sense experience giving rise to craving and suffering. A mendicant overhears him, and the Buddha urges him to remember that teaching.

children.title: 2. World and the Kinds of Sensual Stimulation
Māra’s Snare (1st)
children.description: A mendicant who craves the senses is under the sway of Māra.

children.title: Māra’s Snare (2nd)
children.description: A mendicant who craves the senses is under the sway of Māra.

children.title: Traveling to the End of the World
children.description: The Buddha states that the end of the world cannot be reached by traveling, yet it is impossible to end suffering without reaching the end of the world. The mendicants ask Ānanda to explain this enigmatic statement.

children.title: The Kinds of Sensual Stimulation
children.description: While practicing for awakening, the Buddha reflected that he should be diligent when his mind strayed to sense pleasures of the past, future, or present. He urges the mendicants to realize that place where the senses completely cease, and they ask Ānanda to explain this to them.

children.title: The Question of Sakka
children.description: Sakka asks the Buddha why some become awakened in this very life, while others do not.

children.title: The Question of Pañcasikha
children.description: The fairy Pañcasikha asks the Buddha why some become awakened in this very life, while others do not.

children.title: Sāriputta and the Protégé
children.description: A mendicant informs Sāriputta that one of his friends had disrobed. Sāriputta attributes this to lack of sense restraint, eating too much, and not being wakeful.

children.title: Advice to Rāhula
children.description: Realizing that his son Rāhula was ripe for awakening, the Buddha takes him for a personal teaching. He questions Rāhula on the impermanence of all the factors of sense experience, leading Rāhula to realize full freedom.

children.title: Things That Tighten Fetters
children.description: The exterior sense fields are the things that fetter, the craving is the fetter.

children.title: Things That Fuel Grasping
children.description: The exterior sense fields are the things that are graspable, the craving is the grasping.

children.title: At Vesālī
children.description: At the Great Wood, the householder Ugga of Vesālī asks the Buddha why some become awakened in this very life, while others do not.

children.title: In the Land of the Vajjis
children.description: At Hatthigāma, the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma asks the Buddha why some become awakened in this very life, while others do not.

children.title: At Nāḷandā
children.description: At Nālandā, the householder Upāli asks the Buddha why some become awakened in this very life, while others do not.

children.title: With Bhāradvāja
children.description: King Udena of Kosambi asks Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja how even young monks can maintain the celibate life. Piṇḍola says it’s because they see women as their sisters, mothers, or daughters. If this doesn’t work, they meditate on the ugliness of the body. Finally they exercise sense restraint.

children.title: With Soṇa
children.description: At Rājagaha, the householder Soṇa asks the Buddha why some become awakened in this very life, while others do not.

children.title: With Ghosita
children.description: The householder Ghosita asks Ānanda about the diversity of elements, and he answers in terms of the elements of sense experience.

children.title: With Hāliddikāni
children.description: The householder Hāliddakāni asks Mahākaccāna about the relation between the diversity of elements and the diversity of contacts, and he answers in terms of the elements of sense experience.

children.title: Nakula’s Father
children.description: At Suṁsumāragira, the householder Nakulapitā asks the Buddha why some become awakened in this very life, while others do not.

children.title: With Lohicca
children.description: Students of the brahmin Lohicca make a racket while collecting firewood near Mahākaccāna’s hut. Mahākaccāna hushes them and recites a series of verses contrasting the virtuous brahmins of old with those of today. Taking umbrage, they tell Lohicca, who goes to Mahākaccāna to ascertain the truth. But when Lohicca hears what Mahākaccāna teach on the six senses, he is so impressed he goes for refuge.

children.title: Verahaccāni
children.description: A student of the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan recommends to her the teaching of Venerable Udāyı̄, so she invites him for a meal. But when she displays a conceited attitude, he leaves without teaching. However, she corrects herself so he teaches her that pleasure and pain depend on the senses.

children.title: At Devadaha
children.description: Not all mendicants have completed their work with regards to the six senses, but some of them have.

children.title: Opportunity
children.description: The Buddha speaks of the hell named the “six senses” where all one experiences is sheer pain and unpleasantness.

children.title: Liking Sights (1st)
children.description: Gods and humans take delight in the six sense, but the Realized One does not. This teaching is illustrated with a long series of verses.

children.title: Liking Sights (2nd)
children.description: Gods and humans take delight in the six sense, but the Realized One does not.

children.title: Not Yours (1st)
children.description: Let go of what is not yours: the six interior sense fields. You wouldn’t be upset if someone took the grass and sticks from the monastery grounds, so why worry over the senses?

children.title: Not Yours (2nd)
children.description: Let go of what is not yours: the six exterior sense fields. You wouldn’t be upset if someone took the grass and sticks from the monastery grounds, so why worry over the senses?

children.title: Interior and Cause Are Impermanent
children.description: Since the causes of the six interior sense fields are impermanent, how can the senses be permanent?

children.title: Interior and Cause Are Suffering
children.description: Since the causes of the six interior sense fields are suffering, how can the senses be free of suffering?

children.title: Interior and Cause Are Not-Self
children.description: Since the causes of the six interior sense fields are not-self, how can the senses be self?

children.title: Exterior and Cause Are Impermanent
children.description: Since the causes of the six exterior sense fields are impermanent, how can the senses be permanent?

children.title: Exterior and Cause Are Suffering
children.description: Since the causes of the six exterior sense fields are suffering, how can the senses be free of suffering?

children.title: Exterior and Cause Are Not-Self
children.description: Since the causes of the six exterior sense fields are not-self, how can the senses be self?

children.title: The Cessation of Deeds
children.description: The six interior sense fields are not yours, but are old kamma, generated by choices in past lives. This is explained in terms of the four noble truths.

children.title: The Impermanent as Conducive to Extinguishment
children.description: The way suitable for realizing extinguishment is to contemplate the process of sense experience as impermanent.

children.title: The Suffering as Conducive to Extinguishment
children.description: The way suitable for realizing extinguishment is to contemplate the process of sense experience as suffering.

children.title: Not-Self as Conducive to Extinguishment
children.description: The way suitable for realizing extinguishment is to contemplate the process of sense experience as not-self.

children.title: A Practice Conducive to Extinguishment
children.description: The way suitable for realizing extinguishment is to contemplate the process of sense experience as impermanent, suffering, and not-self.

children.title: A Resident Pupil
children.description: One with no “student” and no “teacher” dwells in happiness. Here the Buddha plays with the Pali words such that “student” means “one who dwells within” and “teacher” means “one who assails”.

children.title: What’s the Goal of the Spiritual Life?
children.description: If anyone asks why we live the holy life, it is for the ending of suffering.

children.title: Is There a Method?
children.description: How is it that a mendicant can declare their awakening? By understanding whether any desire arises from sense stimuli.

children.title: Endowed With Faculties
children.description: One is accomplished in the sense faculties by being freed from attachment to them.

children.title: A Dhamma Speaker
children.description: A speaker on the Dhamma is someone who teaches for letting go of the senses.

children.title: The Interior and the End of Relishing
children.description: Right view is seeing the interior sense fields as they are, impermanent, and this leads to freedom.

children.title: The Exterior and the End of Relishing
children.description: Right view is seeing the exterior sense fields as they are, impermanent, and this leads to freedom.

children.title: Focus, the Interior, and the End of Relishing
children.description: Focusing properly on the interior sense fields you see them as they are and become free.

children.title: Focus, the Exterior, and the End of Relishing
children.description: Focusing properly on the exterior sense fields you see them as they are and become free.

children.title: On Immersion at Jīvaka’s Mango Grove
children.description: A mendicant should develop immersion (samādhi) in order to truly understand the origin and ending of the process of sense experience.

children.title: On Retreat at Jīvaka’s Mango Grove
children.description: A mendicant should make an effort in seclusion in order to truly understand the origin and ending of the process of sense experience.

children.title: With Koṭṭhita on Impermanence
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita asks for a teaching to take on retreat. The Buddha says to give up desire for what is impermanent, i.e. the process of sense experience.

children.title: With Koṭṭhita on Suffering
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita asks for a teaching to take on retreat. The Buddha says to give up desire for what is suffering, i.e. the process of sense experience.

children.title: With Koṭṭhita on Not-Self
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita asks for a teaching to take on retreat. The Buddha says to give up desire for what is not-self, i.e. the process of sense experience.

children.title: Giving Up Wrong View
children.description: Wrong view arises due to grasping the process of sense experience.

children.title: Giving Up Substantialist View
children.description: Identity view arises due to grasping the process of sense experience.

children.title: Giving Up Theory of Self
children.description: View of self arises due to grasping the process of sense experience.

children.title: Desire and Greed for the Impermanent Interior
Desire, Etc. for the Suffering Interior
Desire, Etc. for the Not-Self Interior
Desire, Etc. for the Impermanent Exterior
Desire, Etc. for the Suffering Exterior
Desire, Etc. for the Not-Self Exterior
The Interior Was Impermanent in the Past
The Interior Will Be Impermanent in the Future
The Interior is Impermanent in the Present
The Interior as Suffering in the Three Times
The Interior as Not-Self in the Three Times
The Exterior as Impermanent in the Three Times
The Exterior as Suffering in the Three Times
The Exterior as Not-Self in the Three Times
The Interior and What’s Impermanent in the Past
The Interior and What’s Impermanent in the Future
The Interior and What’s Impermanent in the Present
The Interior and What’s Suffering in the Three Times
The Interior and What’s Not-Self in the Three Times
The Exterior and What’s Impermanent in the Three Times
The Exterior and What’s Suffering in the Three Times
The Exterior and What’s Not-Self in the Three Times
The Ocean (1st)
children.description: In the Buddha’s teaching the “ocean” is the sense organs, the current is the sense objects.

children.title: The Ocean (2nd)
children.description: In the Buddha’s teaching the “ocean” is the delights of sense stimuli.

children.title: The Simile of the Angler
children.description: Sense pleasures are like a baited hook.

children.title: The Simile of the Latex-Producing Tree
children.description: Like a tree that yields sap when cut, so long as desire is present it will be activated by the senses.

children.title: With Koṭṭhita
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita asks Sāriputta whether the interior and exterior sense fields are the fetters of each other. No; it is desire that is the fetter, like the yoke that binds two oxen. One with no desire still experiences the senses but without fetters.

children.title: With Kāmabhū
children.description: Kāmabhū asks Ānanda whether the interior and exterior sense fields are the fetters of each other. No; it is desire that is the fetter. One with no desire still experiences the senses but without fetters.

children.title: With Udāyī
children.description: Udāyı̄ notes to Ānanda that the Buddha has taught the body as not-self; what then of consciousness? Ānanda then explains how consciousness arises dependent on conditions.

children.title: The Exposition on Burning
children.description: It would be better for the sense organs to be pierced with red-hot spikes than to get attached to a pleasant sense experience.

children.title: The Simile of Hands and Feet (1st)
children.description: So long as this body exists there is suffering due to the senses.

children.title: The Simile of Hands and Feet (2nd)
children.description: So long as this body exists there is suffering due to the senses.

children.title: The Simile of the Vipers
children.description: The Buddha strings a series of powerful similes—vipers, murderers, an empty village, and more—into an extended parable of the dangers of existence and the way of escape.

children.title: The Simile of the Chariot
children.description: When a mendicant has three qualities they live happily: sense restraint, moderation in eating, and wakefulness.

children.title: The Simile of the Tortoise
children.description: A parable of a jackal who fails to eat a tortoise who stays still, with limbs retracted, like a mendicant guarding the senses.

children.title: The Simile of the Tree Trunk (1st)
children.description: The Buddha gives a parable of a large log floating downstream, which, if it steers clear of the many obstacles, will eventually reach the ocean. A mendicant asks for an explanation, and the Buddha clarifies each item. A cowherd named Nanda was listening, and determined to go forth.

children.title: The Simile of the Tree Trunk (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha gives a parable of a large log floating downstream, which, if it steers clear of the many obstacles, will eventually reach the ocean. Venerable Kimbila asks for an explanation, and the Buddha clarifies each item.

children.title: The Explanation on the Festering
children.description: The Buddha is invited to teach in a new hall in Kapilavatthu. Late at night, after teaching the Sakyans, the Buddha invites Moggallāna to teach. He speaks on the mental corruption that flows from attachment to the senses.

children.title: Entailing Suffering
children.description: The Buddha defines the things that entail suffering as the five aggregates, and urges mendicants to be free of desire for the six senses, giving a series of vivid similes. He then speaks of how even for a mendicant practicing restraint a lapse of mindfulness might occur from time to time.

children.title: The Simile of the Parrot Tree
children.description: A mendicant goes to a series of teachers and asks how vision is purified. Dissatisfied with all their answers, he complains to the Buddha, who illustrates his quandary with the famous simile of the Kiṁsuka tree. Just as the same Kiṁsuka tree might be described differently by people focusing on the leaves, or the fruit, or the bark, etc., so too the various teachers each speak of the aspect of Dhamma most meaningful to them.

children.title: The Simile of the Harp
children.description: One should restrain the senses like a farmer watching over a field. The Buddha gives the parable of a man bewitched when he first hears a lute. He takes apart the instrument in search of the sound, but is disillusioned when no sound is found.

children.title: The Simile of Six Animals
children.description: The senses are like a snake, a crocodile, a bird, a dog, a jackal, and a monkey all tied up together, pulling this way and that. Mindfulness is like a post that keeps them grounded.

children.title: The Sheaf of Barley
children.description: The six senses are like a sheaf of barley struck with six flails; and the desire for rebirth is a seventh flail. The Buddha goes on to speak of the cunning trap of the gods; but the trap of Māra, conceit, is even more subtle.

children.title: 2. Feelings
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Feelings” contains 31 discourses on the three kinds of feeling. In Sinhalese-script manuscripts, this is reckoned as the last portion of the section on six sense fields. The term “feelings” renders vedanā, which is the simple affective or hedonic tone of experience as pleasant, painful, and neutral, rather than the complex states we call “emotions”. In the process of experience, feeling emerges from sense contact, and stimulates craving. One of the aims of mental development is to first loosen, then eliminate that second link, so that one still has feelings, but does not experience craving for them. The current collection includes a number of rich and significant discourses on this theme.

children.title: Immersion
children.description: There are three feelings, and a meditator practicing immersion can understand them.

children.title: Pleasure
children.description: There are three feelings, and all of them are suffering.

children.title: Giving Up
children.description: One should give up desire for pleasant feeling, aversion for painful feeling, and ignorance regarding neutral feeling.

children.title: The Abyss
children.description: Ordinary people think the ocean is a bottomless abyss; but really, it is the three feelings.

children.title: Should Be Seen
children.description: See pleasant feeling as painful, painful feeling as a dart, and neutral feeling as impermanent.

children.title: An Arrow
children.description: Both ordinary and awakened people experience the three feelings. The difference is that when an ordinary person is stricken with feeling, they react, creating more suffering, whereas an awakened person responds with equanimity.

children.title: The Infirmary (1st)
children.description: A mendicant should await their death mindful and aware. They should bear the feelings of approaching death with wisdom and equanimity.

children.title: The Infirmary (2nd)
children.description: A mendicant should await their death mindful and aware. They should bear the feelings of approaching death with wisdom and equanimity.

children.title: Impermanent
children.description: The three feelings are impermanent.

children.title: Rooted in Contact
children.description: The three feelings are each produced by the appropriate contact.

children.title: In Private
children.description: A mendicant wonders how there can be three kinds of feeling, yet all of them are suffering.

children.title: In the Atmosphere (1st)
children.description: Feelings arise in the body like winds blowing in the sky. With illustrative verses.

children.title: In the Atmosphere (2nd)
children.description: Feelings arise in the body like winds blowing in the sky.

children.title: A Guest House
children.description: Feelings arise in the body like guests in a hotel.

children.title: With Ānanda (1st)
children.description: The Buddha explains the feelings to Ānanda in terms of arising, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: With Ānanda (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha asks about the feelings to Ānanda in terms of arising, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: With Several Mendicants (1st)
children.description: The Buddha explains the feelings to several mendicants in terms of arising, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: With Several Mendicants (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha asks about the feelings to several mendicants in terms of arising, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: With Pañcakaṅga
children.description: The chamberlain Pañcakaṅga disagreed with Venerable Udāyī about how many kinds of feeling the Buddha taught. The Buddha affirms that each is a genuine teaching, valid in different contexts.

children.title: A Mendicant
children.description: The Buddha has taught many different kinds of feeling, valid in different contexts.

children.title: 3. Explanation of the Hundred and Eight
With Sīvaka
children.description: When the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka asks if all feelings are caused by karma in past lives. The Buddha denies this, asserting that feelings have many different causes.

children.title: The Explanation of the Hundred and Eight
children.description: The Buddha explains the different kinds of feelings analyzed into 108 aspects.

children.title: With a Mendicant
children.description: A mendicant asks the Buddha to explain the feelings in terms of the four noble truths.

children.title: Before
children.description: Before his awakening the Buddha reflected on feeling in terms of arising, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: Knowledge
children.description: At his awakening, the Buddha saw feeling in terms of arising, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: With Several Mendicants
children.description: Several mendicants ask the Buddha to explain the feelings in terms of the four noble truths.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (1st)
children.description: One who does not truly understand feeling is no true ascetic.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: One who does not truly understand feeling is no true ascetic.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (3rd)
children.description: One who does not truly understand feeling is no true ascetic.

children.title: Plain Version
children.description: There are three feelings: painful, pleasant, neutral.

children.title: Not of the Flesh
children.description: The Buddha explains feelings as spiritual and carnal, associated with worldly states and with deep meditation.

children.title: 3. Females
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Females” contains 34 discourses regarding various qualities of women. Note that the Pali texts use two distinct terms for women, itthī and mātugāma, the latter of which can be translated as “females”. These texts deal with such themes as the kinds of suffering unique to women, why women are reborn in various states, or the qualities that lead to a woman taking charge in her marriage.

children.title: A Lady
children.description: Five things that make a woman either agreeable or disagreeable to men.

children.title: A Man
children.description: Five things that make a man either agreeable or disagreeable to women.

children.title: Particular Suffering
children.description: Five kinds of suffering that only women are subject to, not men.

children.title: Three Qualities
children.description: A woman who is selfish, envious, and lustful has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Irritable
children.description: A woman with five bad qualities has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Acrimony
children.description: A woman with five bad qualities has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Jealous
children.description: A woman with five bad qualities has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Stingy
children.description: A woman with five bad qualities has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Adultery
children.description: A woman with five bad qualities has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Unethical
children.description: A woman with five bad qualities has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Unlearned
children.description: A woman with five bad qualities has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Lazy
