children.description: A woman with five bad qualities has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Unmindful
children.description: A woman with five bad qualities has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Five Threats
children.description: A woman who doesn’t keep five precepts has a bad rebirth.

children.title: Loving
children.description: A woman with five good qualities has a good rebirth.

children.title: Free of Acrimony
children.description: A woman with five good qualities has a good rebirth.

children.title: Free of Jealousy
children.description: A woman with five good qualities has a good rebirth.

children.title: Free of Stinginess
children.description: A woman with five good qualities has a good rebirth.

children.title: Not Adulterous
children.description: A woman with five good qualities has a good rebirth.

children.title: Ethical
children.description: A woman with five good qualities has a good rebirth.

children.title: Very Learned
children.description: A woman with five good qualities has a good rebirth.

children.title: Energetic
children.description: A woman with five good qualities has a good rebirth.

children.title: Mindful
children.description: A woman with five good qualities has a good rebirth.

children.title: Five Precepts
children.description: A woman who keeps the five precepts has a good rebirth.

children.title: Assured
children.description: A woman with five powers lives confident at home.

children.title: Under Her Thumb
children.description: A woman with five powers lives at home having won over her husband.

children.title: Mastered
children.description: A woman with five powers lives at home with her husband under her control.

children.title: One
children.description: A man with one power has a woman under his control: authority.

children.title: In That Respect
children.description: A woman may be complete with five powers.

children.title: They Send Her Away
children.description: A woman lacking in ethical conduct may be expelled from a family.

children.title: Cause
children.description: It is not because of beauty, wealth, relatives, or sons that a woman has a good rebirth, but because of ethical conduct.

children.title: Things
children.description: For a woman who has not made merit, five things are hard to come by.

children.title: Living With Self-Assurance
children.description: A woman with five qualities lives confidently at home.

children.title: Growth
children.description: A woman who grows in faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom acquires the best.

children.title: 4. Jambukhādaka
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Jambukhādaka” contains 16 discourses recording the answers given by Sāriputta to the questions of a wanderer named Jambukhādaka. The questions cover a wide range of themes, from the nature of extinguishment to the difficulty of practicing the Dhamma. This chapter is practically identical to the next, differing only in the name of the wanderer.

children.title: A Question About Extinguishment
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta about extinguishment and the path to realize it.

children.title: A Question About Perfection
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta about perfection (arahantship) and the path to realize it.

children.title: Principled Speech
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta who in the world are proponents of Dhamma.

children.title: What’s the Goal?
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta about the purpose of the spiritual path.

children.title: Solace
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta about who has attained consolation.

children.title: Ultimate Solace
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta about who has attained supreme consolation.

children.title: A Question About Feeling
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta what is feeling.

children.title: A Question About Defilements
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta what is a defilement.

children.title: A Question About Ignorance
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta what is ignorance.

children.title: A Question About Craving
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta what is craving.

children.title: A Question About Floods
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta what are the floods.

children.title: A Question About Grasping
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta what is grasping.

children.title: A Question About States of Existence
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta about the three realms of rebirth.

children.title: A Question About Suffering
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta about suffering.

children.title: A Question About Substantial Reality
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta what is identity.

children.title: A Question About What’s Hard to Do
children.description: The wanderer Jambukhādaka asks Sāriputta what is difficult to do in this teaching and training.

children.title: 5. Sāmaṇḍaka
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Sāmaṇḍaka” contains 16 discourses recording the answers given by Sāriputta to the questions of a wanderer named Sāmaṇḍaka. The questions cover a wide range of themes, from the nature of extinguishment to the difficulty of practicing the Dhamma. This chapter is practically identical to the previous, differing only in the name of the wanderer, and the Pali editions abbreviate, instructing that it is to be expanded.

children.title: Hard to Do
children.description: The wanderer Sāmaṇḍaka asks Sāriputta what is difficult to do in this teaching and training.

children.title: 6. Moggallāna
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Moggallāna” contains 11 discourses featuring Moggallāna, one of the chief disciples. He tells the monks of his struggles in meditation, and how he was encouraged by the Buddha. In the last two discourses, he visits the heavens and teaches the gods.

children.title: A Question About the First Absorption
children.description: Moggallāna speaks to the mendicants of a time when his practice of the first absorption was faltering. He expresses his gratitude for the Buddha, who urged him to stabilize that attainment.

children.title: A Question About the Second Absorption
children.description: Moggallāna speaks to the mendicants of a time when his practice of the second absorption was faltering. He expresses his gratitude for the Buddha, who urged him to stabilize that attainment.

children.title: A Question About the Third Absorption
children.description: Moggallāna speaks to the mendicants of a time when his practice of the third absorption was faltering. He expresses his gratitude for the Buddha, who urged him to stabilize that attainment.

children.title: A Question About the Fourth Absorption
children.description: Moggallāna speaks to the mendicants of a time when his practice of the fourth absorption was faltering. He expresses his gratitude for the Buddha, who urged him to stabilize that attainment.

children.title: A Question About the Dimension of Infinite Space
children.description: Moggallāna speaks to the mendicants of a time when his practice of the dimension of infinite space was faltering. He expresses his gratitude for the Buddha, who urged him to stabilize that attainment.

children.title: A Question About the Dimension of Infinite Consciousness
children.description: Moggallāna speaks to the mendicants of a time when his practice of the dimension of infinite consciousness was faltering. He expresses his gratitude for the Buddha, who urged him to stabilize that attainment.

children.title: A Question About the Dimension of Nothingness
children.description: Moggallāna speaks to the mendicants of a time when his practice of the dimension of nothingness was faltering. He expresses his gratitude for the Buddha, who urged him to stabilize that attainment.

children.title: A Question About the Dimension of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception
children.description: Moggallāna speaks to the mendicants of a time when his practice of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception was faltering. He expresses his gratitude for the Buddha, who urged him to stabilize that attainment.

children.title: A Question About the Signless
children.description: Moggallāna speaks to the mendicants of a time when his practice of the signless immersion was faltering. He expresses his gratitude for the Buddha, who urged him to stabilize that attainment.

children.title: With Sakka
children.description: Moggallāna ascended to the heaven of the Thirty-Three to address Sakka, the lord of gods, and his extensive retinue. He spoke in praise of going for refuge, as it leads to heaven. Sakka affirmed this on multiple occasions, adding that gods who had gone for refuge and kept ethics surpassed the other deities in the heavens.

children.title: With Candana, Etc.
children.description: The dialogue in SN 40.10 is repeated with a series of other deities.

children.title: 7. Citta the Householder
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Citta” contains 10 discourses featuring the householder Citta, who was praised by the Buddha as the foremost lay disciple in speaking on the Dhamma. Here he engages in a series of insightful and sharp-witted dialogues with various monks. Citta emerges as a distinctive personality, knowledgeable and witty, curious and incisive, with no lack of humor. But he is more than just a clever speaker, for he also lays claim to exalted meditation and spiritual attainments.

children.title: The Fetter
children.description: Citta the householder hears of a conversation among the monks regarding the distinction between the fetters and the things that are fettered. He goes to ask them on this topic, but they are unable to give a satisfactory answer, so he explained it to them. It is desire that is the fetter, like the yoke that binds two oxen.

children.title: Isidatta (1st)
children.description: Citta the householder invites some mendicants to his home for a meal. He asks them about the diversity of the elements, but only the junior monk, Isidatta, is able to answer.

children.title: With Isidatta (2nd)
children.description: Citta the householder invites some mendicants to his home for a meal. He asks them what is the cause of the ten metaphysical questions and the 62 views of the Brahmajāla Sutta, but only the junior monk, Isidatta, is able to answer. Citta realizes that Isidatta is in fact an unseen friend of his from Avantī. He offers to support him with requisites, but Isidatta left, never to return.

children.title: Mahaka’s Demonstration
children.description: Citta the householder invites some mendicants to his home for a meal. When they left he followed them, and witnessed the junior monk Venerable Mahaka performing a psychic feat. Citta approached Mahaka in his hut and asked him to demonstrate his skills, and Mahaka obliged. Citta offers to support him with requisites, but Mahaka left, never to return.

children.title: With Kāmabhū (1st)
children.description: Venerable Kāmabhū asks Citta to explain an enigmatic verse on a “one-spoked chariot”. After a brief consideration, Citta is able to explain it in detail.

children.title: With Kāmabhū (2nd)
children.description: Citta asks Kāmabhū about the different kinds of processes (saṅkhāra) in a series of questions that lead to the most profound of meditation experiences.

children.title: With Godatta
children.description: Venerable Godatta asks Citta whether the liberations of measurelessness, nothingness, emptiness, and signlessness are different states, or just different words for the same thing. Citta explains that they are both: they are terms for different meditation experiences, but may also be used of perfection or arahantship.

children.title: The Jain Ascetic of the Ñātika Clan
children.description: The Jain leader Mahāvīra, known as Nigaṇṭha Nātaputa in the Buddhist tradition, is visited by Citta. Mahāvīra asks him whether he believes in a certain state of immersion. When Citta replies that he doesn’t go by faith in the Buddha on this point, Mahāvīra is delighted. But it turns out Citta doesn’t need faith, as he experiences such a state for himself.

children.title: With Kassapa, the Naked Ascetic
children.description: Citta meets with the naked ascetic Kassapa, an old friend of his, and asks what gains he has realized from the spiritual life. Kassapa admits he has realized no higher attainments, whereupon Citta reveals he has realized many such attainments. Kassapa decides to ordain as a Buddhist mendicant.

children.title: Seeing the Sick
children.description: When Citta was on his deathbed, rather than receiving comfort, he gave comfort and teaching to those present.

children.title: 8. Chiefs
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Chiefs” contains 13 discourses featuring various headmen or chiefs. They sometimes ask questions relating to their professions, from entertainers to warriors, while several discourses touch on familiar Dhamma themes, such as overcoming anger, the validity of brahmanical rites, or whether monastics should use money. Some of the chiefs are quite adversarial, aiming to trip up the Buddha in debate, or accusing him of being a magician. In the end, though, the Buddha’s compassionate and measured responses win them over.

children.title: Fury
children.description: A headman known for his aggressive nature approaches the Buddha and asks how to give up irritability. The Buddha points out that such reactions are fueled by greed, hate, and delusion.

children.title: With Tālapuṭa
children.description: Talapuṭa the head of a troupe of performers asks the Buddha whether the belief that performers have a good rebirth is correct. The Buddha tries to dissuade him, but ultimately reveals that by inciting lust they head to a bad rebirth. Talapuṭa is distressed and asks to ordain.

children.title: A Warrior
children.description: Yodhājı̄va the professional warrior asks the Buddha whether the belief that warriors have a good rebirth is correct. The Buddha tries to dissuade him, but ultimately reveals that by following the way of violence they head to a bad rebirth. Yodhājı̄va is distressed and takes refuge.

children.title: An Elephant Marshal
children.description: Hatthāroha the elephant warrior asks the Buddha whether the belief that warriors have a good rebirth is correct. The Buddha tries to dissuade him, but ultimately reveals that by following the way of violence they head to a bad rebirth. Hatthāroha is distressed and takes refuge.

children.title: A Cavalryman
children.description: Assāroha the cavalry warrior asks the Buddha whether the belief that warriors have a good rebirth is correct. The Buddha tries to dissuade him, but ultimately reveals that by following the way of violence they head to a bad rebirth. Yodhājı̄va is distressed and asks to ordain.

children.title: With Asibandhaka’s Son
children.description: The chief Asibandhakaputta asks whether the rituals advocated by the western brahmins can bring a person to heaven. The Buddha asserts that only good deeds can take you to a good rebirth, and rituals have no effect.

children.title: The Simile of the Field
children.description: The chief Asibandhakaputta asks the Buddha why, if he has equal compassion for all, he teaches some more than others. The Buddha answers with a simile of a field: a farmer knows to put most of their effort into the fertile land.

children.title: A Horn Blower
children.description: The Buddha asks the chief Asibandhakaputta, a Jain, how Mahāvīra the Jain leader teaches his followers. He replies that you go to a rebirth depending on what you usually do. But the Buddha points out that even a killer only spends a small amount of time actually killing. The Buddha’s approach is to point out that deeds have results, and to encourage the abandoing of bad deeds and the adoption of good deeds.

children.title: Families
children.description: Mahāvīra asks Asibandhakaputta to refute the Buddha on behalf of the Jains. He suggests to try to trap the Buddha with a dilemma: he claims to have compassion for householders, yet visits them with a large Saṅgha in a time of scarcity. But the Buddha says no family has been harmed from this.

children.title: With Maṇicūḷaka
children.description: In Rājagaha, some in the royal court say Buddhist mendicants may accept offerings of money. Chief Maṇicūḷaka rebuts them, then visits the Buddha for confirmation. The Buddha categorically denies the accusation.

children.title: With Bhadraka
children.description: The chief Bhadraka asks the Buddha about the origin and ending of suffering, and the Buddha points out that a loss among Bhadraka’s own community would cause him suffering, due to his attachment.

children.title: With Rāsiya
children.description: The chief Rāsiya asks whether the Buddha completely rejects all forms of asceticism. The Buddha denies that this is the case, and explains what he means by the middle way in a lengthy disquisition, covering useful and useless forms of asceticism.

children.title: With Pāṭaliya
children.description: The chief Pāṭaliya asks whether the Buddha knows magic. He says he does—but that does not make him a magician.

children.title: 9. Unconditioned
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Unconditioned” contains 44 discourses on the theme of the unconditioned, i.e. nibbāna or “extinguishment”. They focus on the various practices that lead to the unconditioned. This chapter includes an extensive range of terms and idioms describing the final goal of Buddhist practice.

children.title: Placing the Mind and Keeping it Connected
10. Undeclared
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Undeclared” contains 11 discourses on the theme of the ten “undeclared” questions. These are a stock series of metaphysical hypotheses, which the Buddha dismissed as being based on the implicit assumption of a self, and hence as being counterproductive to liberation. The first discourse here features a conversation between King Pasenadi and the nun Khemā on this topic.

children.title: With Khemā
children.description: While staying in Toraṇavatthu, King Pasenadi wishes to visit a spiritual teacher, and the nun Khemā is highly recommended to him. He asks her about whether a realized one still exists after death, and she says this is not answerable. Later he visits the Buddha, who replies in exactly the same way.

children.title: With Anurādha
children.description: Venerable Anurādha is questioned by a number of ascetics, and ends up by saying that a realized one is described in terms other than “still existing after death” and so on. The wanderers say he’s a fool, so he checks with the Buddha, who says that a realized one is not even apprehended in this life, so how can they be described after death?

children.title: With Sāriputta and Koṭṭhita (1st)
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita asks Sāriputta whether a Realized One exists after death. Sāriputta says that to answer this would be to get involved in the five aggregates, something that a Realized One is free from.

children.title: With Sāriputta and Koṭṭhita (2nd)
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita asks Sāriputta whether a Realized One exists after death. Sāriputta says that one who understands the five aggregates would not think in such terms.

children.title: With Sāriputta and Koṭṭhita (3rd)
children.description: Mahākoṭṭhita asks Sāriputta whether a Realized One exists after death. Sāriputta says that only someone who has desire for the five aggregates would think in such terms.

children.title: With Sāriputta and Koṭṭhita (4th)
children.description: Sāriputta asks Mahākoṭṭhita whether a Realized One exists after death. Mahākoṭṭhita says that only someone who delights in the five aggregates would think in such terms, and offers a variety of further explanations of the same point.

children.title: With Moggallāna
children.description: The wanderer Vacchagotta asks Moggallāna the ten metaphysical questions, starting with whether the cosmos is eternal. Moggallāna says such questions would only be answered by someone who identifies with the six senses. Vacchagotta then asks the Buddha the same questions.

children.title: With Vacchagotta
children.description: The wanderer Vacchagotta asks the Buddha the ten metaphysical questions, starting with whether the cosmos is eternal. He says such questions would only be answered by someone who identifies with the five aggregates.

children.title: The Debating Hall
children.description: The wanderer Vacchagotta reports to the Buddha a conversation among ascetics on the views of the six heretical teachers as to where a perfected one is reborn. Unsure of what the Buddha’s position was, he asks how it is to be understood. The Buddha says it is like a flame that burns dependent on fuel, and goes out when that fuel is extinguished.

children.title: With Ānanda
children.description: Vacchagotta asks the Buddha whether a self exists, but the Buddha is silent. When Ānanda later asks him why he didn’t answer, the Buddha replied that it was to avoid misunderstanding.

children.title: With Sabhiya Kaccāna
children.description: The wanderer Vacchagotta asks Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna whether a Realized One exists after death. He answers that the basis for describing a Realized One no longer applies. Vacchagotta is impressed that such a junior monk understands this subtle matter.

children.title: 5. The Group of Path
children.description: The “Great Book” is the last and largest of the five books of the Linked Discourses. It consists of twelve saṁyuttas, almost all of which deal with an aspect of Buddhist practice, or the path. The first of these, indeed, is the “Section on the Path” (Maggasaṁyutta), and in the northern canons the book as a whole is referred to as the “Book of the Path” (Maggavagga). The first seven of the saṁyuttas treat the familiar set of seven groups of factors on Buddhist practice known to the later traditions as the bodhipakkhiyā dhammā, or “qualities leading to awakening”. This book is the primary source for these teachings. Subsequent saṁyuttas deal with the path from different perspectives, while the final two deal with stream-entry and the four noble truths respectively.

children.title: 1. Eightfold Path
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Path” contains 180 discourses on the noble eightfold path, the “middle way” which is the first and most important of all the Buddha’s teachings on the path of spiritual practice. It is mentioned in the first discourse as the fourth noble truth. It begins with “right view” which is initially an accurate conceptual understanding, based on hearing the teachings and reflecting on their meaning. The second factor is right intention, referring to the attitude or motivation that shapes practice. Next come three factors dealing with ethical conduct. And the final three factors directly deal with meditation. Once all these factors are mature, “right immersion” or the four absorptions (jhānas) enables the initial conceptual understanding to ascend to a higher level of insight and letting go. While this and subsequent chapters contains many substantive discourses on this theme, the large number of discourses is mainly attributable to the formulaic “repetition series” which append each chapter.

children.title: Ignorance
children.description: Following ignorance comes the wrong eightfold path. But the right eightfold path follows true knowledge.

children.title: Half the Spiritual Life
children.description: When Ānanda says that good friendship is half the spiritual path, the Buddha rebukes him, saying that it is in fact the whole of the spiritual path. Based on good friendship, the eightfold path is fulfilled.

children.title: Sāriputta
children.description: When Sāriputta says that good friendship is the whole of the spiritual path, the Buddha praises him. Based on good friendship, the eightfold path is fulfilled.

children.title: Regarding the Brahmin Jānussoṇi
children.description: Ānanda sees the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi resplendent on his all-white chariot. He asks the Buddha whether there is a similarly divine vehicle in Buddhism. The Buddha responds by drawing a detailed set of analogies between the eightfold path and a chariot.

children.title: What’s the Goal?
children.description: When asked what is the purpose of the spiritual path, you should answer that it is the ending of suffering.

children.title: A Mendicant (1st)
children.description: A mendicant asks what is the purpose of the spiritual path, and the Buddha answers that it is the ending of suffering.

children.title: A Mendicant (2nd)
children.description: A mendicant asks about Nibbāna and the deathless.

children.title: Analysis
children.description: The Buddha presents the eightfold path together with a detailed analysis of each factor. It should be assumed that these explanations apply wherever the eightfold path is taught.

children.title: A Spike
children.description: A mendicant with wrong view will develop the path in the wrong way, harming themselves as if grabbing a sharp spike the wrong way.

children.title: With Nandiya
children.description: The wanderer Nandiya asks how many things lead to extinguishment.

children.title: Meditation (1st)
children.description: The Buddha goes on retreat for a fortnight. When he emerges, he describes his meditation on the conditionality of the eightfold path, which was similar to a practice he did shortly after awakening.

children.title: Meditation (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha goes on retreat for a fortnight. When he emerges, he describes his meditation on the conditionality of the eightfold path, which was similar to a practice he did shortly after awakening.

children.title: A Trainee
children.description: A mendicant asks how a person is a “trainee”.

children.title: Arising (1st)
children.description: The eightfold path does not arise apart from a Realized One.

children.title: Arising (2nd)
children.description: The eightfold path does not arise apart from a Holy One’s training.

children.title: Purified (1st)
children.description: The eight pure factors of the path do not arise apart from a Realized One.

children.title: Purified (2nd)
children.description: The eight pure factors of the path do not arise apart from a Holy One’s training.

children.title: At the Chicken Monastery (1st)
children.description: In a short discourse evidently set shortly after the Buddha’s passing, Venerable Bhadda asks Ānanda about the unholy life, or the unspiritual path. It is the wrong eightfold path.

children.title: At the Chicken Monastery (2nd)
children.description: In a short discourse evidently set shortly after the Buddha’s passing, Venerable Bhadda asks Ānanda about the holy life, or the spiritual path. It is the right eightfold path.

children.title: At the Chicken Monastery (3rd)
children.description: In a short discourse evidently set shortly after the Buddha’s passing, Venerable Bhadda asks Ānanda about the spiritual path, one who follows the spiritual path, and the goal of the spiritual path.

children.title: The Wrong Way
children.description: The wrong eightfold path is a wrong state; the right eightfold path is a right state.

children.title: Unskillful Qualities
children.description: The factors of the wrong eightfold path are unskillful qualities; those of the right eightfold path are skillful qualities.

children.title: Practice (1st)
children.description: The wrong eightfold path is the wrong way; the right eightfold path is the right way.

children.title: Practice (2nd)
children.description: Regardless of whether one is a lay person or a renunciate, the Buddha praises the right way, not the wrong way. The wrong eightfold path is the wrong way; the right eightfold path is the right way.

children.title: An Untrue Person (1st)
children.description: A bad person practices wrong eightfold path; a good person practices the right eightfold path.

children.title: An Untrue Person (2nd)
children.description: A bad person practices wrong eightfold path, and a worse person has wrong knowledge and wrong liberation, too; a good person is the opposite.

children.title: Pots
children.description: Someone without the eightfold path is easily knocked over, like a pot without a stand.

children.title: Immersion
children.description: The eightfold path is the necessary prerequisite for right immersion (samādhi).

children.title: Feeling
children.description: The eightfold path is developed to understand the three feelings.

children.title: With Uttiya
children.description: The Buddha taught the eightfold path in order to give up the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

children.title: Practice (1st)
children.description: The wrong eightfold path is wrong practice; the right eightfold path is right practice.

children.title: Practice (2nd)
children.description: Practicing the wrong eightfold path is wrong; practicing the right awakening path is right.

children.title: Missed Out
children.description: Neglecting the eightfold path you neglect the path to the end of suffering.

children.title: Going to the Far Shore
children.description: The eightfold path leads from the near to the far shore. With a long set of verses.

children.title: The Ascetic Life (1st)
children.description: The eightfold path is the ascetic life. Its fruits are stream-entry, once-return, non-return, and perfection.

children.title: The Ascetic Life (2nd)
children.description: The eightfold path is the ascetic life. Its fruits are the end of greed, hate, and delusion.

children.title: The Brahmin Life (1st)
children.description: The eightfold path is brahminhood. Its fruits are stream-entry, once-return, non-return, and perfection.

children.title: The Brahmin Life (2nd)
children.description: The eightfold path is brahminhood. Its fruits are the end of greed, hate, and delusion.

children.title: The Spiritual Path (1st)
children.description: The eightfold path is the spiritual path. Its fruits are stream-entry, once-return, non-return, and perfection.

children.title: The Spiritual Path (2nd)
children.description: The eightfold path is the spiritual path. Its fruits are the end of greed, hate, and delusion.

children.title: 5. Abbreviated Texts on Followers of Other Paths
The Fading Away of Greed
children.description: If others ask why you follow the spiritual path, say it’s for the fading away of lust.

children.title: Six Discourses on Giving Up Fetters, Etc.
children.description: If others ask why you follow the spiritual path, say it’s for giving up fetters, etc.

children.title: Extinguishment With No Fuel For Grasping
children.description: If others ask why you follow the spiritual path, say it’s for final extinguishment without anything left over.

children.title: Good Friends (1st)
children.description: As the dawn precedes the sun, good friendship precedes the eightfold path.

children.title: Five Discourses on Accomplishment in Ethics, Etc. (1st)
children.description: As the dawn precedes the sun, ethics, enthusiasm, confidence, right view, and diligence precede the eightfold path.

children.title: Accomplishment in Rational Application of Mind (1st)
children.description: As the dawn precedes the sun, proper attention precedes the eightfold path.

children.title: Five Discourses on Accomplishment in Ethics, Etc. (2nd)
Accomplishment in Rational Application of Mind (2nd)
Five Discourses on Accomplishment in Ethics, Etc. (1st)
Accomplishment in Rational Application of Mind (1st)
Five Discourses on Accomplishment in Ethics, Etc. (2nd)
Accomplishment in Rational Application of Mind (2nd)
Five Discourses on Accomplishment in Ethics, Etc.
Accomplishment in Rational Application of Mind
Five Discourses on Accomplishment in Ethics, Etc.
Accomplishment in Rational Application of Mind (2nd)
Five Discourses on Slanting to the Ocean
Five Discourses on Sloping to the East
Craving
children.description: Develop the eightfold path to abandon the three cravings. This sutta is doubled by replacing taṇhā with another form of the same word, tasina. This variation is found in Burmese but not Sinhalese manuscripts.

children.title: 2. Awakening Factors
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Awakening Factors” contains 184 discourses on the seven awakening factors. These are qualities such as mindfulness and investigation which lead the meditator to awakening. The focus here is specifically on meditation, rather than the more holistic approach included in the previous chapter on the Path. Some distinctive features of this collection include the use recitation of the awakening factors in order to inspire those who are sick, and the frequent contrast between the seven awakening factors and the five hindrances.

children.title: The Himalaya
children.description: Dragons nurture their strength in the Himalayas, then enter the rivers and reach the ocean. So too, a mendicant nurtures ethics and then develops the seven awakening factors.

children.title: The Body
children.description: Just as the body depends on food, the awakening factors depend on nutriment. The Buddha gives specific conditions for each of the factors.

children.title: Ethics
children.description: Here the awakening factors are described in the context of hearing the teachings and reflecting on them. This leads to full enlightenment, or at least to some lesser attainment.

children.title: Clothes
children.description: The various awakening factors can be donned at different times of the day, like a man who puts on bright colored clothes whenever he wants.

children.title: A Monk
children.description: They’re called awakening factors because they lead to awakening.

children.title: Kuṇḍaliya
children.description: The wanderer Kuṇḍaliya points out that some ascetics argue for the sake of winning debates. But the Buddha says his path is for the sake of liberation. Kuṇḍaliya asks what leads to liberation, and the Buddha traces a sequence of conditions back to sense restraint.

children.title: A Bungalow
children.description: The awakening factors lead to extinguishment, like rafters holding up the roof peak.

children.title: With Upavāṇa
children.description: Sāriputta asks Upavāṇa how one can reflect and see the awakening factors in oneself.

children.title: Arisen (1st)
children.description: The awakening factors do not arise apart from a Realized One.

children.title: Arisen (2nd)
children.description: The awakening factors do not arise apart from a Holy One’s training.

children.title: Living Creatures
children.description: Just as living creatures are based on the earth, the awakening factors are based on ethics.

children.title: The Simile of the Sun (1st)
children.description: Just as the dawn precedes the sun, good friendship precedes the awakening factors.

children.title: The Simile of the Sun (2nd)
children.description: Just as the dawn precedes the sun, proper attention precedes the awakening factors.

children.title: Sick (1st)
children.description: When Mahākassapa was sick, the Buddha taught him the awakening factors, inspiring him to a swift recovery.

children.title: Sick (2nd)
children.description: When Mahāmoggallāna was sick, the Buddha taught him the awakening factors, inspiring him to a swift recovery.

children.title: Sick (3rd)
children.description: When the Buddha was sick, Mahācunda taught him the awakening factors, inspiring him to a swift recovery.

children.title: Going to the Far Shore
children.description: The awakening factors lead from the near to the far shore.

children.title: Missed Out
children.description: Those who neglect the awakening factors neglect the path to the end of suffering.

children.title: Noble
children.description: The awakening factors are noble and emancipating.

children.title: Disillusionment
children.description: The awakening factors lead to disenchantment.

children.title: To Awakening
children.description: They’re called awakening factors because they lead to awakening.

children.title: A Teaching on the Awakening Factors
children.description: A simple statement on the awakening factors.

children.title: Grounds
children.description: Frequently focusing on things tends to promote similar qualities, whether good (awakening factors) or bad (hindrances).

children.title: Irrational Application of Mind
children.description: Improper attention grows the hindrances, proper attention grows the awakening factors.

children.title: Non-decline
children.description: The awakening factors lead to non-decline.

children.title: The Ending of Craving
children.description: The awakening factors lead to the ending of craving.

children.title: The Cessation of Craving
children.description: The awakening factors lead to the cessation of craving.

children.title: Helping Penetration
children.description: The awakening factors partake of penetration.

children.title: One Thing
children.description: Nothing is as effective for getting rid of fetters as the awakening factors.

children.title: With Udāyī
children.description: Venerable Udāyı̄ celebrates his progress on the path, gaining faith as a householder, going forth, and realizing the Dhamma. Now he develops the awakening factors for the end of suffering.

children.title: Skillful (1st)
children.description: Skillful qualities are rooted in diligence, which promotes the awakening factors.

children.title: Skillful (2nd)
children.description: Skillful qualities are rooted in proper attention, which promotes the awakening factors.

children.title: Corruptions
children.description: Hindrances sully the mind like impurities in gold.

children.title: Not Corruptions
children.description: Awakening factors purify the mind and lead to liberation.

children.title: Irrational Application of Mind
children.description: Improper attention promotes the hindrances; proper attention promotes the awakening factors.

children.title: Growth
children.description: The awakening factors lead to growth and non-decline.

children.title: Obstacles
children.description: Hindrances sully the mind, awakening factors purify it.

children.title: Without Obstacles
children.description: Listening to the teaching, the hindrances are given up and the awakening factors developed.

children.title: Trees
children.description: As some large trees with small seeds will overgrow and ruin other trees, so the hindrances overgrow and ruin the mind.

children.title: Hindrances
children.description: The hindrances cause blindness, the awakening factors cause vision.

children.title: Discriminations
children.description: Anyone who abandons the three kinds of discrimination does so due to the awakening factors.

children.title: A Wheel-Turning Monarch
children.description: As the Wheel-turning Monarch manifests seven treasures, the Realized One manifests the seven awakening factors.

children.title: About Māra
children.description: The awakening factors crush Māra’s army.

children.title: Witless
children.description: A stupid person has not developed the awakening factors.

children.title: Wise
children.description: A wise person has developed the awakening factors.

children.title: Poor
children.description: A person who has not developed the awakening factors is called “poor”.

children.title: Prosperous
children.description: A person who has developed the awakening factors is called “prosperous”.

children.title: The Sun
children.description: As the dawn precedes the sunrise, so too good friendship precedes the awakening factors.

children.title: Interior
children.description: No internal factor helps the awakening factors so much as proper attention.

children.title: Exterior
children.description: No external factor helps the awakening factors so much as good friendship.

children.title: Nourishing
children.description: The Buddha spells out in detail the factors that nourish the hindrances, and those that nourish the awakening factors.

children.title: Is There a Way?
children.description: Some wanderers tell some Buddhist mendicants that they, too, teach the five hindrances and the seven awakening factors, so what is the difference? The Buddha explains by giving a detailed analytical treatment that he says is beyond the scope of the wanderers.

children.title: Fire
children.description: Which awakening factors should be developed when the mind is tired, and which when it is energetic? And what is always useful?

children.title: Full of Love
children.description: Some wanderers tell some Buddhist mendicants that they, too, teach the five hindrances and the four Brahmā meditations, so what is the difference? The Buddha explains the detailed connection between the Brahmā meditations and the awakening factors, which taken together lead to liberation.

children.title: With Saṅgārava
children.description: The brahmin Saṅgārava asks why sometimes verses stay in memory while other times they don’t. The Buddha replies that it is due to the presence of either the hindrances of awakening factors. He gives a set of similes illustrating each of the hindrances with different bowls of water.

children.title: With Prince Abhaya
children.description: Prince Abhaya reports Pūraṇa Kassapa’s view that there is no cause for ignorance or knowledge, and asks the Buddha’s opinion. The Buddha replies that the cause of ignorance is the hindrances, and the cause of knowledge is the awakening factors.

children.title: A Skeleton
children.description: A series of passages on the benefits of meditating on a skeleton. Some editions treat the sections as separate suttas.

children.title: 14. Another Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on the Ganges
Another Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on the Ganges
3. Mindfulness Meditation
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Mindfulness Meditation” contains 104 discourses on the four kinds of mindfulness meditation (satipaṭṭhāna, otherwise known as the “foundations of mindfulness” or “establishments of mindfulness”). These are the body, feelings, mind, and principles. The last of these is translated in various ways, but a close reading of the texts in this chapter shows that it originally referred to the “principles” of causality underlying the process of meditation itself. These discourses on this fundamental topic are much less known than the longer “Discourse on Mindfulness Meditation” found in versions in MN 10 and DN 22; however, they are historically earlier than that late compilation. Where MN 10 emphasizes insight meditation, in this collection we frequently find mindfulness closely connected to absorption, as it is the factor of the path that leads directly to “right immersion”. Insight is mentioned only rarely. The root meaning of the term mindfulness (sati) is “memory”, and when used in meditation it refers to not “forgetting” one’s meditation, but keeping focus on the breath or other theme of meditation. This collection presents a range of perspectives on mindfulness meditation; one of its most memorable features is a series of similes or parables illustrating the practice. The partner of mindfulness (sati) is “situational awareness” (sampajañña, sometimes rendered as “clear comprehension”), which refers to keeping a broad awareness and understanding especially in daily activities.

children.title: In Ambapālī’s Mango Grove
children.description: At Ambapālī’s mango grove, the Buddha teaches the mendicants about the “way to convergence”, the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: Mindful
children.description: At Ambapālī’s mango grove, the Buddha teaches the mendicants about the four kinds of mindfulness meditation and the practice of situational awareness.

children.title: A Monk
children.description: When a mendicant asks for a teaching to take on retreat, the Buddha issues an unexpected rebuke. Evidently the mendicant had been badly behaved; but now, he insists, he is sincere. The Buddha relents, and teaches the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, well grounded on ethics.

children.title: At Sālā
children.description: Newly ordained mendicants should practice the four kinds of mindfulness meditation; trainees are practicing them, and perfected ones have perfected the practice.

children.title: A Heap of the Unskillful
children.description: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation are a complete heap of what is skillful.

children.title: A Hawk
children.description: The parable of the quail and the hawk. When the quail ventured outside her ancestral territory, she became vulnerable. And what is a mendicant’s ancestral territory? The four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: A Monkey
children.description: The parable of the foolish monkey who gets trapped in tar when it ventures outside its ancestral territory. And what is a mendicant’s ancestral territory? The four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: Cooks
children.description: The parable of the cook. They present different kinds of dishes to the king, and observe which the king likes. In the same way, a mendicant observes why their meditation succeeds or fails. When the four kinds of mindfulness meditation succeeds it leads to giving up hindrances and entering immersion.

children.title: Sick
children.description: The Buddha decides to spend his final rains retreat at Vesālī in Beluvagāmaka. During the retreat he becomes very ill, but later recovers. Ānanda wonders who will guide the Saṅgha when the Buddha dies, but the Buddha says they should be their own refuge, grounded on the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: The Nuns’ Quarters
children.description: When Ānanda visits the nuns’s quarters they tell him that their meditation is prospering to higher and higher levels. Ānanda reporrts the good news to the Buddha, who speaks of two ways of developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation: directed and undirected.

children.title: A Great Man
children.description: Sāriputta asks the Buddha what is a great man, and the Buddha says it is someone whose mind has been freed by developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: At Nāḷandā
children.description: Sāriputta boldly claims that no-one has ever, or will ever, be more enlightened than the Buddha. He admits that he cannot read the minds of all the Buddhas, but he understands a principle of the Dhamma: all those who become awakened do so by giving up the five hindrances, practicing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, and developing the seven awakening factors.

children.title: With Cunda
children.description: Sāriputta dies of illness, and the novice Cunda together with Ānanda take his bowl and robes and report the sad news to the Buddha. The Buddha dispels Ānanda’s sadness by speaking of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: At Ukkacelā
children.description: After the passing of Sāriputta and Moggallāna (whose actual death is unrecorded in the canon), the Buddha says the Saṅgha looks empty; yet he is not sad.

children.title: With Bāhiya
children.description: When Venerable Bāhiya asks for a teaching to take on retreat, the Buddha teaches the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, well grounded on ethics.

children.title: With Uttiya
children.description: When Venerable Uttiya asks for a teaching to take on retreat, the Buddha teaches the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, well grounded on ethics.

children.title: Noble
children.description: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation lead to the end of suffering.

children.title: Divinity
children.description: Just after the Buddha’s awakening, Brahmā Sahampati supports the Buddha’s reflection that the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the way to convergence.

children.title: At Sedaka
children.description: Two acrobats discuss whether one should support the other, or the other way around. The Buddha says they should support each other. In the same way we should practice the four kinds of mindfulness meditation both for one’s own benefit and to protect others.

children.title: The Finest Lady in the Land
children.description: A parable that sets up an impossible challenge: to walk between a popular performer and the crowd jostling to see her, carrying a bowl of oil filled to the brim, while a man with a drawn sword waits to chop off your head if you spill a drop. That’s mindfulness!

children.title: Ethics
children.description: Venerable Bhadda asks Ānanda about the ethical virtues encouraged by the Buddha—what is their purpose? To develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: Long Lasting
children.description: Venerable Bhadda asks Ānanda about the conditions under which the true teaching lasts long or does not last long after the Buddha’s passing. Ānanda says it depends on whether the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are practiced.

children.title: Decline
children.description: Venerable Bhadda asks Ānanda about the conditions under which the true teaching declines. Ānanda says it depends on whether the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are practiced.

children.title: Plain Version
children.description: A simple teaching on the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: A Certain Brahmin
children.description: A brahmin asks the Buddha about the conditions under which the true teaching lasts long or does not last long after the Buddha’s passing. The Buddha says it depends on whether the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are practiced.

children.title: Partly
children.description: Sāriputta asks Anuruddha what makes someone a trainee. It is someone who has partly developed the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: Completely
children.description: Sāriputta asks Anuruddha what makes someone an adept. It is someone who has fully developed the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: The World
children.description: Anuruddha claims to have developed the various direct knowledges by practicing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: With Sirivaḍḍha
children.description: When the householder Sirivaḍḍha is sick, Ānanda visits him and encourages him to practice mindfulness meditation. But he has already developed them, and abandoned the five lower fetters.

children.title: With Mānadinna
children.description: When the householder Mānadinna is sick, Ānanda visits him and encourages him to practice mindfulness meditation. But he has already developed them, and abandoned the five lower fetters.

children.title: Not Learned From Anyone Else
children.description: The full knowledge of mindfulness meditation was not learned before the Buddha.

children.title: Fading Away
children.description: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation lead to peace.

children.title: Missed Out
children.description: Someone who has neglected the four kinds of mindfulness meditation has neglected the noble path.

children.title: Developed
children.description: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation lead from the near to the far shore.

children.title: Mindful
children.description: Mindfulness is the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. Situational awareness is watching the arising and passing of feelings, thoughts, and perceptions.

children.title: Enlightenment
children.description: When the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are developed, perfection or non-return may be expected.

children.title: Desire
children.description: Developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, desire is abandoned.

children.title: Complete Understanding
children.description: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation lead to realizing the deathless.

children.title: Development
children.description: The development of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: Analysis
children.description: The Buddha teaches the simple passage on the four kinds of mindfulness meditation and an advanced analysis, which involves contemplating them as impermanent.

children.title: Freedom From Death
children.description: Develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, don’t let the deathless be lost.

children.title: Origin
children.description: The causes for the origination and cessation of the phenomena upon which the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are grounded.

children.title: The Path
children.description: The Buddha tells the mendicants how, just after his awakening, Brahmā Sahampati supported the Buddha’s reflection that the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the way to convergence

children.title: Mindful
children.description: Be mindful by developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: A Heap of the Skillful
children.description: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation are a heap of the skillful.

children.title: Restraint in the Monastic Code
children.description: When a mendicant asks for a teaching to take on retreat, the Buddha teaches the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, well grounded on restraint in the code of monastic rules.

children.title: Bad Conduct
children.description: When a mendicant asks for a teaching to take on retreat, the Buddha teaches the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, well grounded on good bodily, verbal, and mental conduct.

children.title: Friends
children.description: You should encourage your friends to practice the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: Feelings
children.description: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation help to understand the three feelings.

children.title: Defilements
children.description: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation help to give up the defilements.

children.title: 4. Faculties
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Faculties” contains 178 discourses on various sets of “faculties” (indriya). The “five faculties” of faith, energy, mindfulness, immersion, and wisdom are the most natural fit in this context. However the chapter also finds room for discourses on a wider range of 22 faculties, including the six sense faculties, five affective faculties (kinds of feeling), three faculties relating the process of enlightenment, and three concerning biology and gender. This flexible category thus serves as a link between the teachings on wisdom and those on the path.

children.title: Plain Version
children.description: The five faculties are faith, energy, mindfulness, immersion, and wisdom.

children.title: A Stream-Enterer (1st)
children.description: One who understands the gratification, the drawback, and the escape regarding the five faculties is a stream-enterer.

children.title: A Stream-Enterer (2nd)
children.description: One who understands the origin, the passing, the gratification, the drawback, and the escape regarding the five faculties is a stream-enterer.

children.title: A Perfected One (1st)
children.description: One who is freed after understanding the gratification, the drawback, and the escape regarding the five faculties is a perfected one.

children.title: A Perfected One (2nd)
children.description: One who is freed after understanding the origin, the passing, the gratification, the drawback, and the escape regarding the five faculties is a perfected one.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (1st)
children.description: A true ascetic understands the five faculties in terms of gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: A true ascetic understands the five faculties in terms of the four noble truths.

children.title: Should Be Seen
children.description: Each of the five faculties should be seen in a particular set of teachings.

children.title: Analysis (1st)
children.description: The Buddha gives a short explanation of each of the five faculties.

children.title: Analysis (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha gives a detailed explanation of each of the five faculties.

children.title: Gain
children.description: The Buddha explains the five faculties in terms of how they are obtained.

children.title: In Brief (1st)
children.description: One who has developed the five faculties fully is a perfected one. Developing them to a lesser degree, one reaches lesser attainments.

children.title: In Brief (2nd)
children.description: One who has developed the five faculties fully is a perfected one. Developing them to a lesser degree, one reaches lesser attainments. A difference in faculties leads to a difference in fruits.

children.title: In Brief (3rd)
children.description: One who has developed the five faculties fully is a perfected one. Developing them to a lesser degree, one reaches lesser attainments. The faculties are not barren.

children.title: In Detail (1st)
children.description: One who has developed the five faculties fully is a perfected one. Developing them to a lesser degree, one reaches lesser attainments.

children.title: In Detail (2nd)
children.description: One who has developed the five faculties fully is a perfected one. Developing them to a lesser degree, one reaches lesser attainments. A difference in faculties leads to a difference in fruits.

children.title: In Detail (3rd)
children.description: One who has developed the five faculties fully is a perfected one. Developing them to a lesser degree, one reaches lesser attainments. The faculties are not barren.

children.title: Practicing
children.description: One who has developed the five faculties fully is a perfected one. Developing them to a lesser degree, one reaches lesser attainments. One who has none of them at all is an outsider.

children.title: Endowed
children.description: Someone who develops the faculties is said to be equipped with faculties.

children.title: The Ending of Defilements
children.description: The five faculties lead to the ending of defilements in this very life.

children.title: Future Lives
children.description: The Buddha did not claim to be awakened until he realized the five faculties.

children.title: The Life Faculty
children.description: Three faculties: femininity, masculinity, and vitality.

children.title: The Faculty of Enlightenment
children.description: Three faculties relating to stages in the realization of awakening.

children.title: A One-Seeder
children.description: Depending on the strength of the five faculties, one is perfected, or reaches a lesser attainment.

children.title: Plain Version
children.description: Six faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

children.title: A Stream-Enterer
children.description: Six faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. One who understand these is a stream-enterer.

children.title: A Perfected One
children.description: Six faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. One who is freed by understanding these is perfected.

children.title: Awakened
children.description: The Buddha did not claim to be awakened until he realized the origin, the passing, the gratification, the drawback, and the escape regarding the six faculties.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (1st)
children.description: A true ascetic understands the six faculties in terms of gratification, drawback, and escape.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: A true ascetic understands the six faculties in terms of the four noble truths.

children.title: Plain Version
children.description: Five faculties: pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity.

children.title: A Stream-Enterer
children.description: One who understands the gratification, the drawback, and the escape regarding the five faculties of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity is a stream-enterer.

children.title: A Perfected One
children.description: One who is freed after understanding the gratification, the drawback, and the escape regarding the five faculties of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity is a perfected one.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (1st)
children.description: A true ascetic understands the five faculties of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity in terms of the four noble truths.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: A true ascetic understands the five faculties of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity in terms of the four noble truths.

children.title: Analysis (1st)
children.description: The five faculties of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity are analyzed in detail.

children.title: Analysis (2nd)
children.description: The five faculties of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity are analyzed in detail. In addition, each is to be seen in one of the three feelings.

children.title: Analysis (3rd)
children.description: The five faculties of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity are analyzed in detail. In addition, each is to be seen in one of the three feelings.

children.title: The Simile of the Fire Sticks
children.description: The five faculties of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity arise dependent on the appropriate contact, like sticks making fire.

children.title: Irregular Order
children.description: The five faculties of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity are taught in a detailed exposition that treats them in an unusual order. The abandoning of each is related to the attainment of a particular meditative absorption.

children.title: Old Age
children.description: When Ānanda sees the Buddha’s sense faculties fading, the Buddha speaks on the decrepitude of old age, including verses.

children.title: The Brahmin Uṇṇābha
children.description: The brahmin Uṇṇābha points out that the five physical sense faculties do not share a common domain, so where do they come together? In the mind. Uṇṇābha pursues the teaching all the way to Nibbāna.

children.title: At Sāketa
children.description: The Buddha discusses the five faculties and the five powers. They are like a river that flows around a central island. From one point of view they can be considered different, but from another they are just the same stream.

children.title: At the Eastern Gate
children.description: Sāriputta does not rely on faith in saying that the five faculties lead to the deathless, for he has seen this for himself.

children.title: At the Eastern Monastery (1st)
children.description: Having developed wisdom a mendicant may declare their awakening, as wisdom fulfills the other faculties.

children.title: At the Eastern Monastery (2nd)
children.description: Having developed wisdom and immersion a mendicant may declare their awakening.

children.title: At the Eastern Monastery (3rd)
children.description: Having developed energy, mindfulness, immersion, and wisdom a mendicant may declare their awakening.

children.title: At the Eastern Monastery (4th)
children.description: Having developed faith, energy, mindfulness, immersion, and wisdom a mendicant may declare their awakening.

children.title: About Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer
children.description: Having developed mindfulness, immersion, and wisdom the mendicant Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja declared his awakening.

children.title: At Āpaṇa
children.description: The Buddha asks Sāriputta whether a noble disciple doubts the Buddha. Not only does he have faith, replies Sāriputta, but the other faculties each come to be developed in turn.

children.title: At Sālā
children.description: Just as the lion is the king of beasts, wisdom is the chief of qualities that lead to awakening.

children.title: In the Land of the Mallas
children.description: Only when noble wisdom arises do the other four faculties become stable.

children.title: A Trainee
children.description: How does someone recognize that they are a trainee? By understanding the four noble truths and the five faculties. But only a perfected one fully embodies these qualities.

children.title: Footprints
children.description: Just as all footprints fit into that of an elephant, wisdom is the chief of qualities that lead to awakening.

children.title: Heartwood
children.description: Just as red sandalwood is the best of fragrances, wisdom is the chief of qualities that lead to awakening.

children.title: Grounded
children.description: When established in diligence, the five faculties come to be developed.

children.title: With the Divinity Sahampati
children.description: Just after the Buddha’s awakening, Brahmā Sahampati supports the Buddha’s reflection that the five faculties lead to the deathless.

children.title: The Boar’s Cave
children.description: A mendicant honors the Realized One and his teaching for the sake of the supreme sanctuary.

children.title: Arising (1st)
children.description: The five faculties only arise in the dispensation of a Realized One.

children.title: Arising (2nd)
children.description: The five faculties only arise in the training of a Holy One.

children.title: 13. Another Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on the Ganges
Another Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on the Ganges
Another Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on the Ganges
5. Right Efforts
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Right Efforts” contains 54 discourses, which are, however, a mere instantiation of the standard repetition series as applied to the four right efforts. There are many discourses on right effort throughout the Pali nikāyas, but for some reason the redactors did not collect them here.

children.title: 6. Five Powers
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Five Powers” contains 108 discourses, which are, however, a mere instantiation of the standard repetition series as applied to the five powers. These powers are effectively identical with the five faculties, as stated at SN 48.43, being merely distinguished as a different teaching approach. There are several discourses on these qualities found mainly in the Aṅguttara Fives, but for some reason the redactors did not collect them here.

children.title: 6. Another Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on the Ganges
Another Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on the Ganges
7. Bases of Psychic Power
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Bases of Psychic Power” contains 86 discourses dealing with the qualities of enthusiasm or desire for practice, energy, higher consciousness, and inquiry, which are said to lead to the development of various psychic powers. The purpose of Buddhism, of course, is not to develop such powers. But they are a matter of constant interest and intrigue among spiritual practitioners—not just in ancient India—and it seems the Buddha formulated this approach to the path to inspire those interested in them. The emphasis is on the development of deep meditation immersion (samādhi) through applying effort.

children.title: 1. The Chapter at the Cāpāla Shrine
From the Near Shore
children.description: The four bases of psychic power lead from the near to the far shore.

children.title: Missed Out
children.description: One who has neglected the four bases of psychic power has neglected the path to the end of suffering.

children.title: A Noble One
children.description: The four bases of psychic power are noble and emancipating.

children.title: Disillusionment
children.description: The four bases of psychic power lead to dispassion.

children.title: Partly
children.description: Those who have developed psychic powers in part have developed the four bases of psychic power in part.

children.title: Completely
children.description: Those who have developed psychic powers in full have developed the four bases of psychic power in full.

children.title: A Mendicant
children.description: Whatever mendicants realize perfection do so by developing the four bases of psychic power.

children.title: Awakened
children.description: It is because of developing the four bases of psychic power that the Realized One is called a Buddha.

children.title: Knowledge
children.description: On the night of his awakening, understanding and vision came to the Buddha regarding the four bases of psychic power.

children.title: At the Cāpāla Shrine
children.description: The Buddha says he could live to the end of the eon due to developing the four bases of psychic power. But Ānanda doesn’t get the hint.

children.title: Before
children.description: The Buddha recounts the process of inquiry that lead to him fully understanding the four bases of psychic power, as well as the powers that result from that.

children.title: Very Fruitful
children.description: The four bases of psychic power are very beneficial.

children.title: Immersion Due to Enthusiasm
children.description: An analysis of the four bases of psychic power showing how enthusiasm, energy, higher consciousness, and inquiry work in the context of advanced meditation.

children.title: With Moggallāna
children.description: When lazy monks were wasting time, the Buddha asks Moggallāna to stir them up. He shakes with his toe the large building in which they were staying, terrifying the monks. They sought refuge in the Buddha, and he taught them the four bases of psychic power.

children.title: The Brahmin Uṇṇābha
children.description: Ānanda explains to the brahmin Uṇṇābha that the spiritual path is lived to give up desire through the the four bases of psychic power. But Uṇṇābha says this is a contradiction, as desire is itself one of the four bases. Ānanda resolves the contradiction with the simile of a man walking to a park.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (1st)
children.description: Whatever ascetics are of great spiritual power have developed the four bases of psychic power.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: Whatever ascetics are of great spiritual power have developed the four bases of psychic power.

children.title: A Mendicant
children.description: It is because of developing the four bases of psychic power that a mendicant ends the defilements.

children.title: A Teaching on Psychic Power, Etc.
children.description: The Buddha distinguishes between psychic powers, the basis for psychic power, and the development of the bases for psychic power.

children.title: Analysis
children.description: The Buddha teaches the bases for psychic power and analyzes them in detail.

children.title: The Path
children.description: Before his awakening, the Buddha reflected on the path for developing the bases of psychic power.

children.title: The Iron Ball
children.description: Ānanda asks the Buddha whether he travels to the Brahmā realm in a mind-made body or in a physical body.

children.title: A Mendicant
children.description: It is because of developing the four bases of psychic power that a mendicant ends the defilements.

children.title: Plain Version
children.description: The four bases for psychic power are desire, energy, higher mind, and inquiry.

children.title: Fruits (1st)
children.description: The four bases for psychic power lead to perfection or once-return.

children.title: Fruits (2nd)
children.description: The four bases for psychic power lead to seven benefits; perfection or one of the lesser attainments.

children.title: With Ānanda (1st)
children.description: The Buddha explains to Ānanda the difference between psychic powers, the basis for psychic power, and the development of the bases for psychic power.

children.title: With Ānanda (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha explains to Ānanda the difference between psychic powers, the basis for psychic power, and the development of the bases for psychic power.

children.title: Several Mendicants (1st)
children.description: The Buddha explains to several mendicants the difference between psychic powers, the basis for psychic power, and the development of the bases for psychic power.

children.title: Several Mendicants (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha explains to several mendicants the difference between psychic powers, the basis for psychic power, and the development of the bases for psychic power.

children.title: About Moggallāna
children.description: Moggallāna is so very powerful due to developing the four bases for psychic power.

children.title: The Realized One
children.description: The Realized One is so very powerful due to developing the four bases for psychic power.

children.title: 8. Anuruddha
children.description: The “Linked Discourses with Anuruddha” contains 24 discourses with Anuruddha, famous for his powers of clairvoyance, but here revealed as an exponent of mindfulness meditation. It is to mindfulness meditation that he attributes his spiritual attainments, whether psychic powers, absorptions, or awakening. This series of texts can be regarded as a supplement to SN 47.

children.title: In Private (1st)
children.description: While meditating alone, Anuruddha reflected that one who has neglected the four kinds of mindfulness meditation has neglected the path to the end of suffering. Moggallāna reads his mind and visits to question him on this. Anuruddha speaks of developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation internally and externally, in terms of origin and cessation, and developing power over perceptions.

children.title: In Private (2nd)
children.description: While meditating alone, Anuruddha reflected that one who has neglected the four kinds of mindfulness meditation has neglected the path to the end of suffering. Moggallāna reads his mind and visits to question him on this. Anuruddha speaks of developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation internally and externally.

children.title: On the Bank of the Sutanu
children.description: When some mendicants ask Anuruddha how he attained such higher knowledge, he replies it is from developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: At Thorny Wood (1st)
children.description: Sāriputta and Moggallāna ask Anuruddha what a trainee mendicant should practice. He replies that it is the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: At Thorny Wood (2nd)
children.description: Sāriputta and Moggallāna ask Anuruddha what an adept mendicant should practice. He replies that it is the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: At Thorny Wood (3rd)
children.description: When Sāriputta ask Anuruddha how he attained such higher knowledge, he replies it is from developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: The Ending of Craving
children.description: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation lead to the ending of craving.

children.title: The Salaḷa Tree Hut
children.description: Even if kings beg them to disrobe, a mendicant who has developed the four kinds of mindfulness meditation is unmoved. Their mind flows to Nibbāna like the Ganges to the sea.

children.title: In Ambapālī’s Mango Grove
children.description: Sāriputta asks why Anuruddha looks so peaceful, and he replies it is due to developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: Gravely Ill
children.description: Some mendicants ask Anuruddha how he remains equanimous even though ill. He replies that it is due to the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

children.title: A Thousand Eons
children.description: By developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation Anuruddha surveys a thousand world systems.

children.title: Where All Paths of Practice Lead
9. Absorption
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Absorption” contains 54 discourses on the topic of absorption meditation (jhāna), which however merely apply the standard repetition series to the formula for the four absorptions.

children.title: 10. Breath Meditation
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Breath Meditation” contains 20 discourses on breath meditation (ānāpānassati), the most revered form of meditation from early Buddhism until the present day. It was practiced by the Buddha himself. The meditation is taught in a detailed series of sixteen steps. These are partially sequential, but also overlap in some cases. The development of these fulfills all four kinds of mindfulness meditation and the seven factors of awakening. Thus this one form of meditation can lead to awakening; which is not, however, to say that it is invariably the best approach. The Buddha taught many different meditations for a reason; each has its own qualities and benefits. Breath meditation is seen as a peaceful and pleasant meditation which helps still distracting thoughts. It is a simple practice broadly suitable for most meditators, but leading to profound depths.

children.title: One Thing
children.description: Breath meditation is very beneficial. It is developed by going into seclusion, establishing mindfulness on the breath, and proceeding through sixteen stages.

children.title: Awakening Factors
children.description: Breath meditation is very beneficial. It is developed together with the seven factors of awakening.

children.title: Plain Version
children.description: Breath meditation is very beneficial. It is developed by going into seclusion, establishing mindfulness on the breath, and proceeding through sixteen stages.

children.title: Fruits (1st)
children.description: Breath meditation is very beneficial. When developed it leads to perfection or non-return.

children.title: Fruits (2nd)
children.description: Breath meditation is very beneficial. When developed it leads to perfection or one of the lesser attainments.

children.title: With Ariṭṭha
children.description: When the Buddha asks Venerable Ariṭṭha about breath meditation, his answer, while not incorrect, does not do full justice to the practice.

children.title: About Mahākappina
children.description: The Buddha sees Venerable Mahākappina meditating nearby and points out that his steadiness and tranquility are due to practicing breath meditation.

children.title: The Simile of the Lamp
children.description: Before his awakening the Buddha generally practiced breath meditation, which kept him alert and peaceful and led to the ending of defilements. One who wishes for any of the higher fruits of the renunciate life should practice the same way.

children.title: At Vesālī
children.description: The Buddha taught the meditation on the ugliness of the body, then left to go on retreat. However, many monks, misconstruing the teachings, ending up killing themselves. The Buddha taught breath meditation as a peaceful and pleasant abiding.

children.title: With Kimbila
children.description: When the Buddha asks Venerable Kimbila about breath meditation, he is unable to answer. At Ānanda’s urging, the Buddha explains in detail.

children.title: Icchānaṅgala
children.description: The Buddha goes on a three month retreat, and later says that during that time he mostly practiced breath meditation.

children.title: In Doubt
children.description: Venerable Lomasavaṅgīsa explains to Mahānāma that the difference between a trainee and the Realized One is that the trainees practice to give up the hindrances, whereas the Realized One has already ended all defilements.

children.title: With Ānanda (1st)
children.description: Answering Ānanda, the Buddha explains how one thing fulfills four things, four things fulfill seven things, and seven things fulfill two things.

children.title: With Ānanda (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha explains to Ānanda how one thing fulfills four things, four things fulfill seven things, and seven things fulfill two things.

children.title: Several Mendicants (1st)
children.description: Answering some mendicants, the Buddha explains how one thing fulfills four things, four things fulfill seven things, and seven things fulfill two things.

children.title: Several Mendicants (2nd)
