children.description: The Buddha explains to some mendicants how one thing fulfills four things, four things fulfill seven things, and seven things fulfill two things.

children.title: Completely Understanding the Course of Time
11. Stream-Entry
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on Stream-Entry” contains 74 discourses on the topic of stream-entry, or more precisely, two sets of four qualities, one of which distinguishes a person as a stream-enterer, and one which help lead to stream-entry. The primary qualities of the first set are faith and ethical conduct. For the second, it is hearing the teaching and practicing accordingly. Note that these sets do not exhaust the qualities of a stream-enterer, many others of which are described elsewhere, but serve to emphasis the crucial role especially of faith.

children.title: A Wheel-Turning Monarch
children.description: Even a universal monarch may have a bad rebirth, but someone who has the four factors of stream-entry—experiential faith in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and ethical conduct—is freed from such destinies.

children.title: The Objective of the Spiritual Life
children.description: Someone who has the four factors of stream-entry—experiential faith in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and ethical conduct—is a stream-enterer, destined for awakening.

children.title: With Dīghāvu
children.description: The lay follower Dīghāvu is ill and he asks for the Buddha to visit. Dīghāvu confirms that he possesses the four factors of stream-entry and in addition six contemplations leading to insight. Yet he is still worried that his father will miss him when he dies.

children.title: With Sāriputta (1st)
children.description: Sāriputta explains to Ānanda that someone who has the four factors of stream-entry—experiential faith in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and ethical conduct—is a stream-enterer, destined for awakening.

children.title: With Sāriputta (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha asks Sāriputta about the four factors for stream-entry: association with good people, hearing the teaching, proper attention, and right practice. He also defines the “stream” and the “stream-enterer”.

children.title: The Chamberlains
children.description: After the rainy season, the chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa hear that the Buddha is approaching and go to see him. They describe their joy at knowing when the Buddha is approaching, and speak of their special duties guarding the royal harem. The Buddha says they have four factors of stream-entry—experiential faith in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha; and here generosity rather than ethics as the final factor.

children.title: The People of Bamboo Gate
children.description: The brahmin householders of Bamboo Gate ask the Buddha how to live well in the home. The Buddha teaches them seven principles they can apply to themselves, which are practical applications of the Golden Rule. Someone with these seven principles and the four factors of stream-entry is a stream-enterer.

children.title: In the Brick Hall (1st)
children.description: Ānanda asks the Buddha about the rebirths of several disciples. The Buddha confirms those details, and proposes a way for people to know for themselves by reflecting on the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: At the Brick Hall (2nd)
children.description: Ānanda asks the Buddha about the rebirths of several disciples. The Buddha confirms those details, and proposes a way for people to know for themselves by reflecting on the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: At the Brick Hall (3rd)
children.description: Ānanda asks the Buddha about the rebirths of several disciples. The Buddha confirms those details, and proposes a way for people to know for themselves by reflecting on the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: A Saṅgha of a Thousand Nuns
children.description: The Buddha teaches a thousand nuns the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: The Brahmins
children.description: The Buddha contrasts a foolish brahmanical ritual called “going upwards” with the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: With the Senior Monk Ānanda
children.description: Sāriputta asks Ānanda how many things are given up and how many things possessed by the stream-enterer.

children.title: Fear of the Bad Place
children.description: A noble disciple has transcended fears of a bad rebirth.

children.title: Fear of the Bad Place, the Underworld
children.description: A noble disciple has transcended fears of a bad rebirth.

children.title: Friends and Colleagues (1st)
children.description: You should encourage your friends in the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: Friends and Colleagues (2nd)
children.description: You should encourage your friends in the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: A Visit to the Gods (1st)
children.description: Moggallāna visits the gods of the Thirty-Three and encourages them in the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: A Visit to the Gods (2nd)
children.description: Moggallāna visits the gods of the Thirty-Three and encourages them in the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: A Visit to the Gods (3rd)
children.description: The Buddha visits the gods of the Thirty-Three and encourages them in the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: With Mahānāma (1st)
children.description: Mahānāma the Sakyan expresses his fear that if he dies unmindful he may go to a bad rebirth. The Buddha tells him not to fear, as he will definitely go to a good place, since he has long practiced the Dhamma.

children.title: With Mahānāma (2nd)
children.description: Mahānāma the Sakyan expresses his fear that if he dies unmindful he may go to a bad rebirth. The Buddha tells him not to fear, as he will definitely go to a good place, since he has the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: With Godhā the Sakyan
children.description: Mahānāma and Godhā the Sakyans discuss whether a stream-enterer has three or four factors. They go to the Buddha to settle it, and Mahānāma testifies to his faith.

children.title: About Sarakāni (1st)
children.description: When Sarakāni the Sakyan died the Buddha declared him a stream-enterer. But others complained, since he was known as a drinker. However, the Buddha confirmed to Mahānāma that Sarakāni had undertaken the precepts on his deathbed.

children.title: About Sarakāni the Sakyan (2nd)
children.description: When Sarakāni the Sakyan died the Buddha declared him a stream-enterer. But others complained, since he was known as a drinker. However, the Buddha confirmed to Mahānāma that Sarakāni had undertaken the precepts on his deathbed.

children.title: Anāthapiṇḍika (1st)
children.description: When the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sick, Sāriputta reminds him of his considerable accomplishments in the Dhamma, analyzing stream-entry in ten factors, at which Anāthapiṇḍika recovers. Later he invited Sāriputta and Ānanda for a meal, and Sāriputta thanked him with verses.

children.title: With Anāthapiṇḍika (2nd)
children.description: When the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sick, Ānanda reminds him of the four factors of stream-entry, which Anāthapiṇḍika claims to possess.

children.title: Fears and Enmities (1st)
children.description: A noble disciple who is a layperson has eliminated the fear that comes from breaking precepts, possesses the four factors of stream-entry, and understands dependent origination.

children.title: Fears and Enmities (2nd)
children.description: A noble disciple who is a layperson has eliminated the fear that comes from breaking precepts, possesses the four factors of stream-entry, and understands dependent origination.

children.title: With Nandaka the Licchavi
children.description: The Buddha teaches the four factors of stream-entry to Nandaka, the minister of the Licchavis. When his servant tells him it is time for his ritual bath, he says that the inner bathing of the Dhamma is enough.

children.title: Overflowing Merit (1st)
children.description: The four factors of stream-entry—with ethics as the fourth—are streams of merit.

children.title: Overflowing Merit (2nd)
children.description: The four factors of stream-entry—with generosity as the fourth—are streams of merit.

children.title: Overflowing Merit (3rd)
children.description: The four factors of stream-entry—with wisdom as the fourth—are streams of merit.

children.title: Footprints of the Gods (1st)
children.description: The four factors of stream-entry are footprints of the gods.

children.title: Footprints of the Gods (2nd)
children.description: The four factors of stream-entry are footprints of the gods, for the gods hold non-violence as supreme.

children.title: In Common With the Gods
children.description: When a person possesses the four factors of stream-entry, the gods regard them as similar to themselves.

children.title: With Mahānāma
children.description: The Buddha explains to Mahānāma what is a lay follower, what is a virtuous lay follower, and a lay follower accomplished in faith, generosity, and wisdom.

children.title: Rain
children.description: Like rain falling on the mountain top, the four factors of stream-entry flow on to the ending of defilements.

children.title: With Kāḷigodhā
children.description: Kāḷigodhā the Sakyan lady confirms to the Buddha that she possesses the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: Nandiya the Sakyan
children.description: Someone who completely lacks the four factors of stream-entry is an ordinary person. But even a stream-enterer may be negligent if they do not make further effort in meditation.

children.title: Overflowing Merit (1st)
children.description: The four factors of stream-entry—with ethics as the fourth—are streams of merit, and like the ocean cannot be counted. With verses.

children.title: Overflowing Merit (2nd)
children.description: The four factors of stream-entry—with generosity as the fourth—are streams of merit, and like the ocean cannot be counted. With verses.

children.title: Overflowing Merit (3rd)
children.description: The four factors of stream-entry—with wisdom as the fourth—are streams of merit, and like the ocean cannot be counted. With verses.

children.title: Rich (1st)
children.description: A noble disciple with the four factors of stream-entry is said to be prosperous.

children.title: Rich (2nd)
children.description: A noble disciple with the four factors of stream-entry is said to be prosperous.

children.title: Plain Version
children.description: A noble disciple with the four factors of stream-entry is a stream-enterer.

children.title: With Nandiya
children.description: A noble disciple with the four factors of stream-entry is a stream-enterer.

children.title: With Bhaddiya
children.description: A noble disciple with the four factors of stream-entry is a stream-enterer.

children.title: With Mahānāma
children.description: A noble disciple with the four factors of stream-entry is a stream-enterer.

children.title: Factors
children.description: Four factors for stream-entry: association with good people, hearing the teaching, proper attention, and right practice.

children.title: With Verses
children.description: A noble disciple with the four factors of stream-entry is a stream-enterer. With verses.

children.title: One Who Completed the Rains
children.description: When a monk comes from Sāvatthī to Kapilavatthu, the Sakyans visit him and ask as to the health of the Buddha and the Saṅgha. Then they ask what the monk has learned. He replies that the number of perfected ones is few, and those on lower levels of attainment are greater in number.

children.title: With Dhammadinna
children.description: The lay follower Dhammadinna leads a group of 500 to visit the Buddha. He encourages them to study deep discourses, but they protest that they don’t have enough time. So the Buddha encourages them in the four factors of stream-entry.

children.title: Sick
children.description: Mahānāma asks the Buddha how a lay follower should teach a wise lay follower who is ill. He should first be encouraged in the four factors of stream-entry, and then urged to let go of attachments, until he realizes full freedom.

children.title: The Fruit of Stream-Entry
children.description: Association with good people, hearing the teaching, proper attention, and right practice lead to the fruit of stream-entry.

children.title: 12. Truths
children.description: The “Linked Discourses on the Truths” contains 131 discourses on the four noble truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. These formed the main subject of the Buddha’s first discourse, which is included here as SN 56.11. The Buddha said that all of his teaching was comprised within the four noble truths. Indeed, the overall structure of the main doctrinal Saṁyuttas can be seen as an expanded example of this: The sections on the Aggregates and the Sense Fields deal with the first noble truth; Dependent Origination deals with the second and third; and the chapters on the Path deal with the final truth. This chapter thus provides an overall perspective on the other teachings, and the chapter occurs at the end just as the realization of the four noble truths emerges from the path.

children.title: Immersion
children.description: Mendicants should develop immersion so as to understand the four noble truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

children.title: Retreat
children.description: Mendicants should develop seclusion so as to understand the four noble truths.

children.title: A Gentleman (1st)
children.description: Members of good families go forth to understand the four noble truths.

children.title: A Gentleman (2nd)
children.description: Members of good families go forth to penetrate the four noble truths.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (1st)
children.description: True ascetics understand the four noble truths.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
children.description: True ascetics become awakened through understanding the four noble truths.

children.title: Thoughts
children.description: Don’t think bad thoughts. Instead, think of the four noble truths.

children.title: Thought
children.description: Don’t think in useless ways. Instead, reflect on the four noble truths.

children.title: Arguments
children.description: Don’t argue. Instead, converse on the four noble truths.

children.title: Low Talk
children.description: Don’t gossip. Instead, talk about the four noble truths.

children.title: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma
Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma
children.description: The famous first discourse, taught at Varanasi to the group of five ascetics. It begins by rejecting the extremes of asceticism and indulgence and recommends the middle way of the eightfold path. Then it defines the four noble truths and analyzes them in twelve aspects. It ends with Venerable Kondañña becoming the first person apart from the Buddha to realize the Dhamma.

children.title: The Realized Ones
children.description: All Realized Ones understand the four noble truths in their twelve aspects.

children.title: Aggregates
children.description: The four noble truths are defined, with the five aggregates under the truth of suffering.

children.title: Interior Sense Fields
children.description: The four noble truths are defined, with the six sense fields under the truth of suffering.

children.title: Remembering (1st)
children.description: The Buddha asks the mendicants how they remember the four noble truths.

children.title: Remembering (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha asks the mendicants how they remember the four noble truths.

children.title: Ignorance
children.description: Ignorance is not knowing the four noble truths.

children.title: Knowledge
children.description: Understanding is knowing the four noble truths.

children.title: Expressions
children.description: Each of the four noble truths has innumerable implications.

children.title: Real
children.description: Each of The four noble truths are real, not otherwise.

children.title: 3. The Chapter at the Village of Koṭi
At the Village of Koṭi (1st)
children.description: It is because of not understanding the four noble truths that both the Buddha and others have wandered for so long in transmigration. With verses.

children.title: At the Village of Koṭi (2nd)
children.description: True ascetics understand the four noble truths. With verses.

children.title: The Fully Awakened Buddha
children.description: The Realized One is called the Buddha because he understands the four noble truths.

children.title: The Perfected Ones
children.description: All Buddhas become awakened through the four noble truths.

children.title: The Ending of Defilements
children.description: Only by knowing and seeing the four noble truths are the defilements ended.

children.title: Friends
children.description: You should encourage your friends in the four noble truths.

children.title: Real
children.description: The four noble truths are real, not otherwise, that is why they are noble.

children.title: The World
children.description: In this world, the Realized One is the noble one, that is why the four truths are noble.

children.title: Should Be Completely Understood
children.description: The first truth is to be understood; the second is to be given up; the third is to be realized; and the fourth is to be developed.

children.title: With Gavampati
children.description: Some mendicants are discussing whether the four truths are necessarily seen together. Venerable Gavampati asserts that he has learned it from the Buddha that they are: if you see one, you see them all.

children.title: 4. The Chapter in a Rosewood Forest
In a Rosewood Forest
children.description: In a siṁsapā grove, the Buddha holds up a handful of leaves, and compares it to all the leaves in the forest. So too, he has taught the four noble truths, which is only a fraction of what he knows.

children.title: Acacia Leaves
children.description: Just as it’s impossible to keep water in a basket of pine needles, it’s impossible to end suffering without penetrating the four noble truths.

children.title: A Stick
children.description: Beings who have not seen the four noble truths roam on from one birth to another, like a stick thrown end to end.

children.title: Clothes
children.description: Even more than if your clothes are on fire, you should make an effort to understand the four noble truths.

children.title: A Hundred Spears
children.description: Even more than if you’re being tortured with spikes, you should make an effort to understand the four noble truths.

children.title: Living Creatures
children.description: The small creatures in the ocean are greater in number than all the foliage in the jungles of India. Still, your rebirths are more than this.

children.title: The Simile of the Sun (1st)
children.description: As the dawn precedes the sunrise, right view precedes the penetration of the four noble truths.

children.title: The Simile of the Sun (2nd)
children.description: As long as there are no sun and moon, the world is in darkness. So too, as long as the Realized One has not arisen and declared the four noble truths, the world is in darkness.

children.title: Indra’s pillar
children.description: One who has not seen the four noble truths is as feeble as a tuft of cotton wool, while one who has seen them is like a deep-rooted pillar.

children.title: Looking For a Debate
children.description: No-one can refute you if you are well grounded in the four noble truths.

children.title: Speculation About the World
children.description: The Buddha tells the curious tale of a man who sat by a lotus pond to speculate about the world, and saw an army enter a lotus stalk. He thought he was going mad. The Buddha said that no, the army was real. Nevertheless, you should not speculate about such things, but should reflect on the four noble truths.

children.title: A Cliff
children.description: The Buddha takes the mendicants to a steep precipice, and points out that those who do not understand the four noble truths fall into a still deeper precipice.

children.title: The Great Scorching
children.description: The Buddha speaks of a hell called the great inferno, and points out that those who do not understand the four noble truths fall into a still fiercer inferno.

children.title: A Bungalow
children.description: Just as it’s impossible to climb the upper floor without building the lower floors first, it’s impossible to end suffering without penetrating the four noble truths.

children.title: Splitting Hairs
children.description: Ānanda sees Licchavi youths shoot arrows through keyholes. But seeing the four noble truths is even harder.

children.title: Darkness
children.description: Interstellar space is dark and empty; but not seeing the four noble truths is even worse.

children.title: A Yoke With a Hole (1st)
children.description: A blind turtle would put its head through a yoke with a hole in it floating in the ocean sooner than someone in the lower realms would be reborn as a human.

children.title: A Yoke With a Hole (2nd)
children.description: A blind turtle would put its head through a yoke with a hole in it floating in the ocean sooner than someone in the lower realms would be reborn as a human.

children.title: Sineru, King of Mountains (1st)
children.description: As seven bits of gravel are smaller than Mount Sineru, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: Sineru, King of Mountains (2nd)
children.description: As seven bits of gravel are smaller than Mount Sineru, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: A Fingernail
children.description: As a bit of dirt under a nail compared to the whole earth, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: A Lotus Pond
children.description: As a drop of water on a blade of grass compared to a massive dam, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: Where the Waters Join Together (1st)
children.description: As a few drops of water compared to the confluence of great rivers, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: Where the Waters Join Together (2nd)
children.description: As a few drops of water compared to confluence of the great rivers, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: The Earth (1st)
children.description: As a few jujube seeds compared to the great earth, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: The Earth (2nd)
children.description: As a few jujube seeds compared to the great earth, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: The Ocean (1st)
children.description: As a few drops of water compared to the ocean, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: The Ocean (2nd)
children.description: As a few drops of water compared to the ocean, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: A Mountain (1st)
children.description: As seven bits of gravel are smaller than the Himalayas, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: A Mountain (2nd)
children.description: As seven bits of gravel are smaller than the Himalayas, so is the suffering remaining to one who has seen the four noble truths.

children.title: 7. The First Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on Raw Grain
8. The Second Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on Raw Grain
9. The Third Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on Raw Grain
10. The Fourth Chapter of Abbreviated Texts on Raw Grain
Passing Away as Humans and Reborn in Hell
Passing Away as Humans and Reborn as Animals
Passing Away as Humans and Reborn as Ghosts
Passing Away as Humans and Reborn as Gods
Passing Away as Gods and Reborn as Gods
Dying as Gods and Reborn as Humans
Dying in Hell and Reborn as Humans
Dying in Hell and Reborn as Gods
Dying as Animals and Reborn as Humans
Dying as Animals and Reborn as Gods
Dying as Ghosts and Reborn as Humans
Dying as Ghosts and Reborn as Gods
Dying as Ghosts and Reborn as Ghosts
1. The Serpent Chapter
children.description: Twelve poems beginning with a set of similes comparing a liberated one with a serpent who sheds its skin. The poems are diverse in style and content, and appear to have been collected from different sources. This chapter includes many perennial favorites such as the Mettā Sutta on Love and the warnings of the Parābhava Sutta on downfalls.

children.title: The Snake
children.description: One who advances far along the path sloughs off the near shore and far, like a snake who sloughs off its skin.

children.title: With Dhaniya the Cowherd
children.description: A poetic dialogue contrasting the wealth and security of lay life with the wealth and security of a person who has lived the renunciate life to its culmination. If you have trouble relating to someone like Dhaniya who measures his wealth in cattle, then when reading this poem substitute stocks and bonds for cows and bulls, and economic downturn for rain.

children.title: The Rhinoceros Horn
children.description: If you can’t find a good teacher, it’s better to wander alone.

children.title: With Bhāradvāja the Farmer
children.description: The Buddha answers a farmer who claims that monks do no useful work and so don’t deserve to eat.

children.title: With the Smith Cunda
children.description: Four different types of contemplatives and how to recognize them.

children.title: Downfalls for a Lay Follower
children.description: The various actions and attitudes that lead to spiritual decline.

children.title: The Lowlife
children.description: Being an outcaste is a matter of behavior, not birth.

children.title: The Discourse on Love
children.description: The practice of developing universal goodwill: the practices that form a foundation for the practice, the attitude of universal goodwill itself, and the steps that lead from goodwill to awakening.

children.title: The Buddha Teaches Sātāgira and Hemavata the Native Spirits
children.description: The Buddha explains to a yakkha how one crosses over the flood.

children.title: Āḷavaka the Native Spirit
children.description: A yakkha challenges the Buddha with riddles and threatens to “hurl out his mind, rip open his heart, or hurl him across the River Ganges” if he doesn’t solve the riddles to the yakkha’s satisfaction.

children.title: Victory
children.description: Victory over the defilements through contemplation of the unattractiveness of the body.

children.title: The Sage
children.description: The characteristics of the ideal sage, who finds happiness and security in living the solitary life. (This sutta is apparently one of the series of passages that King Asoka recommended for study and reflection by all practicing Buddhists.)

children.title: 2. The Lesser Chapter
children.description: Thirteen diverse poems similar to the previous chapter.

children.title: Gems
children.description: The many treasures to be found in the Triple Gem.

children.title: Carrion
children.description: People are defiled, not by eating meat, but by engaging in evil conduct.

children.title: Conscience
children.description: How to recognize a true friend.

children.title: True Blessings
children.description: A list of the types of skillful behavior that give blessings and protection.

children.title: Spiky the Native Spirit
children.description: Another yakkha challenges the Buddha with riddles and threatens to “hurl out his mind, rip open his heart, or hurl him across the River Ganges” if he doesn’t solve the riddles to the yakkha’s satisfaction.

children.title: A Righteous Life
children.description: The Buddha encourages the monks to avoid monks who are evil in their desires.

children.title: Brahmanical Traditions
children.description: How brahmans, through greed, abandoned the good principles of their ancestors.

children.title: The Boat
children.description: A good teacher, like a good boatman, is one who knows firsthand how to cross to the further shore.

children.title: What Morality?
children.description: The attitudes and behavior that enable one best to learn and benefit from the Dhamma.

children.title: Get up! Make an Effort!
children.description: Get up! Don’t let the opportunity for practice pass you by.

children.title: With Rāhula
children.description: Rāhula reflects on the teachings he received from his father, the Buddha.

children.title: Vaṅgīsa and his Mentor Nigrodhakappa
children.description: Vaṅgīsa, the foremost poet among the Buddha’s disciples, praises the Buddha in verse.

children.title: The Right Way to Wander
children.description: The sort of person who, having gone forth, is fit to wander through the world.

children.title: With Dhammika
children.description: The proper code of conduct for lay followers of the Dhamma.

children.title: 3. The Great Chapter
children.description: Twelve longer poems that expand into sometimes legendary narrative. The first two discourses and the Nalaka Sutta offer early glimpses at crucial episodes in the Buddha’s life. While some of these poems are found elsewhere in the canon, the Dvayatānupassanā offers a unique perspective on dependent origination and other topics typically found in prose texts.

children.title: The Going Forth
children.description: The young Bodhisatta (Buddha-to-be), soon after leaving home, explains why he refuses King Bimbisāra’s offer of a position in his court.

children.title: Striving
children.description: Māra attempts to dissuade the Bodhisatta from his path.

children.title: Well-Spoken Words
children.description: Four characteristics of well-spoken speech.

children.title: With Bhāradvāja of Sundarika on the Sacrificial Cake
children.description: A brahman questions the Buddha to see if the latter deserves to receive the cake resulting from his sacrifice.

children.title: With Māgha on Giving
children.description: What are the qualities of a recipient that produce the most merit from a gift?

children.title: Sabhiya’s Questions
children.description: A sutta dating from early in the Buddha’s teaching career. A wanderer, disappointed in the teachings he has received from other teachers, approaches the Buddha with his questions.

children.title: With Sela
children.description: Sela the brahman praises the Buddha to see how the latter responds to praise.

children.title: The Dart
children.description: Death and loss are inevitable, but grief is not.

children.title: With Vāseṭṭha
children.description: Is one worthy of respect because of one’s birth, or because of one’s actions?

children.title: To Kokāliya on the Results of Slander
children.description: A follower of Devadatta slanders Ven. Sāriputta and Ven. Moggallāna and, after suffering a painful disease, falls into hell. The sutta then gives a graphic description of the sufferings awaiting him there.

children.title: The Sages Asita and Nālaka
children.description: A sutta in two parts. The first part gives an account of events soon after the birth of the Bodhisatta. The second part describes the way of the sage.

children.title: Contemplating Pairs
children.description: Not all dualities are misleading. This sutta teaches ways to contemplate the duality of the origination and cessation of stress and suffering so as to reach awakening.

children.title: 4. Eights
children.description: This chapter, which has parallels in Chinese, and received an early commentary in the Niddesa, is often regarded as one of the earliest texts in the canon. Shorn of literary embellishments, it is direct and  powerful. A distinctive aspect is the critique of meaningless debates and attachments to views. The Attadaṇḍa Sutta gives an alternative account of the reasons for the Buddha’s going forth.

children.title: Sensual Pleasures
children.description: The drawbacks of sensual desires.

children.title: Eight on the Cave
children.description: Those who remain attached to the body, to sensuality, and to their sense of “mine” will have a hard time freeing themselves from fear of death and from further becoming.

children.title: Eight on Malice
children.description: Freedom isn’t to be found by boasting of your precepts and practices or by debating your views.

children.title: Eight on the Pure
children.description: How to avoid the trap of letting go of one thing only to cling to something more subtle.

children.title: Eight on the Ultimate
children.description: The conceit that comes from clinging to practices or views—even if they’re supreme—is a fetter preventing full freedom.

children.title: Old Age
children.description: Life is short. Possessiveness brings grief. Freedom comes from abandoning any sense of “mine.”

children.title: To Tissametteyya on the Dangers of Sex
children.description: The drawbacks of falling away from the celibate life.

children.title: To Pasūra on Debate
children.description: The drawbacks of engaging in debates, for winners and losers alike.

children.title: With Māgaṇḍiya
children.description: Māgandiya offers the Buddha his daughter in marriage. The Buddha refuses and further subdues Māgandiya’s pride by describing a state of peace that Māgandiya doesn’t understand.

children.title: Before the Breakup
children.description: How to live at peace.

children.title: Quarrels and Disputes
children.description: The Buddha is questioned on the source of quarrels and disputes, and on the highest level of spiritual attainment.

children.title: The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
children.description: If the truth is one, how should a person behave in a world where many different truths are taught?

children.title: The Longer Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
children.description: How to maintain freedom in a world full of disputes.

children.title: Speedy
children.description: The attitudes and behavior of a monk training for the sake of total release.

children.title: Taking Up Arms
children.description: The Buddha speaks in poignant terms of the saṁvega that led him to leave the household life. He concludes with recommendations for practice and a description of the person who has attained the goal of true peace and security.

children.title: The Questions of Sāriputta
children.description: When a monk, disaffected with the world, takes up the life of seclusion, what fears should he overcome? What dangers should he beware of? How should he train to blow away the impurities in his heart?

children.title: 5. Way to the Beyond
children.description: This is perhaps the most sophisticated and moving poetic composition in early Buddhism. It begins with a brahmin, suffering an unwanted curse, who sends his students to seek the Buddha. At the end of a long journey they ask questions, the nature of which indicate their subtle philosophy and deep meditation. It concludes with an emotional declaration of faith and determination.

children.title: Introductory Verses
children.description: A brahman teacher sends his students to the Buddha to see if the latter is truly awakened.

children.title: The Questions of the Student Ajita
children.description: A brahman questions the Buddha about mindfulness, discernment, and the cessation of name-and-form.

children.title: The Questions of the Student Tissametteyya
children.description: Who in the world is truly contented, truly free, truly a great person?

children.title: The Questions of the Student Puṇṇaka
children.description: Birth and aging can be overcome, not through sacrificial rituals, but through training the mind to go beyond perturbation.

children.title: The Questions of the Student Mettagū
children.description: How does one cross the flood of birth and old age, sorrow and grief?

children.title: The Questions of the Student Dhotaka
children.description: How can one become freed of all doubt?

children.title: The Questions of the Student Upasīva
children.description: What support should one hold on to in order to cross over the flood of craving? Can an awakened person be described?

children.title: The Questions of the Student Nanda
children.description: Who deserves to be called a sage? Who has crossed over birth and aging?

children.title: The Questions of the Student Hemaka
children.description: How do you cross over entanglements in the world?

children.title: The Questions of the Student Todeyya
children.description: How to recognize an emancipated person.

children.title: The Questions of the Student Kappa
children.description: What is the island above the flood of the great danger of birth?

children.title: The Questions of the Student Jatukaṇṇī
children.description: How does one abandon birth and aging?

children.title: The Questions of the Student Bhadrāvudha
children.description: Bhadrāvudha asks the Buddha: How did you come to know the Dhamma?

children.title: The Questions of the Student Udaya
children.description: How to reach unbinding and bring consciousness to a halt.

children.title: The Questions of the Student Posala
children.description: How to develop insight after mastering the perception of nothingness.

children.title: The Questions of the Student Mogharāja
children.description: How should one view the world so as to escape the king of Death?

children.title: The Questions of the Student Piṅgiya
children.description: Alarmed by the deterioration of his aging body, Piṅgiya asks the Buddha how to conquer birth and decay.

children.title: Homage to the Way to the Beyond
children.description: The questions and events are summarized.

children.title: Preserving the Way to the Beyond
children.description: Piṅgiya, after becoming a non-returner, explains to his former teacher his devotion to the Buddha.

children.title: Sumanā, Who Went Forth Late in Life
To Abhayā’s Mother From Her Daughter
Paṭācārā, Who Had a Following of Five Hundred
1. Awakening
children.description: This chapter begins with a series of discourses set immediately after the Buddha’s awakening, which are shared with the first chapter of the Khandhakas. It establishes the fundamental thesis of Buddhism: that awakening is possible through one’s own efforts. Each discourse deals with the idea of the true “brahmin”, defined not according to hereditary caste, but freedom from defilements.

children.title: Upon Awakening (1st)
children.description: The Buddha, soon after awakening, contemplates specific conditionality and dependent co-arising.

children.title: Upon Awakening (2nd)
children.description: The Buddha, soon after awakening, contemplates specific conditionality and dependent co-arising.

children.title: Upon Awakening (3rd)
children.description: The Buddha, soon after awakening, contemplates specific conditionality and dependent co-arising.

children.title: The Mystic Syllable Huṁ
children.description: A brahmin who recites the mystic syllable huṁ asks the Buddha who is the true brahmin.

children.title: The Brahmin
children.description: The Buddha redefines the term “brahmin” to mean anyone, regardless of birth, who is awakened.

children.title: With Mahākassapa
children.description: Ven. Mahā Kassapa chooses to go for alms among the poor rather than among the devas.

children.title: At Ajakalāpaka
children.description: An awakened person has gone beyond fear.

children.title: With Saṅgāmaji
children.description: A monk’s former wife tries to use their child to lure him back into the lay life.

children.title: Dreadlocked Ascetics
children.description: The mind is cleansed and purified, not by ablutions, but by truth and rectitude.

children.title: With Bāhiya
children.description: The ascetic Bāhiya becomes an arahant after receiving a brief teaching about adding nothing to sensory experience.

children.title: 2. Mucalinda
children.description: The Buddha’s awakening has shown him a spiritual happiness that is better than any worldly happiness. This chapter focusses on the emotional dimension of enlightenment.

children.title: With Mucalinda
children.description: Shortly after the Buddha’s awakening, a dragon protects him from a storm.

children.title: Kings
children.description: When monks have gathered, they shouldn’t spend their time gossiping about kings.

children.title: A Stick
children.description: A lesson to young boys: If you don’t want to suffer from pain, don’t inflict pain on other beings.

children.title: Esteem
children.description: On how to deal with abusive language.

children.title: A Lay Follower
children.description: The drawbacks of having.

children.title: The Pregnant Woman
children.description: More drawbacks of having.

children.title: An Only Son
children.description: The sorrow that comes from having those who are dear.

children.title: Suppavāsā
children.description: After a long and difficult pregnancy, Suppavāsā invites the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal.

children.title: With Visākhā
children.description: The drawbacks of having to do business with kings.

children.title: With Bhaddiya
children.description: A former king, now monk, exclaims over the bliss of solitude.

children.title: 3. Nanda
children.description: The discourses in this chapter focus on equanimity in the face of pleasure and pain. There are several examples of monastic conduct of poise and balance.

children.title: Born of the Fruits of Deeds
children.description: A monk meditates in pain engendered by past kamma but without being struck down by it.

children.title: With Nanda
children.description: The Buddha makes a deal with his step-brother: Stay a monk, and you’ll be rewarded with nymphs in the next life.

children.title: With Yasoja
children.description: A group of monks, rebuked by the Buddha, take it as an encouragement to reach awakening.

children.title: With Sāriputta
children.description: Ven. Sāriputta meditates, his mind as solid as rock.

children.title: With Mahāmoggallāna
children.description: Ven. Mahā Moggallāna meditates.

children.title: With Pilindavaccha
children.description: Some old habits die hard.

children.title: Sakka’s Heartfelt Saying
children.description: A deva-king disguises himself to give alms to Ven. Mahā Kassapa.

children.title: One Who Eats Only Almsfood
children.description: The Buddha rebukes monks who are chatting about the agreeable things that one can encounter on almsround.

children.title: Professions
children.description: More lessons in what monks should and shouldn’t talk about.

children.title: The World
children.description: Shortly after awakening, the Buddha contemplates future rebirth.

children.title: 4. Meghiya
children.description: If a practitioner fails to achieve such balance, their undisciplined mind leads to harming themselves and others.

children.title: With Meghiya
children.description: A monk leaves the Buddha to go into solitude, only to find his mind overcome by unskillful thoughts.

children.title: Restless
children.description: The need to protect body and mind.

children.title: The Cowherd
children.description: A cowherd is murdered after presenting a meal to the Buddha and the Sangha.

children.title: The Spirit’s Blow
children.description: A spirit gives Ven. Sāriputta a blow on the head.

children.title: A Bull Elephant
children.description: The Buddha, hemmed in by his followers, goes into seclusion.

children.title: The Alms-Gatherer
children.description: Ven. Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja meditates.

children.title: With Sāriputta
children.description: Ven. Sāriputta meditates.

children.title: With Sundarī
children.description: Wanderers of other sects kill a woman and blame her murder on the Sangha.

children.title: With Upasena
children.description: Ven. Upasena Vaṅgantaputta contemplates: “Fortunate has been my life; fortunate will be my death.”

children.title: The Peacefulness of Sāriputta
children.description: Ven. Sāriputta meditates.

children.title: 5. Soṇa
children.description: Broadening the focus from the individual practitioner, this chapter deals with the “all”, and shows how the Dhamma is inclusive of all beings, from kings to little fish.

children.title: Who is More Dear?
children.description: King Pasenadi asks his queen, “Is there anyone dearer to you than yourself?”

children.title: Short-lived
children.description: Ven. Ānanda comments on how the Buddha’s mother died shortly after his birth.

children.title: With Suppabuddha the Leper
children.description: A leper becomes a stream-enterer, dies, and is reborn as a deva.

children.title: The Boys
children.description: A lesson to young boys: If you don’t want to suffer from pain, don’t inflict pain on other beings.

children.title: Sabbath
children.description: Ven. Mahā Moggallāna expels a sham monk from a meeting of the Sangha.

children.title: With Soṇa
children.description: A young man in a remote part of India is able to ordain only after many delays.

children.title: With Revata the Doubter
children.description: Ven. Revata meditates.

children.title: Schism in the Saṅgha
children.description: Devadatta announces that he will cause a split in the Sangha.

children.title: Teasing
children.description: A group of youths jeer at the monks.

children.title: With Cūḷapanthaka
children.description: Ven. Cūḷa Panthaka meditates.

children.title: 6. Blind From Birth
children.description: Returning to stories about the Buddha’s life, this chapter skips ahead to near the end. Meanwhile, it reminds us of those who have lost their way.

children.title: Surrendering the Life Force
children.description: The Buddha relinquishes the forces that will keep him living.

children.title: Seven Matted-Hair Ascetics
children.description: How to know another person’s character.

children.title: The Buddha’s Reviewing
children.description: The Buddha reflects on the unskillful qualities that he has abandoned.

children.title: Followers of Various Other Religions (1st)
children.description: The blind people and the elephant.

children.title: Followers of Various Other Religions (2nd)
children.description: Wanderers of other sects dispute over the self, pleasure, pain, and the nature of the world.

children.title: Followers of Various Other Religions (3rd)
children.description: Wanderers of other sects dispute over the self, pleasure, pain, and the nature of the world.

children.title: With Subhūti
children.description: Ven. Subhūti meditates.

children.title: The Courtesan
children.description: Two factions fight over a courtesan.

children.title: Hastening By
children.description: Insects fly into the flames of lamps set out at night.

children.title: Arising
children.description: Other sectarians shine only as long as a Buddha hasn’t appeared in the world.

children.title: 7. The Lesser Chapter
children.description: This chapter returns to the awakening of the Buddha, and employing water-based imagery, it reinforces the power of the Dhamma to carry us across the flood.

children.title: Bhaddiya the Dwarf (1st)
children.description: A dwarf becomes an arahant.

children.title: Bhaddiya the Dwarf (2nd)
children.description: Ven. Sāriputta doesn’t realize that his listener has already become an arahant.

children.title: Clinging (1st)
children.description: Attachment to sensual pleasures keeps you from crossing over the flood.

children.title: Clinging (2nd)
children.description: Attachment to sensual pleasures keeps you trapped like a fish.

children.title: Another Discourse with Bhaddiya the Dwarf
children.description: Inner and outer beauty.

children.title: The Ending of Craving
children.description: Ven. Aññata Koṇḍañña meditates.

children.title: The Ending of Proliferation
children.description: The Buddha contemplates his own abandoning of the perceptions and categories of proliferation.

children.title: Kaccāna
children.description: Ven. Mahā Kaccāyana meditates.

children.title: The Well
children.description: Wanderers of other sects try to keep the Buddha from drinking the water in a well.

children.title: King Udena
children.description: Five hundred awakened women die in a fire.

children.title: 8. the Pāṭali Villagers
children.description: The final chapter deals with the Buddha’s final passing away and the crisis of faith that this created. It begins with series of solemn declarations on Nibbana and ends with the spectacular passing of the monk Dabba.

children.title: About Extinguishment (1st)
children.description: The nature of extinguishment.

children.title: About Extinguishment (2nd)
children.description: On seeing extinguishment.

children.title: About Extinguishment (3rd)
children.description: The escape from conditions is areal.

children.title: About Extinguishment (4th)
children.description: Extinguishment as independence.

children.title: With Cunda
children.description: The Buddha’s last meal.

children.title: The Layfolk of Pāṭali Village
children.description: The rewards of virtue and of dedicating merit to the devas.

children.title: A Fork in the Road
children.description: One of the Buddha’s attendants disobeys him.

children.title: With Visākhā
children.description: Lady Visākhā wishes for many grandchildren.

children.title: With Dabba (1st)
children.description: Ven. Dabba Mallaputta performs a miracle on his death.

children.title: Dabba (2nd)
children.description: There’s no destination to describe for those rightly released.

children.title: Greed
children.description: Abandon greed, and you’re guaranteed non-return.

children.title: Hate
children.description: Abandon aversion, and you’re guaranteed non-return.

children.title: Delusion
children.description: Abandon delusion, and you’re guaranteed non-return.

children.title: Anger
children.description: Abandon anger, and you’re guaranteed non-return.

children.title: Disdain
children.description: Abandon contempt, and you’re guaranteed non-return.

children.title: Conceit
children.description: Abandon conceit, and you’re guaranteed non-return.

children.title: Complete Understanding of All
children.description: When the mind, cleansed of passion for the All, abandons it, you are capable of putting an end to suffering.

children.title: Complete Understanding of Conceit
children.description: When the mind, cleansed of passion for conceit, abandons it, you are capable of putting an end to suffering.

children.title: Complete Understanding of Greed
children.description: When the mind, cleansed of passion for greed, abandons it, you are capable of putting an end to suffering.

children.title: Complete Understanding of Hate
children.description: When the mind, cleansed of passion for aversion, abandons it, you are capable of putting an end to suffering.

children.title: Complete Understanding of Delusion
children.description: When the mind, cleansed of passion for delusion, abandons it, you are capable of putting an end to suffering.

children.title: Complete Understanding of Anger
children.description: When the mind, cleansed of passion for anger, abandons it, you are capable of putting an end to suffering.

children.title: Complete Understanding of Disdain
children.description: When the mind, cleansed of passion for contempt, abandons it, you are capable of putting an end to suffering.

children.title: The Hindrance of Ignorance
children.description: Hindered by the hindrance of ignorance, people go wandering and transmigrating on for a long, long time.

children.title: The Fetter of Craving
children.description: Fettered with the fetter of craving, beings go wandering and transmigrating on for a long, long time.

children.title: A Trainee (1st)
children.description: Appropriate attention as the prime internal factor to help those in training.

children.title: A Trainee (2nd)
children.description: Friendship with admirable people as the prime external factor to help those in training.

children.title: Schism in the Saṅgha
children.description: Schism in the Sangha leads to the detriment and unhappiness of many beings, both human and divine.

children.title: Harmony in the Saṅgha
children.description: Concord in the Sangha leads to the welfare and happiness of many beings, both human and divine.

children.title: A Corrupted Mind
children.description: Corrupt-mindedness leads to rebirth in the planes of deprivation.

children.title: A Pure Mind
children.description: Clear-mindedness leads to rebirth in a heavenly world.

children.title: The Benefits of Love
children.description: “Acts of merit” is a synonym for what is blissful, desirable, pleasing, endearing, charming. The Buddha recalls the results he himself has experienced from doing meritorious deeds.

children.title: Both Kinds of Benefit
children.description: Heedfulness with regard to skillful qualities keeps both kinds of benefit secure: benefit in this live and benefit in lives to come.

children.title: A Heap of Bones
children.description: In this course of transmigrating, one person would leave behind a heap of bones as large as a mountain—if there were someone to collect the bones and the collection were not destroyed.

children.title: Lying
children.description: A person who tells a deliberate lie is capable of any evil deed.

children.title: Giving
children.description: If you knew, as the Buddha did, the results of giving and sharing, you wouldn’t eat without having shared.

children.title: The Meditation on Love
children.description: Goodwill far outshines all other ways of making merit.

children.title: Living in Suffering
children.description: Not guarding the doors of the sense faculties and knowing no moderation in food leads to suffering in this life and the next.

children.title: Living in Happiness
children.description: Guarding the doors of the sense faculties and knowing moderation in food leads to ease in this life and the next.

children.title: Mortifying
children.description: Two things that cause remorse.

children.title: Not Mortifying
children.description: Two things that cause lack of remorse.

children.title: Ethics (1st)
children.description: A person of evil habits and evil views goes to hell.

children.title: Ethics (2nd)
children.description: A person of auspicious habits and auspicious views goes to heaven.

children.title: Keen
children.description: To lack ardency and compunction makes you incapable of unbinding.

children.title: Deceit and Flattery (1st)
children.description: The holy life is lived for the purpose of restraint and abandoning.

children.title: Deceit and Flattery (2nd)
children.description: The holy life is lived for the purpose of direct knowledge and full comprehension.

children.title: Happiness
children.description: A sense of urgency and appropriate exertion bring ease here-and-now, and lead to the ending of the defilements.

children.title: Thoughts
children.description: Two thoughts that often occur to the Buddha as he delights in non-ill will and seclusion.

children.title: Teaching
children.description: Two Dhamma sequences: see evil as evil, and become released from it.

children.title: Knowledge
children.description: Ignorance leads to lack of conscience and prudence.

children.title: Bereft of Wisdom
children.description: The rewards of noble discernment.

children.title: Bright Things
children.description: Conscience and prudence safeguard the world.

children.title: Unborn
children.description: The existence of an unfabricated dimension allows for the escape from conditions.

children.title: Facets of Quenching
children.description: Two unbinding properties: with fuel remaining and with no fuel remaining.

children.title: Retreat
children.description: Live enjoying aloofness, delighting in aloofness, inwardly committed to awareness-tranquility, not neglecting jhāna, endowed with clear-seeing insight, and frequenting empty buildings.

children.title: The Benefits of Training
children.description: Live with the trainings as your reward, with discernment uppermost, with release the essence, and with mindfulness the governing principle.

children.title: Wake Up
children.description: Be wakeful, mindful, alert, centered, sensitive, clear, and calm. And there you should, at the appropriate times, see clearly into skillful mental qualities.

children.title: Bound for Loss
children.description: Two types of behavior that lead to hell.

children.title: Misconceptions
children.description: How those with vision differ from those who adhere to craving for rebirth and those who slip past into craving to be annihilated.

children.title: Roots
children.description: Three roots of what is unskillful.

children.title: Elements
children.description: Three properties: form, formlessness, cessation.

children.title: Feelings (1st)
children.description: Three feelings.

children.title: Feelings (2nd)
children.description: How the three types of feeling should be viewed.

children.title: Searches (1st)
children.description: Three searches: for sensuality, for rebirth, for a holy life.

children.title: Searches (2nd)
children.description: Three searches: for sensuality, for rebirth, for a holy life.

children.title: Defilements (1st)
children.description: Three defilements.

children.title: Defilements (2nd)
children.description: Three defilements.

children.title: Craving
children.description: Three cravings.

children.title: Māra’s Sway
children.description: Three qualities that lead beyond Māra’s domain.

children.title: Grounds for Making Merit
children.description: Three grounds for meritorious activity.

children.title: The Eye
children.description: Three eyes: the eye of flesh, the divine eye, and the eye of discernment.

children.title: Faculties
children.description: The noble attainments described in terms of three faculties.

children.title: Periods
children.description: Three time periods and the importance of comprehending signs.

children.title: Bad Conduct
children.description: Three kinds of misconduct.

children.title: Good Conduct
children.description: Three kinds of good conduct.

children.title: Purity
children.description: Three kinds of cleanliness: bodily, verbal, and mental.

children.title: Sagacity
children.description: Three forms of sagacity: bodily, verbal, and mental.

children.title: Greed (1st)
children.description: One whose passion, aversion, and delusion are abandoned is freed from Māra’s power.

children.title: Greed (2nd)
children.description: To abandon passion, aversion, and delusion is like crossing over the dangers of the ocean.

children.title: Having Wrong View
children.description: The Buddha reports having seen, for himself, beings reborn in planes of deprivation in line with their wrong views and evil actions.

children.title: Having Right View
children.description: The Buddha reports having seen, for himself, beings reborn in good destinations in line with their right views and good actions.

children.title: Elements of Escape
children.description: Three properties for escape: from sensuality, from form, and from whatever is fabricated and dependently co-arisen.

children.title: More Peaceful
children.description: Formless phenomena are more peaceful than forms; cessation, more peaceful than formless phenomena.

children.title: A Child
children.description: Three types of sons and daughters (when compared to their parents): of heightened birth, of similar birth, and of lowered birth.

children.title: A Rainless Cloud
children.description: Three types of people: one like a cloud without rain, one who rains locally, and one who rains everywhere.

children.title: Wishing for Happiness
children.description: Aspiring to three forms of bliss, wise people should guard their virtue.

children.title: Fragile
children.description: This body falls apart; consciousness is subject to fading; all acquisitions are inconstant, sufferingful, subject to change.

children.title: Converging Elements
children.description: Like attracts like. It’s in accordance with their properties—either low or admirable—that beings come together and associate with one another.

children.title: Decline
children.description: Three things lead to the falling away of a monk in training.

children.title: Thoughts
children.description: Three kinds of unskillful thinking.

children.title: Esteem
children.description: The dangers of letting your mind be overcome by the fact that you either receive offerings or don’t receive offerings.

children.title: The Cry of the Gods
children.description: Three occasions on which devas give voice to joy over the behavior of human beings.

children.title: Five Warning Signs
children.description: Five omens that appear when a deva is about to pass away, and the encouragement that other devas give at that time.

children.title: For the Welfare of the People
children.description: Three people who appear for the benefit of the world.

children.title: Observing Ugliness
children.description: The rewards of focusing on the foulness of the body, of establishing mindfulness of breathing to the fore, and of focusing on the inconstancy of all conditions.

children.title: Practicing In Line With the Teaching
children.description: Practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma.

children.title: Destroyers of Sight
children.description: Three kinds of unskillful thinking; three kinds of skillful thinking.

children.title: Inner Stains
children.description: Three inside stains.

children.title: About Devadatta
children.description: Conquered by three forms of false Dhamma, Devadatta was incurably doomed to deprivation.

children.title: The Best Kinds of Confidence
children.description: Three supreme objects of confidence: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.

children.title: Lifestyle
children.description: Why reasonable people take up the life of alms-going, and the dangers that lie in wait if they do not train their minds.

children.title: The Corner of the Cloak
children.description: To see the Dhamma is to see the Buddha and to be close to him, even when physically far away.

children.title: Fire
children.description: The three fires: of passion, aversion, and delusion.

children.title: Examination
children.description: On having consciousness neither externally scattered and diffused, nor internally positioned.

children.title: Provided With Pleasure
children.description: Three ways in which devas obtain sensual pleasures.

children.title: Attached to Sensual Pleasures
children.description: The yoke of sensuality and the yoke of rebirth.

children.title: Good Morals
children.description: Admirable virtue, admirable qualities, and admirable discernment defined.

children.title: Giving
children.description: Two kinds of gifts, sharing, and assistance: in material things and in Dhamma.

children.title: The Three Knowledges
children.description: The three knowledges that characterize a brahman in the Buddha’s sense of the word.

children.title: The Holy Offering of the Teaching
children.description: The Buddha as doctor; the monks as his heirs in Dhamma, not in material things.

children.title: Easy to Find
children.description: The four basic requisites are easy to gain and blameless. To be content with them is a factor of the contemplative life.

children.title: The Ending of Defilements
children.description: For one knowing and seeing the four noble truths, there is the ending of suffering.

children.title: Ascetics and Brahmins
children.description: To see the four noble truths is to count as a true contemplative.

children.title: Accomplished in Ethics
children.description: The rewards of associating with those who genuinely count as admirable friends.

children.title: The Arising of Craving
children.description: Where a monk’s craving takes birth.

children.title: With Brahmā
children.description: Mother and father as the Brahmās and first teachers of their children.

children.title: Very Helpful
children.description: The reciprocal ways in which monks and lay supporters benefit one another.

children.title: Deceivers
children.description: Monks who are and who are not the Buddha’s true followers.

children.title: A River
children.description: An extended metaphor for the dangers of “going with the flow.”

children.title: Walking
children.description: What it means to have ardency and compunction.

children.title: Accomplishment in Ethics
children.description: When one is consummate in virtue, what more is to be done?

children.title: The World
children.description: The qualities that entitle the Buddha to be called Tathāgata.

children.title: The Three Refuges
children.description: The three refuges formula

children.title: The Ten Precepts
children.description: The ten precepts of a novice mendicant

children.title: The Thirty-two Parts of the Body
children.description: The thirty-two parts of the body for reflection

children.title: The Boy’s Questions
children.description: A list of ten doctrinal factors

children.title: True Blessings
children.description: A list of the types of skillful behavior that give blessings and protection.

children.title: Gems
children.description: The many treasures to be found in the Triple Gem.

children.title: Without the Walls
children.description: The Supreme Buddha explains how to share merit with past relatives.

children.title: Storing Your Savings
children.description: Merit is the only sure investment

children.title: The Teaching on Love
children.description: The practice of developing universal goodwill: the practices that form a foundation for the practice, the attitude of universal goodwill itself, and the steps that lead from goodwill to awakening.

The Conduct of a Mother’s Provider
The Conduct of the Dragon of Campeyya
The Conduct of the Buffalo King
The Conduct of the Deer-king Ruru

The Conduct of the Scholar Soṇa

Guaranteed
children.description: This discourse regarding Truth was delivered by the Blessed One, while he was dwelling in the Great Monastery at Jetavana near Savatthi. But who, you ask, was it that led up to this tale?

children.title: The Sandy Track
children.description: “Untiring, deep they dug.”—This discourse was delivered by the Blessed One whilst he was dwelling at Savatthi.

children.title: The Merchant Seriva
children.description: “If in this faith.” This lesson too was taught by the Blessed One while at Savatthi, also about a Brother who gave up persevering.

children.title: The Shorter Tale of the Financier
children.description: “With humblest start.” This story was told by the Master about the Elder named Little Wayman, while in Jivaka’s Mango-grove near Rajagaha.

children.title: A Little Rice
children.description: “Dost ask how much a peck of rice is worth?”—This was told by the Master, whilst at Jetavana, about the Elder Udayi, called the Dullard.

children.title: Godlike
children.description: “Those only ‘godlike’ call.”—This story was told by the Blessed One while at Jetavana, about a wealthy Brother.

children.title: The King and the Stick-Collector
children.description: “Your son am I.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about the story of Vasabha-Khattiya, which will be found in the Twelfth Book in the Bhaddasala-jataka.

children.title: Prince Gāmaṇi
children.description: “Their heart’s desire.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about a Brother who gave up persevering. In this Jataka both the Introductory Story and the Story of the Past will be given in the Eleventh Book in connexion with the Samvara-jataka; the incidents are the same both for that Jataka and for this, but the stanzas are different.

children.title: King Makhadeva
children.description: “Lo! these grey hairs.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about the Great Renunciation, which has already been related in the Nidana-Katha.

children.title: One Who Lives Happily
children.description: “The man who guards not.”—This story was told by the Master while in the Anupiya Mango-grove near the town of Anupiya, about the Elder Bhaddiya (the Happy), who joined the Brotherhood in the company of the six young nobles with whom was Upali. Of these the Elders Bhaddiya, Kimbila, Bhagu, and Upali attained to Arahatship; the Elder Ananda entered the First Path; the Elder Anuruddha gained all-seeing vision; and Devadatta obtained the power of ecstatic self-abstraction. The story of the six young nobles, up to the events at Anupiya, will be related in the Khandahala-jataka.

children.title: The Lucky Deer
children.description: “The upright man.”—This story was told by the Master in the Bamboo-grove near Rajagaha about Devadatta. The story of Devadatta will be related, up to the date of the Abhimara-employment, in the Khandahala-jataka; up to the date of his dismissal from the office of Treasurer, in the Cullahamsa-jataka; and, up to the date of his being swallowed up by the earth, in the Sixteenth Book in the Samudda-vanija-jataka.

children.title: The Banyan Deer
children.description: “Keep only with the Banyan Deer.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about the mother of the Elder named Prince Kassapa. The daughter, we learn, of a wealthy merchant of Rajagaha was deeply rooted in goodness and scorned all temporal things; she had reached her final existence, and within her breast, like a lamp in a pitcher, glowed her sure hope of winning Arahatship. As soon as she reached knowledge of herself, she took no joy in a worldly life but yearned to renounce the world. With this aim, she said to her mother and father, “My dear parents, my heart takes no joy in a worldly life; fain would I embrace the saving doctrine of the Buddha. Suffer me to take the vows.”

children.title: The Dart
children.description: “Cursed be the dart of love.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about the temptation caused to Brethren by the wives of their mundane life. This will be related in the Indriya-jataka in the Eighth Book. Said the Blessed One to the Brother, “Brother, it was because of this very woman that in bygone days you met your death and were roasted over glowing embers.” The Brethren asked the Blessed One to explain this. The Blessed One made clear what had been concealed from them by re-birth.

children.title: The Wind-antelope
children.description: “There’s nothing worse.” This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana, about the Elder Tissa, called Direct-alms the Less. Tradition says that, while the Master was dwelling at the Bamboo-grove near Rajagaha, the scion of a wealthy house, Prince Tissa by name, coming one day to the Bamboo-grove and there hearing a discourse from the Master, wished to join the Brotherhood, but, being refused because his parents would not give their consent, obtained their consent by following Rattha-pala’s example and refusing food for seven days, and finally took the vows with the Master.

children.title: With Kharādiya
children.description: “For when a deer.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about an unruly Brother. Tradition says that this Brother was unruly and would not heed admonition. Accordingly, the Master asked him, saying, “Is it true, as they say, that you are unruly and will not heed admonition?”

children.title: The Deer With Three Ruses
children.description: “In all three postures.”—This story was told by the Master while dwelling do the Badarika Monastery in Kosambi, about the Elder Rahula whose heart was set on observing the rules of the Brotherhood.

children.title: The Breeze
children.description: “In light or dark.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about two Brethren who had joined the Brotherhood in their old age. Tradition says that they were living in a forest-dwelling in the Kosala country, and that one was named the Elder Dark and the other the Elder Light. Now one day Light said to Dark, “Sir, at what time does what is called cold appear?” “It appears in the dark half of the month.” And one day Dark said to Light, “Sir, at what time does what is called cold appear?” “It appears in the light half of the month.”

children.title: Feasts for the Dead
children.description: “If folk but knew.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about Feasts for the Dead. For at this time the folk were putting to death goats, sheep, and other animals, and offering them up as what is called a Feast for the Dead, for the sake of their departed kinsmen. Finding them thus engaged, the Brethren asked the Master, saying, “Just now, sir, the folk are taking the lives of many living creatures and offering them up as what is called a Feast for the Dead. Can it be, sir, that there is any good in this?”

children.title: Sacrifice to Fulfill a Wish
children.description: “Take thought of life hereafter.” This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about the offering of a sacrifice under vow to gods. Tradition says that in those days folk when going a journey on business, used to slay living creatures and offer them as a sacrifice to gods, and set out on their way, after making this vow,—“If we come safely back with a profit, we will give you another sacrifice.” And when they did come safely back with a profit, the Idea that this was all due to gods made them slay a number of living creatures and offer them up as a sacrifice to obtain a release from their vow.

children.title: Drinking With Straws
children.description: “I found the footprints.” This story was told by the Master whilst journeying on an alms-pilgrimage through Kosala, when he had come to the village of Nalaka-pana (Cane-drink) and was dwelling at Ketaka-vana near the Pool of Nalaka-pana, about cane-sticks. In those days the Brethren, after bathing in the Pool of Nalaka-pana, made the novices get them cane-sticks for needle-cases, but, finding them hollow throughout, went to the Master and said, “Sir, we had cane-sticks got in order to provide needle-cases; and from top to bottom they are quite hollow. Now how can that be?”

children.title: The Antelope
children.description: “The antelope knows well.”—This story was told by the Master while at the Bamboo-grove about Devadatta. For once when the Brethren were gathered together in the Hall of Truth, they sat talking reproachfully of Devadatta, saying, “Sirs, with a view to destroy the Buddha Devadatta hired bowmen, hurled down a rock, and let loose the elephant Dhana-palaka; in every way he goes about to slay the Lord of Wisdom.” Entering and seating himself on the seat prepared for him, the Master asked, saying, “Sirs, what is the theme you are discussing here in conclave?” “Sir,” was the reply, “we were discussing the wickedness of Devadatta, saying that he was always going about to slay you.” Said the Master, “It is not only in these present days, Brethren, that Devadatta goes about seeking to slay me; he went about with the like intent in bygone days also,—but was unable to slay me.” And so saying, he told this story of the past.

children.title: The Dog
children.description: “The dogs that in the royal palace grow.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana, about acting for the good of kinsfolk, as will be related in the Twelfth Book in the Bhaddasala-jataka. It was to drive home that lesson that he told this story of the past.

children.title: The Destrier
children.description: “Though prostrate now.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about a Brother who gave up persevering. For it was then that the Master addressed that Brother and said, “Brethren, in bygone days the wise and good persevered even amid hostile surroundings, and, even when they were wounded, still did not give in.” And, so saying, he told this story of the past.

children.title: The Thoroughbred
children.description: “No matter when or where.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about another Brother who gave up persevering. But, in this case, he addressed that Brother and said, “Brethren, in bygone days the wise and good still persevered even when wounded.” And, so saying, he told this story of the past.

children.title: The Bathing-place
children.description: “Change thou the spot.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana, about an ex-goldsmith, who had become a Brother and was co-resident with the Captain of the Faith (Sariputta).

children.title: Damsel-face the Brigand
children.description: “Through hearing first.”—This story was told by the Master while at the Bamboo-grove, about Devadatta, who, having secured the adherence of Prince Ajata-sattu, had attained both gain and honour. Prince Ajata-sattu had a Monastery built for Devadatta at Gaya-sisa, and every day brought to him five hundred kettles of perfumed three-year-old rice flavoured with all the choicest flavourings. All this gain and honour brought Devadatta a great following, with whom Devadatta lived on, without ever stirring out of his Monastery.

children.title: Familiarity
children.description: “No morsel can he eat.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana, about a lay-disciple and an aged Elder.

children.title: The Bull Named Ample Joy
children.description: “Speak only words of kindness.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana, about the bitter words spoken by the Six. For, in those days the six, when they disagreed with respectable Brethren, used to taunt, revile and jeer them, and load them with the ten kinds of abuse. This the Brethren reported to the Blessed One, who sent for the Six and asked whether this charge was true. On their admitting its truth, he rebuked them, saying, “Brethren, hard words gall even animals: in bygone days an animal made a man who had used harsh language to him lose a thousand pieces.” And, so saying, he told this story of the past.

children.title: The Bull Named Black
children.description: “With heavy loads.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana, about the Double Miracle, which, together with the Descent from Heaven, will be related in the Thirteenth Book, in the Sarabhamiga-jataka.

children.title: The Pig Named Munika
children.description: “Then envy not poor Munika.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana about being seduced by a plump young woman, as will be related in the Thirteenth Book in the Culla-Narada-Kassapa-jataka.

children.title: The Nestling Birds
children.description: “Let all the forest’s nestlings.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana, about a brother who drank water without straining it.

children.title: Dancing
children.description: “A pleasing note.” This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana, about a Brother with many belongings. The incident is just the same as in the Devadhamma-jataka supra.

children.title: Mutual Appreciation
children.description: “While concord reigns.” This story was told by the Master while dwelling in the Banyan-grove near Kapilavatthu, about a squabble over a porter’s head-pad, as will be related in the Kunala-jataka.

children.title: The Fish
children.description: “’Tis not the cold.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana, about being seduced by the wife of one’s mundane life before joining the Brotherhood. Said the Master on this occasion, “Is it true, as I hear, Brother, that you are passion-tost?”

children.title: The Quail
children.description: “With, wings that fly not.”—This story was told by the Master, whilst on an alms-pilgrimage through Magadha, about the going-out of a jungle fire.

children.title: The Bird
children.description: “Ye denizens of air.”—This story was told by the Master while at Jetavana, about a Brother whose cell was burnt down.

children.title: The Partridge, the Monkey, and the Elephant
